guide.whatIs: The AI SDK is Vercel's provider-agnostic TypeScript toolkit for building LLM applications and agents. One API (generateText, streamText, structured output via zod schemas, tool calls) works across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and other providers: either through the Vercel AI Gateway with plain model strings like 'anthropic/claude-opus-4.6', or through per-provider packages such as @ai-sdk/openai. Companion UI packages add useChat-style hooks for React, Svelte, Vue, and Angular, and the ToolLoopAgent class runs multi-step tool loops server side with a typed message protocol down to the browser.
useIf: You want to swap model providers without rewriting call sites: the model is a string or provider function and the surrounding code stays identical
You are building chat UI in Next.js, React, Svelte, or Vue and want streaming, message state, and tool rendering handled by useChat instead of hand-rolled SSE
You need typed structured output: zod schema in, validated object out
You are building tool-using agents and want the tool loop, streaming, and UI message protocol as one coherent stack
skipIf: You call exactly one provider with plain prompts: the official openai or @anthropic-ai/sdk client is a smaller, more direct dependency
You need provider-specific beta features the day they ship: the unified abstraction usually trails the raw provider APIs
Your team dislikes fast-moving majors: the SDK is on major version 7 with about 1,750 open issues and PRs, and every major brings a migration guide you actually have to read
You work outside TypeScript/JavaScript: this stack is TS-only, so Python teams should use provider SDKs or another toolkit
guide.setupReality: npm install ai requires Node 22+. The quick path routes calls through the Vercel AI Gateway using bare model strings, which needs a gateway credential; direct provider access means installing @ai-sdk/openai, @ai-sdk/anthropic, and so on separately, each reading its own API key env var. UI hooks live in yet another package per framework (@ai-sdk/react and friends). The recurring cost is churn: majors arrive fast, and message formats, tool definitions, and helper names have all been renamed across versions, so pin your version and budget upgrade time.

alternatives.name: openai
alternatives.when: You only call OpenAI models and want the official client with newest features first

alternatives.name: @anthropic-ai/sdk
alternatives.when: Anthropic-only apps that want the raw Messages API without an abstraction layer

alternatives.name: langchain
alternatives.when: You care more about chains, retrievers, and a large integration catalog than typed UI streaming

guide.verdict: The default for TypeScript LLM apps, especially anything with streaming chat UI in Next.js. You pay for its pace: pin versions and read the migration notes on every major.

apiStability.why: Seven majors in roughly three years; the generateText/streamText core endures but message types, tool definitions, and the UI protocol have all moved between majors

docsQuality.why: ai-sdk.dev has thorough guides, a full API reference, and starter templates; the version churn means older blog posts and examples on the web go stale fast

maintenance.why: Vercel-staffed with pushes landing daily and a rapid patch cadence (7.0.52 current); the roughly 1,750 open issues and PRs track heavy usage, not neglect

ecosystem.why: 20M weekly downloads, first-party provider packages for every major model vendor plus community providers and framework hooks; younger and thinner than the raw provider SDK ecosystems

patterns.title: Generate text with a gateway model string
patterns.note: Gateway model strings need no provider package installed, but they do need an AI Gateway credential in the environment.

patterns.title: Stream a completion to stdout
patterns.note: streamText starts immediately and does not reject on model errors; errors arrive as part of the stream, so try/catch alone will not catch them.

patterns.title: Get validated structured output with zod
patterns.note: Read the result from output, not text; schema validation failures throw, so wrap strict schemas in try/catch.

patterns.title: Define a typed tool
patterns.note: The schema field is inputSchema; older examples on the web still show parameters, which no longer type-checks.

patterns.title: Run a multi-step agent with ToolLoopAgent
patterns.note: The agent keeps calling tools until the model stops requesting them; guard expensive tools with your own limits.

patterns.title: Serve an agent from a Next.js route
patterns.note: useChat posts to /api/chat by default; if you change the route path, configure the hook to match.

patterns.title: Build a chat UI with useChat
patterns.note: Messages are arrays of typed parts, not plain strings; render by switching on part.type or tool parts silently disappear.

patterns.title: Render a tool call in the UI by state
patterns.note: Tool parts move through states (input-available, then output-available); render every state or users see nothing while a tool runs.

patterns.title: Call a provider package directly
patterns.note: Provider packages are separate installs and read their own env vars (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY here); the gateway is bypassed entirely.

patterns.title: Use a system prompt with a message history
patterns.note: Pass prompt or messages, never both; the call rejects if the two are combined.

guide.whatIs: aiohttp is the async HTTP workhorse for Python's asyncio: one package that is both an HTTP client (ClientSession, with connection pooling, streaming, and timeouts) and a web server framework (aiohttp.web, with middleware and pluggable routing), plus WebSocket support on both sides. It sits lower level than requests or FastAPI: you write async with blocks and manage session lifetimes yourself, and in exchange you get fine control and high throughput on concurrency-heavy workloads like crawlers, aggregators, and long-lived socket services.
useIf: You need thousands of concurrent HTTP requests from one process (crawler, API aggregator, proxy) where blocking clients would need a thread per call
You need WebSocket client or server support inside asyncio without adding a second dependency
You want client and server in one library, for example a service that both serves HTTP and calls upstream APIs on the same event loop
You want control over pooling, per-request timeouts, and DNS behavior (the README recommends aiodns for speed)
skipIf: Your codebase is synchronous: requests or sync httpx is far simpler, and rebuilding around asyncio for a few HTTP calls is not worth it
You want requests-style ergonomics with async as an option: httpx has a near-identical API in both modes plus HTTP/2
You are picking a framework for a typical JSON API: FastAPI gives you validation and OpenAPI docs; aiohttp's server layer is deliberately minimal
You need HTTP/2 or HTTP/3: the aiohttp client and server speak HTTP/1.1 only
guide.setupReality: pip install aiohttp is quick, and wheels ship for CPython 3.10+ so you rarely compile anything, though unusual platforms may build the C extensions of aiohttp and its multidict/yarl/frozenlist dependencies from source. The real cost is discipline, not installation: everything lives inside async with blocks, a ClientSession must be created once inside a running loop and reused (per-request sessions defeat pooling and leak sockets), and a session you forget to close greets you with the Unclosed client session warning at shutdown.

alternatives.name: httpx
alternatives.when: A requests-like API with both sync and async modes, plus HTTP/2 support

alternatives.name: requests
alternatives.when: Synchronous scripts and tools where async buys you nothing

alternatives.name: fastapi
alternatives.when: Building an API server with validation and OpenAPI docs rather than a low-level client/server toolkit

guide.verdict: The proven pick when raw async HTTP throughput or WebSockets matter, client side or server side. For everyday API servers use FastAPI, and for simple scripts use requests or httpx; aiohttp rewards the workloads that actually need it.

apiStability.why: The 3.x line has been the stable branch for years (3.14.3 current); ClientSession and web.Application APIs barely move and deprecations phase in over multiple releases

docsQuality.why: docs.aiohttp.org is thorough with a maintained changelog and a dedicated page on why the client needs more lines than requests; the asyncio prerequisites still make the on-ramp steeper than the docs admit

maintenance.why: The aio-libs team pushed within the last day, holds 218 open issues and PRs on a 16.5k-star project, ships steady patch releases, and displays an LFX health score in the README

ecosystem.why: 160M weekly downloads and a curated third-party list (sessions, CORS, clients built on top); the middleware and plugin scene is smaller than Flask's or Django's

patterns.title: Fetch a page with ClientSession
patterns.snippet:
import aiohttp
import asyncio

async def main():
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get('https://python.org') as response:
            print('Status:', response.status)
            html = await response.text()

asyncio.run(main())
patterns.note: Both context managers matter: the session owns the connection pool and the response releases its connection back to it.

patterns.title: POST JSON and read a JSON response
patterns.snippet:
async with session.post(url, json={'name': 'demo'}) as resp:
    resp.raise_for_status()
    data = await resp.json()
patterns.note: resp.json() raises ContentTypeError when the server sends a non-JSON content type; pass content_type=None to skip that check.

patterns.title: Create one session for the whole app
patterns.note: One ClientSession per application, created inside a running event loop; per-request sessions are the top aiohttp performance mistake.

patterns.title: Set client timeouts
patterns.snippet:
timeout = aiohttp.ClientTimeout(total=30, connect=5)
async with aiohttp.ClientSession(timeout=timeout) as session:
    async with session.get(url) as resp:
        body = await resp.text()
patterns.note: The default total timeout is 5 minutes; set your own or a slow upstream quietly stalls your workers.

patterns.title: Fetch many URLs concurrently
patterns.snippet:
async def fetch(session, url):
    async with session.get(url) as resp:
        return await resp.text()

async def main(urls):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        pages = await asyncio.gather(
            *(fetch(session, u) for u in urls)
        )
patterns.note: Bound concurrency with an asyncio.Semaphore for large URL lists, or you exhaust sockets and trip rate limits.

patterns.title: Stream a large download to disk
patterns.snippet:
async with session.get(url) as resp:
    with open('big.bin', 'wb') as f:
        async for chunk in resp.content.iter_chunked(1 << 16):
            f.write(chunk)
patterns.note: await resp.read() buffers the entire body in memory; iter_chunked is the way to handle files bigger than RAM.

patterns.title: Connect to a WebSocket as a client
patterns.snippet:
async with session.ws_connect('wss://example.com/ws') as ws:
    await ws.send_str('hello')
    async for msg in ws:
        if msg.type == aiohttp.WSMsgType.TEXT:
            print(msg.data)
        elif msg.type == aiohttp.WSMsgType.ERROR:
            break
patterns.note: Receiving means iterating the socket; the loop ends when the connection closes, so branch on msg.type for ERROR and CLOSE.

patterns.title: Serve HTTP with aiohttp.web
patterns.snippet:
from aiohttp import web

async def handle(request):
    name = request.match_info.get('name', 'Anonymous')
    return web.Response(text=f'Hello, {name}')

app = web.Application()
app.add_routes([
    web.get('/', handle),
    web.get('/{name}', handle),
])

if __name__ == '__main__':
    web.run_app(app)
patterns.note: web.run_app blocks and manages the event loop itself; to embed the server in an existing loop use AppRunner instead.

patterns.title: Handle WebSockets on the server
patterns.snippet:
from aiohttp import web

async def wshandle(request):
    ws = web.WebSocketResponse()
    await ws.prepare(request)

    async for msg in ws:
        if msg.type == web.WSMsgType.text:
            await ws.send_str(f'Hello, {msg.data}')
        elif msg.type == web.WSMsgType.close:
            break

    return ws
patterns.note: Call prepare(request) before any send, and return the WebSocketResponse from the handler when the loop exits.

patterns.title: Add error-handling middleware
patterns.note: Re-raise HTTPException subclasses: aiohttp uses them as control flow (redirects, 404s), not as errors.

guide.whatIs: @angular/core is the runtime of the Angular framework: components, dependency injection, signals for reactive state, lifecycle hooks, and change detection. Angular is a full platform rather than a view library; the official package family covers routing, forms, HTTP, SSR, and animations, and the CLI generates, builds, tests, and migrates projects. Modern Angular is standalone-component and signals based, with template control flow (@if, @for) built into the compiler, and v22 continues that line. You almost never install this package alone; it arrives as part of a CLI-generated workspace.
useIf: You are building a large, long-lived app where one official answer for routing, forms, HTTP, DI, and testing beats assembling a stack from npm
Your team wants strong conventions and TypeScript-first tooling: the CLI scaffolds, builds, and upgrades projects (ng update) with automated migrations
You need structured dependency injection for testability across hundreds of services and components
You maintain enterprise apps where a predictable release schedule and long deprecation windows matter more than novelty
skipIf: You are building a content site or a small widget: the core runtime is about 135 KB gzipped before your own code, and React, Vue, or Svelte get you shipping with less framework to learn
Your team is new to Angular and the deadline is close: DI, RxJS, signals, and the CLI workspace layout are a genuine learning curve compared to Vue or Svelte
You want maximum third-party choice: the component and library scene is noticeably thinner than React's
You dislike scheduled churn: majors land twice a year, and staying supported means running ng update migrations on that clock
guide.setupReality: You do not npm install @angular/core by hand; you install the CLI globally (npm install -g @angular/cli) and run ng new, which generates the workspace and pins the whole @angular/* constellation plus peer dependencies (rxjs, zone.js, @angular/compiler) at matching versions. Version alignment is the recurring pain: every @angular/* package must move together, so upgrades go through ng update rather than editing package.json. New projects are standalone-component based; older codebases carry NgModules until someone runs the migration.

alternatives.name: react
alternatives.when: You want the biggest ecosystem and hiring pool and prefer picking your own router, state, and form libraries

alternatives.name: vue
alternatives.when: You want a batteries-included framework with a gentler learning curve and single-file components

alternatives.name: svelte
alternatives.when: Small bundles and compile-time reactivity matter more than enterprise structure

guide.verdict: Still the strongest option for large enterprise TypeScript apps that value one official way to do everything. For small or fast-moving projects the framework weight and twice-yearly major cadence cost more than they return.

apiStability.why: Majors ship on a published schedule with long deprecation windows and automated ng update migrations; the NgModule-to-standalone and signals transitions still mean older code needs periodic modernization work

docsQuality.why: angular.dev has interactive tutorials, an in-browser playground, a complete API reference, and a per-version-pair update guide

maintenance.why: Google-backed with pushes landing daily, 100k+ stars, about 1,150 open issues and PRs on a very large monorepo, and scheduled releases (22.1.0 current)

ecosystem.why: Official packages plus Angular Material cover most needs; third-party breadth trails React's, and community libraries often lag a major or two behind

patterns.title: Define a standalone component
patterns.note: Components are standalone by default in modern Angular; you no longer write standalone: true or declare them in an NgModule.

patterns.title: Reactive state with signal and computed
patterns.note: Signals are functions: read with count(), not count; forgetting the parentheses binds the function object instead of the value.

patterns.title: Declare a typed signal input
patterns.note: input() replaces the @Input() decorator; input.required has no default, and reading it before the parent binds it throws.

patterns.title: Emit events to a parent with output
patterns.note: output() replaces @Output() with EventEmitter; parents still listen with (saved)="handler($event)" in the template.

patterns.title: Template control flow with @if and @for
patterns.note: track is mandatory in @for; the compiler rejects the block without it, unlike the optional trackBy of the old *ngFor.

patterns.title: Get dependencies with inject()
patterns.note: inject() only works in an injection context (field initializers, constructors, provider factories); calling it inside a method throws NG0203.

patterns.title: Make HTTP calls with HttpClient
patterns.note: HttpClient observables are cold: nothing fires until something subscribes (the async pipe or toSignal counts).

patterns.title: Lazy-load a route with loadComponent
patterns.note: loadComponent lazy-loads a standalone component with no NgModule involved; the bundle split happens automatically at build.

patterns.title: Bootstrap a standalone application
patterns.note: bootstrapApplication replaces platformBrowserDynamic().bootstrapModule; app-wide providers all move into this providers array.

patterns.title: Run side effects when signals change
patterns.note: effect() must be created in an injection context such as a constructor, and re-runs whenever any signal it read changes.

guide.whatIs: The official Python SDK for Anthropic's Claude API. It wraps the Messages API with typed request and response models built on httpx and pydantic, ships both sync and async clients, and includes streaming helpers, tool-use support, and token counting. Optional extras add AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex, an aiohttp transport, MCP types, and webhook verification. It is an API client, not an agent framework: prompts, memory, and orchestration loops stay in your code.
useIf: You call Claude models from Python and want the official typed client instead of hand-rolled httpx requests
You need the same call shapes against the Claude API, AWS Bedrock, or Google Vertex; the SDK ships dedicated client classes and extras for each
You want async support and SSE streaming handled for you, including a context-manager streaming helper that cleans up connections
skipIf: You want provider-agnostic code; a router layer like litellm swaps models without touching call sites, this SDK is Claude-only by design
You are allergic to 0.x churn: the package sits at 0.120.2 with frequent releases, so pin the version and read changelogs, minor bumps can move helper APIs
You expect agent loops, memory, or tool execution out of the box; this is a thin API client and all of that is your code (or a separate agent framework)
guide.setupReality: pip install anthropic plus an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY env var and you are making requests in five lines; the client reads the key by default. The rough edges: max_tokens is a required argument on every messages.create call, the version is still 0.x so unpinned installs can pick up breaking minors, Bedrock and Vertex each need their own extra (anthropic[bedrock], anthropic[vertex]) plus separate cloud auth, and configuration follows httpx idioms (httpx.Timeout objects, proxies on the transport) rather than the requests-style knobs many Python devs reach for first.

alternatives.name: openai
alternatives.when: The equivalent official client if you are on OpenAI models

alternatives.name: litellm
alternatives.when: One interface over many providers, Claude included, when you expect to swap models

alternatives.name: langchain-anthropic
alternatives.when: You are already inside LangChain and want Claude as a chat model there

guide.verdict: If you call Claude from Python, use this; there is no serious case for hand-rolling the HTTP layer. Treat the 0.x version number as real advice: pin it and read release notes before upgrading.

apiStability.why: Still pre-1.0 at 0.120.2 with frequent releases; the core messages.create surface has been steady for a long time, but helper APIs and typed models move between minor versions.

docsQuality.why: The repo README is a short stub that points to platform.claude.com, where the Python SDK docs are thorough with runnable snippets; you live in the platform docs, not the repo.

maintenance.why: Official Anthropic project with pushes the day before this review (2026-08-04) and releases that track new API features closely.

ecosystem.why: 47M weekly downloads, first-class extras for Bedrock, Vertex, aiohttp, MCP, and webhooks, and support in LangChain and litellm; the third-party tooling ring is still smaller than the OpenAI client's.

patterns.title: Send a message to Claude
patterns.snippet:
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

message = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, Claude"}],
)

print(message.content[0].text)
patterns.note: max_tokens is required on every call, unlike the OpenAI SDK; content comes back as a list of typed blocks, not a plain string.

patterns.title: Set a system prompt
patterns.snippet:
message = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="You are a terse code reviewer.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Review this diff..."}],
)
patterns.note: system is a top-level parameter, not a message role; a {'role': 'system'} message raises an error.

patterns.title: Stream a response
patterns.snippet:
with client.messages.stream(
    model="claude-opus-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about CI"}],
) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:
        print(text, end="", flush=True)

final = stream.get_final_message()
patterns.note: The context manager closes the SSE connection for you; text_stream yields only text deltas, and get_final_message() returns the assembled message.

patterns.title: Use the async client
patterns.snippet:
import asyncio
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic

client = AsyncAnthropic()

async def main():
    message = await client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}],
    )
    print(message.content[0].text)

asyncio.run(main())
patterns.note: Sync and async clients mirror each other method for method; do not share one client across event loops.

patterns.title: Define a tool and return its result
patterns.note: The SDK never executes tools; you run the function and send a tool_result block back, echoing the full assistant content in the history.

patterns.title: Send an image
patterns.note: media_type must match the actual bytes (image/png, image/jpeg, image/webp, image/gif) or the API rejects the request.

patterns.title: Handle API errors by type
patterns.note: Rate limits and transient server errors are already retried automatically (default 2 retries) before these exceptions reach you.

patterns.title: Configure retries and timeouts
patterns.snippet:
import httpx
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic(
    max_retries=0,  # default is 2
    timeout=httpx.Timeout(60.0, connect=5.0),
)

# or per request
client.with_options(max_retries=5).messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}],
)
patterns.note: Timeouts are httpx-style; pass a plain float for a global cap or an httpx.Timeout for per-phase control.

patterns.title: Count tokens before sending
patterns.snippet:
count = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model="claude-opus-4-6",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, Claude"}],
)
print(count.input_tokens)
patterns.note: Counting runs server-side without generating anything; counts are model-specific, so pass the same model you will call with.

patterns.title: Call Claude through AWS Bedrock
patterns.snippet:
# pip install 'anthropic[bedrock]'
from anthropic import AnthropicBedrock

client = AnthropicBedrock(aws_region="us-west-2")

message = client.messages.create(
    model="anthropic.claude-opus-4-6-v1:0",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}],
)
patterns.note: Auth comes from the standard AWS credential chain, not ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and Bedrock uses its own model id format; check the ids enabled in your AWS account.

guide.whatIs: Official TypeScript/JavaScript client for the Claude API. Wraps the Messages endpoint with typed requests and responses, streaming helpers, automatic retries with backoff, and typed error classes per HTTP status. Runs on Node 20+, Deno, Bun, Cloudflare Workers, and Vercel Edge; browser use is disabled by default so you cannot accidentally ship your API key to clients. It is a 0.x package that tracks a fast-moving API, so minor releases can carry breaking changes.
useIf: You call the Claude API from server-side TypeScript or JavaScript and want typed params instead of hand-rolled fetch calls
You need streaming with real helpers: client.messages.stream() plus finalMessage() beats parsing SSE yourself
You want tool use, structured outputs validated against Zod schemas, and token counting handled by the library
You deploy to edge runtimes (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge) where many HTTP clients break
skipIf: You are building a browser-only app: the SDK blocks browser use by default because it would expose your secret key; route calls through your own backend instead of setting dangerouslyAllowBrowser
You target React Native: the README states it is not supported
You want one client across OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic models: a multi-provider layer like the ai package saves you maintaining N SDKs
You need a frozen API surface: this is a pre-1.0 package where minor versions have shipped breaking changes, so pin the version and read changelogs before upgrading
guide.setupReality: npm install @anthropic-ai/sdk, set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and new Anthropic() picks it up automatically. No peer dependencies; TypeScript 4.9+ and Node 20+ required. The friction is churn, not setup: the package is 0.x and tracks the API closely, so model ids, beta feature flags, and parameter shapes move between minor versions. Pin your version. Also note Jest only works with the node test environment (jsdom is unsupported), and the client timeout option is in milliseconds, unlike the Python SDK's seconds.

alternatives.name: openai
alternatives.when: Your app targets OpenAI models; the client design is nearly identical

alternatives.name: ai
alternatives.when: You want one interface over several model providers plus framework streaming hooks

alternatives.name: anthropic
alternatives.when: Same official client for the same API, from Python

guide.verdict: The correct way to call Claude from TypeScript: well built, typed end to end, and released in lockstep with the API. Treat it like the 0.x package it is: pin versions and expect steady churn.

apiStability.why: Well-designed surface, but pre-1.0 at 0.115.0: breaking changes land in minor releases and deprecated parameters get removed on short cycles

docsQuality.why: The repo README is deliberately thin; the real docs on platform.claude.com are thorough, with per-feature examples, streaming and tool-use guides, and migration notes

maintenance.why: Generated from the API spec and released alongside API changes; multiple releases per month and pushes on the day of writing

ecosystem.why: 30M weekly downloads and first-party status; a smaller third-party plugin scene than the openai client, but multi-provider layers like the ai package support it

patterns.title: Send a basic message
patterns.note: content is an array of typed blocks; narrow on block.type before reading .text or TypeScript will error.

patterns.title: Set a system prompt
patterns.note: system is a top-level parameter, not a message with role system at index 0.

patterns.title: Stream a response token by token
patterns.note: Use finalMessage() for the complete message; large max_tokens values require streaming to avoid HTTP timeouts.

patterns.title: Let Claude call your function (tool runner)
patterns.note: The tool runner (beta) drives the call-execute-loop cycle for you; drop to a manual stop_reason === 'tool_use' loop only when you need to own the whole loop.

patterns.title: Handle rate limits and API errors by type
patterns.note: Check APIConnectionError before APIError; in this SDK it is a subclass of APIError. The client already retries 429/5xx twice by default.

patterns.title: Count tokens before sending
patterns.note: Counts are model-specific; never estimate Claude tokens with tiktoken, it is OpenAI's tokenizer and undercounts.

patterns.title: Get schema-validated JSON output
patterns.note: parsed_output is null when parsing failed; also note the old top-level output_format parameter is deprecated in favor of output_config.format.

patterns.title: Send an image for analysis
patterns.note: URL sources also work: { type: 'url', url: '...' }. Put images before the text block that asks about them.

patterns.title: Cache a large stable prompt prefix
patterns.note: Caching is a byte-exact prefix match: a timestamp or random id anywhere in the prefix silently kills every cache hit.

patterns.title: Tune timeout and retries
patterns.note: Timeouts are retried too, so worst-case wall clock is timeout times (maxRetries + 1).

guide.whatIs: @aws-sdk/client-s3 is the official AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 client for S3: upload, download, list, copy, and delete objects plus bucket-level operations, with one Command class per API call. v3 split the old monolithic aws-sdk into per-service packages so you ship only the client you use, added first-class TypeScript types, and routes every call through a middleware stack. It also talks to S3-compatible stores (Cloudflare R2, MinIO, Backblaze B2) via a custom endpoint, with caveats.
useIf: You talk to S3 or an S3-compatible store from Node 20+ and want the client AWS itself builds, types, and supports
You need the full surface: multipart uploads, presigned URLs, versioning, checksums, bucket policies
You run on Lambda, where the v3 SDK ships inside the Node.js runtimes so the dependency is effectively free
You bundle for size and want per-service packages plus modular commands that tree shaking can trim
skipIf: You only need to sign a request in a browser or edge runtime: aws4fetch is tiny, while this client drags a wide @smithy dependency tree with it
You maintain v2 aws-sdk code: v3 is a full rewrite (Command objects, streaming bodies, different error shapes), so migration is real work, not find-and-replace
You target S3-compatible services and cannot babysit AWS changes: the v3.729.0 default checksum change broke uploads to R2, MinIO, and others until configs and services caught up
You expect a guided API: the reference docs are generated from service models, so figuring out input shapes often means reading TypeScript definitions
guide.setupReality: npm install @aws-sdk/client-s3 pulls a wide tree of @aws-sdk/* and @smithy/* internals and requires Node 20+. Presigned URLs and managed multipart uploads live in separate packages (@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner, @aws-sdk/lib-storage) that you discover only when something is missing. Versions move almost daily (3.1103.0 at review time), so pin and upgrade deliberately. Credentials flow through the default provider chain, which is painless on AWS infrastructure and confusing everywhere else; local dev usually means env vars or a shared credentials file, and S3-compatible endpoints usually need forcePathStyle plus checksum overrides.

alternatives.name: minio
alternatives.when: A smaller focused client for MinIO and other S3-compatible stores without the AWS dependency tree

alternatives.name: aws4fetch
alternatives.when: You just need SigV4-signed S3 requests from browsers, Cloudflare Workers, or other edge runtimes

alternatives.name: aws-sdk
alternatives.when: A legacy v2 codebase not worth migrating yet; note v2 reached end-of-support and gets no fixes

guide.verdict: If you use S3 from Node, use this client; it is well built once the Command pattern clicks. Budget time for the generated docs, pin versions, and watch release notes, because AWS ships daily and has changed defaults inside the major before.

apiStability.why: The v3 Command API has been stable since general availability in December 2020, but AWS changes behavior inside the major: the v3.729.0 default integrity checksums broke S3-compatible backends in early 2025.

docsQuality.why: The developer guide is decent, but the API reference is generated from service models: exhaustive, accurate, and painful to navigate. Most people end up reading TypeScript types or third-party posts to find input shapes.

maintenance.why: Maintained by AWS with releases nearly every business day (3.1103.0, last push August 2026) and a dedicated team triaging the 140 open issues and PRs on the monorepo.

ecosystem.why: 39M weekly downloads and the entire AWS tooling universe assumes it, but community material is thinner than v2 accumulated over a decade, and helpers are split across many small packages.

patterns.title: Create a client
patterns.snippet:
import { S3Client } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';

const s3 = new S3Client({ region: 'us-east-1' });
patterns.note: Credentials come from the default provider chain (env vars, shared config, IAM role); reuse one client instead of creating one per request.

patterns.title: Upload an object
patterns.note: Body accepts strings, Buffers, and streams, but a stream of unknown length fails; use Upload from @aws-sdk/lib-storage for those.

patterns.title: Read an object into memory
patterns.note: Unlike v2, Body is a stream, not a Buffer; transformToString and transformToByteArray are the easy way out for small objects.

patterns.title: Stream a large object to disk
patterns.note: Pipe instead of buffering; transformToByteArray on a multi-GB object will exhaust the heap.

patterns.title: List all keys under a prefix
patterns.note: ListObjectsV2 returns at most 1000 keys per call; the paginator handles ContinuationToken, and Contents is undefined on empty pages.

patterns.title: Generate a presigned URL
patterns.note: The presigner is a separate package. Expiry caps at 7 days, and URLs signed with temporary credentials die when those credentials expire.

patterns.title: Upload big files with progress
patterns.note: PutObject tops out at 5 GB and cannot report progress; Upload does multipart with parallel parts and handles unknown-length streams.

patterns.title: Check whether a key exists
patterns.note: HeadObject throws NotFound (not NoSuchKey), and you get 403 instead of 404 when the caller lacks s3:ListBucket on the bucket.

patterns.title: Delete multiple objects in one call
patterns.note: Limit is 1000 keys per call, and per-key failures arrive inside a 200 response; always check the Errors array.

patterns.title: Point the client at R2 or MinIO
patterns.note: Since v3.729.0 the SDK sends CRC32 checksums by default, which broke several S3-compatible services; the WHEN_REQUIRED settings restore the old behavior.

patterns.title: Copy an object server-side
patterns.note: CopySource needs URL encoding when the key has special characters, and server-side copy caps at 5 GB before you need multipart copy.

patterns.title: Tune retries and timeouts
patterns.note: Defaults are 3 attempts in standard retry mode and no overall request timeout; a hung socket waits forever unless you set one.

guide.whatIs: Promise-based HTTP client that runs in both the browser (via XMLHttpRequest) and Node.js (via the http module). One API for all request methods with automatic JSON serialization, request and response interceptors, upload and download progress events, cancellation via AbortController, and built-in encoding for multipart/form-data and urlencoded bodies. It sat in nearly every JavaScript project before fetch went universal, and its interceptor model is still the main reason teams keep reaching for it.
useIf: You want request/response interceptors for auth tokens, logging, or error normalization without wrapping fetch yourself
You need one HTTP client that behaves identically in browsers and Node, including Node versions without a stable native fetch
You want automatic JSON parsing, query param serialization, and multipart/form-data encoding out of the box
You need upload or download progress events, which plain fetch still makes awkward
skipIf: You are on Node 18+ or modern browsers and only make simple JSON requests: native fetch does the job with zero dependencies

You call servers you do not fully trust and will not tune config: maxContentLength and maxBodyLength default to unlimited, so a decompression bomb can exhaust your Node process unless you set caps yourself (the README now warns about this)
You need HTTP/2: axios support is experimental in the Node adapter and behavior varies by runtime
You need retries: there is no built-in retry; you have to add axios-retry or write your own interceptor
Bundle size matters: at roughly 18 KB gzipped it is many times heavier than ky or bare fetch
guide.setupReality: npm install axios and it works: no peer dependencies, no config, TypeScript types included. The real work starts when you productionize. Nothing retries by default, timeout defaults to 0 (wait forever), and response size limits default to unlimited, so a serious setup means an axios.create() instance with baseURL, timeout, maxContentLength, and interceptors. Two current gotchas: CancelToken is deprecated in favor of AbortController, and some strict backends reject axios's readable query encoding until you override paramsSerializer.encode with encodeURIComponent.

alternatives.name: ky
alternatives.when: Browser-first fetch wrapper at a fraction of the size, with retries built in

alternatives.name: got
alternatives.when: Node-only projects that want retries, hooks, and streams without plugins

alternatives.name: node-fetch
alternatives.when: You want the plain fetch API shape on Node versions lacking stable native fetch

guide.verdict: Still the safe boring choice when you need interceptors or wide runtime coverage. For new projects on Node 18+ making plain JSON calls, native fetch or ky does the same job without the dependency.

apiStability.why: v1.x has been stable since 2022; the config object and interceptor API are unchanged for years, and deprecated pieces like CancelToken keep working

docsQuality.why: One long, thorough README plus axios-http.com covering every option with examples; finding a specific edge case means scrolling a very large single page

maintenance.why: Active releases (1.19.0 shipped July 2026), pushes within the last day, and only around 60 open issues and PRs on a repo of this size; still largely volunteer-driven

ecosystem.why: 118M weekly downloads, 109k stars, and a big plugin scene (axios-retry, axios-mock-adapter); nearly every JS API wrapper documents an axios example

patterns.title: Fetch JSON with error-aware handling
patterns.note: axios parses JSON automatically and rejects on non-2xx status, unlike fetch which resolves on 404s.

patterns.title: POST a JSON body
patterns.note: Plain objects are serialized to JSON with the right Content-Type header; no JSON.stringify needed.

patterns.title: Create a configured instance
patterns.note: timeout defaults to 0 (never) and maxContentLength to unlimited; set both on every production instance.

patterns.title: Attach an auth token with a request interceptor
patterns.note: Request interceptors run last-registered-first; response interceptors run in registration order.

patterns.title: Distinguish HTTP errors from network errors
patterns.note: err.response exists only when the server answered; timeouts surface as code ECONNABORTED (or ETIMEDOUT with clarifyTimeoutError).

patterns.title: Cancel a request with AbortController
patterns.note: Use AbortController; the older CancelToken API is deprecated since v0.22 and should not appear in new code.

patterns.title: Retry a failed request with an interceptor
patterns.note: axios has no built-in retry; for anything beyond this, use the axios-retry package instead of growing this interceptor.

patterns.title: Send query parameters
patterns.note: By default axios keeps characters like : and $ readable in query strings; some backends require the strict encoding shown here.

patterns.title: Upload a file as multipart/form-data
patterns.note: Do not set the Content-Type header yourself; axios sets the multipart boundary automatically.

patterns.title: Track download progress
patterns.note: e.total is undefined when the server omits Content-Length; guard before computing percentages.

patterns.title: Cap response size against decompression bombs
patterns.snippet:
axios.defaults.maxContentLength = 10 * 1024 * 1024; // 10 MB
axios.defaults.maxBodyLength = 10 * 1024 * 1024;
patterns.note: Both default to -1 (unlimited); a hostile server can return a tiny gzip body that expands to gigabytes in your Node process.

guide.whatIs: bcrypt is the classic Node.js library for hashing passwords. It is a native addon wrapping the OpenBSD bcrypt implementation: you pick a cost factor (rounds), call hash() to get a salted 60-character hash, and later call compare() to check a login attempt. The cost factor makes hashing deliberately slow (2^rounds iterations), which is the whole point: it makes brute-forcing stolen hashes expensive. The async API runs hashing on a thread pool so it does not block the event loop. It does one job, has done it for over a decade, and the API is essentially frozen.
useIf: You store user passwords and need the industry-default hash with salt handling built in
You inherit a database of existing bcrypt hashes ($2a$ or $2b$ prefixes) and need compatibility
You run on standard Node 18+ server platforms where the prebuilt native binaries just work
You want hashing off the event loop: the async API uses a worker thread pool
skipIf: You are starting a new project and can choose freely: OWASP's current first recommendation for password hashing is Argon2id, and the argon2 npm package is just as easy to use
You deploy to edge runtimes or anywhere native addons cannot load (Cloudflare Workers, some bundled Electron setups); bcryptjs is pure JS and produces compatible hashes
Your users may have long or emoji-heavy passwords and you have not planned for it: bcrypt silently uses only the first 72 bytes of the input, the rest is ignored
Your platform has no prebuilt binary: you fall into a node-gyp build that needs Python and a C++ toolchain, historically the top source of issues for this package
You need fast-moving maintenance: releases are infrequent (v6.0.0 shipped May 2025) and the project explicitly supports only stable Node releases
guide.setupReality: On Windows x64/arm64, mainstream Linux (glibc and musl) x64/arm64, and macOS, npm install bcrypt pulls a prebuilt binary via node-gyp-build and you are done. Off that happy path (unusual arch, brand-new Node release before prebuilds land, restricted networks), it compiles from source, which drags in node-gyp, Python, and a C++ toolchain, and on Windows the Visual Studio C++ workload. v6 requires Node 18+. Also plan for the 72-byte input truncation and the fact that TypeScript types are a separate @types/bcrypt install.

alternatives.name: argon2
alternatives.when: New projects: Argon2id is the current OWASP first choice and this binding is well maintained

alternatives.name: bcryptjs
alternatives.when: You need bcrypt-compatible hashes without any native compilation (edge, Electron, odd platforms)

alternatives.name: @node-rs/bcrypt
alternatives.when: You want bcrypt semantics with Rust-built prebuilds and no node-gyp in sight

guide.verdict: Battle-tested and fine for existing systems with bcrypt hashes, but it is no longer the default answer for new code: argon2 is the stronger algorithm and bcryptjs removes the native-build risk. Pick bcrypt for compatibility, not by reflex.

apiStability.why: hash, compare, genSalt, and getRounds have not meaningfully changed in years; v6 was mostly a platform floor bump to Node 18, and old hashes stay verifiable.

docsQuality.why: The README is genuinely good: full API reference, cost-factor timing table, security history, and the 72-byte warning; there is just no docs site beyond it.

maintenance.why: Alive but slow: last release v6.0.0 in May 2025, last repo push April 2026, 38 open issues and PRs; fine for a frozen-scope library, bad if you expect quick fixes.

ecosystem.why: About 5.7M weekly downloads and every Node auth tutorial uses it, but the mindshare is shifting toward argon2 and pure-JS or Rust-based alternatives.

patterns.title: Hash a password before storing it
patterns.note: Never store the plain password anywhere; the 60-char hash string contains algorithm, cost, and salt, so no separate salt column is needed.

patterns.title: Check a login attempt against a stored hash
patterns.note: compare() extracts cost and salt from the stored hash automatically; never compare hash strings with === yourself.

patterns.title: Pick a cost factor deliberately
patterns.note: Benchmark on your production hardware and pick the highest rounds your login latency budget tolerates; 10 is the default, many teams now run 12.

patterns.title: Use async, not the Sync variants, on servers
patterns.note: At cost 12 hashSync freezes your process for hundreds of milliseconds per call; the README itself recommends the async API on servers.

patterns.title: Guard against the 72-byte truncation
patterns.note: The limit is bytes, not characters: emoji and non-Latin scripts hit it far sooner than 72 characters.

patterns.title: Transparently upgrade old hashes at login
patterns.note: Login is the only moment you hold the plain password, so it is the only place you can re-hash at a higher cost.

patterns.title: Registration route with hashing
patterns.note: Do the hashing inside the request handler with await; wrapping hashSync in a route is the classic accidental event-loop stall.

patterns.title: Generate a salt as a separate step
patterns.snippet:
const salt = await bcrypt.genSalt(12);
const hash = await bcrypt.hash(password, salt);
patterns.note: Functionally identical to passing rounds straight to hash(); only useful when you want to log or reuse the salt string.

patterns.title: Inspect the cost factor of a stored hash
patterns.snippet:
const rounds = bcrypt.getRounds('$2b$10$nOUIs5kJ7naTuTFkBy1veuK0kSxUFXfuaOKdOKf9xYT0KKIGSJwFa');
console.log(rounds); // 10
patterns.note: Handy for auditing a user table to see how many hashes still sit at an outdated cost factor.

patterns.title: Avoid user-enumeration via response timing
patterns.note: Without a dummy compare, unknown emails return instantly while known ones take ~100ms, which leaks which emails have accounts.

guide.whatIs: Beautiful Soup parses HTML and XML into a Python object tree you can search and edit. It sits on top of a real parser (html.parser from the standard library, or lxml and html5lib if installed) and gives you find, find_all, CSS selectors, and tree navigation that tolerate the broken markup real websites ship. It is the extraction half of scraping; you still need requests or httpx to fetch the pages.
useIf: You are scraping or cleaning real-world HTML that is malformed, mis-nested, or inconsistently encoded
You want extraction code that reads like the page structure it targets: find_all and select over regex heroics
You need to edit markup (strip tags, rewrite attributes, pull fragments), not just read it
You are prototyping and want results in ten lines using only the standard library parser
skipIf: Throughput matters: bs4 builds a full Python object tree, and lxml or selectolax parse the same pages far faster at bulk-scraping volume
The page renders its content with JavaScript: no HTML parser will ever see that data; you need Playwright or the site's underlying JSON API
You are building a crawling pipeline: Scrapy with parsel gives you XPath plus CSS with request handling, throttling, and retries built in
You are parsing one well-formed XML feed: lxml or the standard library's ElementTree does it without an extra dependency
guide.setupReality: pip install beautifulsoup4 works everywhere because the default backend is Python's own html.parser: no compiled extensions, no wheel drama. Wanting speed means adding lxml, which does need wheels (fine on mainstream platforms, annoying on Alpine). Two classic footguns: the import name is bs4, not beautifulsoup4, and PyPI still hosts an ancient package literally named BeautifulSoup (version 3), so a from-memory install can hand you an abandoned codebase. Also pin your parser explicitly, because different backends build slightly different trees from bad markup.

alternatives.name: lxml
alternatives.when: You need speed and full XPath and can accept a compiled dependency and a stricter API.

alternatives.name: selectolax
alternatives.when: You are CSS-selector-only and want the fastest practical HTML parsing for large crawls.

alternatives.name: parsel
alternatives.when: You want Scrapy-style selectors (XPath plus CSS chained together) with or without Scrapy itself.

guide.verdict: Still the friendliest way to pull data out of messy HTML, and the pure-Python default keeps installs painless. Use it for jobs measured in pages; move to lxml or selectolax when you measure in millions.

apiStability.why: The find/find_all/select API has been stable across the entire 4.x line for over a decade; 4.13 added type hints without changing call signatures.

docsQuality.why: One canonical long-form doc covers everything with examples and multiple translations; it is a single giant page, so you navigate by Ctrl-F rather than structure.

maintenance.why: Actively maintained by its original author with 4.15.0 current; development lives on Launchpad rather than GitHub, so issue visibility and contributor flow are thinner than 118M weekly downloads implies.

ecosystem.why: The default answer in nearly every scraping tutorial since the 2000s, 118M+ weekly downloads, and pluggable parser backends (lxml, html5lib) that slot in without code changes.

patterns.title: Parse a document and grab the title
patterns.snippet:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
print(soup.title.string)
print(soup.h1)
patterns.note: Always name the parser explicitly; leaving it out picks the best installed backend, so the tree can change between machines.

patterns.title: Find tags by name, class, and attributes
patterns.snippet:
links = soup.find_all("a", class_="result", limit=10)
for a in links:
    print(a["href"], a.get_text(strip=True))

row = soup.find("tr", attrs={"data-id": "42"})
patterns.note: It is class_ with a trailing underscore because class is reserved in Python; find returns None on a miss, so chain carefully.

patterns.title: Query with CSS selectors
patterns.snippet:
cells = soup.select("table#prices tr td:nth-of-type(2)")
first = soup.select_one("div.card > h2")
if first is not None:
    print(first.get_text())
patterns.note: select is powered by the bundled soupsieve dependency and supports most modern CSS; select_one returns None rather than raising.

patterns.title: Get clean text out of a subtree
patterns.note: get_text() with no separator glues adjacent strings together into words like 'HomeAbout'; pass separator=' ' for readable output.

patterns.title: Read tag attributes safely
patterns.snippet:
a = soup.find("a")
href = a.get("href")          # None if missing
hard = a["href"]               # KeyError if missing
classes = a.get("class", [])   # class is always a list
patterns.note: Multi-valued attributes like class come back as lists, not strings, which breaks naive == comparisons.

patterns.title: Move between related elements
patterns.snippet:
label = soup.find("th", string="Price")
value = label.find_next_sibling("td")

section = value.find_parent("section")
for child in section.children:
    print(getattr(child, "name", None))
patterns.note: Whitespace between tags counts as text nodes, so .children and .next_sibling often return strings where you expected tags.

patterns.title: Scrape a live page with requests
patterns.snippet:
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

resp = requests.get(url, headers={"User-Agent": "my-bot/1.0"}, timeout=10)
resp.raise_for_status()
soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.content, "html.parser")
patterns.note: Pass resp.content (bytes) rather than resp.text so Beautiful Soup does its own encoding detection instead of trusting the HTTP header.

patterns.title: Strip tags and rewrite content
patterns.snippet:
for tag in soup.find_all(["script", "style"]):
    tag.decompose()

h1 = soup.find("h1")
h1.string = "New title"
h1["class"] = ["headline"]

clean_html = str(soup)
patterns.note: decompose() destroys the element permanently; use extract() instead if you want to keep the removed subtree around.

patterns.title: Parse only part of a big page with SoupStrainer
patterns.snippet:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup, SoupStrainer

only_links = SoupStrainer("a")
soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser", parse_only=only_links)
hrefs = [a.get("href") for a in soup.find_all("a")]
patterns.note: SoupStrainer cuts memory and parse time on large pages, but it does not work with the html5lib backend.

patterns.title: Handle a page with wrong or missing encoding
patterns.snippet:
soup = BeautifulSoup(raw_bytes, "html.parser", from_encoding="iso-8859-1")
print(soup.original_encoding)
patterns.note: Only force from_encoding after checking soup.original_encoding; guessing before the auto-detection fails just adds a new bug.

guide.whatIs: Biome is a formatter and linter for JavaScript, TypeScript, JSX, JSON, CSS, and GraphQL shipped as a single fast native binary written in Rust. The formatter scores 97% compatibility with Prettier; the linter carries more than 500 rules ported from ESLint, typescript-eslint, and other sources, with detailed diagnostics and safe autofixes. It is built for editor-first use through LSP and replaces the usual ESLint plus Prettier plus plugin stack with one tool and one config file.
useIf: You want to collapse ESLint, Prettier, and their config sprawl into one tool with a single biome.json
Lint and format time in CI or pre-commit hooks is a real cost on a large codebase or monorepo
You want sane defaults without assembling plugins; biome check --write formats, lints, and organizes imports in one pass
You need the same binary in the editor, in scripts, and in CI (biome ci), including machines without Node.js
skipIf: Your lint setup depends on ESLint plugins with no Biome equivalent, including custom in-house rules written for ESLint's API
You rely on the full depth of type-aware linting from typescript-eslint; Biome's type inference covers a narrower slice
You format languages Biome does not handle, such as Markdown or YAML, so you would keep Prettier anyway and end up running both tools
Your team treats formatting diffs as sacred: 97% Prettier compatibility means some files will change on migration, so budget a one-shot reformat commit
guide.setupReality: npm install --save-dev --save-exact @biomejs/biome fetches a platform-specific native binary, and biome init writes a starter biome.json. biome migrate eslint --write and biome migrate prettier --write translate existing configs, but rule mapping is not one-to-one, so expect a triage pass of re-enabling rules and adding suppressions. In editors you must disable the ESLint and Prettier extensions or they will fight Biome over formatting. The README's --save-exact hint matters: formatter and rule output can shift between releases, so pin it.

alternatives.name: eslint
alternatives.when: You depend on its plugin ecosystem or need custom rules beyond what Biome has ported

alternatives.name: prettier
alternatives.when: You only want formatting, with the widest language and ecosystem coverage including Markdown and YAML

alternatives.name: oxlint
alternatives.when: You want a fast native linter but plan to keep Prettier as your formatter

guide.verdict: The strongest single-tool replacement for the ESLint plus Prettier stack today: one fast binary, one config, very good defaults. Check the rule and plugin coverage against your current setup before migrating, because that gap is the whole decision.

apiStability.why: CLI verbs have stayed stable, but the 1.x to 2.0 jump renamed config sections (ignore lists became files.includes, import sorting moved under assist); biome migrate exists for a reason

docsQuality.why: biomejs.dev has guides, a per-rule reference with examples, and a WebAssembly playground; migration edge cases still route you to GitHub discussions

maintenance.why: Daily activity, a funded core team via Open Collective and GitHub Sponsors, an enterprise support program, and translated docs in a dozen languages

ecosystem.why: First-party VS Code and Open VSX extensions plus broad LSP editor support, but the third-party rule and plugin ecosystem is young next to ESLint's

patterns.title: Format files in place
patterns.snippet: npx @biomejs/biome format --write
patterns.note: Without --write it only prints the diff and exits non-zero when files would change.

patterns.title: Lint and apply safe fixes
patterns.snippet: npx @biomejs/biome lint --write
patterns.note: --write applies only fixes marked safe; add --unsafe to apply the rest, and review that diff.

patterns.title: Format, lint, and organize imports in one pass
patterns.snippet: npx @biomejs/biome check --write
patterns.note: check is the everyday command; it runs the formatter, linter, and assist actions together.

patterns.title: Fail CI on formatting or lint issues
patterns.snippet: npx @biomejs/biome ci
patterns.note: ci never writes files and exits non-zero on any diagnostic, which is exactly what you want in a pipeline.

patterns.title: Create a starter biome.json
patterns.snippet: npx @biomejs/biome init
patterns.note: Biome works with zero config; init just gives you a file with the schema reference to grow into.

patterns.title: Import an existing ESLint or Prettier config
patterns.snippet:
npx @biomejs/biome migrate eslint --write
npx @biomejs/biome migrate prettier --write
patterns.note: Rules without a Biome equivalent are dropped silently, so diff the generated biome.json against expectations.

patterns.title: Turn individual lint rules on or off
patterns.note: Rules live in groups (suspicious, style, correctness, and so on) with severities off, warn, or error.

patterns.title: Suppress a rule on one line
patterns.snippet:
// biome-ignore lint/suspicious/noExplicitAny: third-party payload is untyped
const data: any = JSON.parse(raw);
patterns.note: The full rule path is required and the explanation after the colon is expected; biome-ignore-all at the top of a file covers the whole file.

patterns.title: Scope which files Biome touches
patterns.note: Biome 2 replaced separate ignore lists with includes plus ! negation patterns; older files.ignore configs need biome migrate.

patterns.title: Respect .gitignore automatically
patterns.note: With useIgnoreFile on, build output ignored by git stays out of lint runs without duplicating globs in biome.json.

patterns.title: Enable import sorting
patterns.note: In Biome 2 import sorting is an assist action that runs during check, not a standalone command.

guide.whatIs: Boto3 is the official AWS SDK for Python, maintained and published by Amazon. It gives you a Python client for essentially every AWS service (S3, EC2, DynamoDB, SQS, Lambda and hundreds more), generated from AWS's own service definitions via the underlying botocore library. It handles credential resolution, request signing, retries, pagination and waiters. If you touch AWS from Python, whether in a script, a server or inside Lambda, this is the tool; there is no serious competitor for direct AWS access.
useIf: You automate or integrate anything on AWS from Python: it is the official, always-current SDK with same-day support for new services
You run code in AWS Lambda, where boto3 is preinstalled in the Python runtime and picks up the execution role's credentials automatically
You need production plumbing done right: built-in paginators, waiters, configurable retry modes and request signing you should never hand-roll
You want AWS-backed support and a maintenance policy rather than a community wrapper
skipIf: You need async: boto3 is synchronous and blocks the event loop; aioboto3 exists but is a community wrapper, not AWS-supported
You mostly move dataframes around: awswrangler (AWS SDK for pandas) wraps boto3 with far less ceremony for S3/Athena/Redshift analytics work
You want typed autocomplete out of the box: clients are generated at runtime, so your editor sees nothing until you add third-party boto3-stubs
You are not on AWS or need multi-cloud abstraction; this SDK is AWS-only by design
guide.setupReality: pip install boto3 works, but the install is heavy: botocore ships JSON service definitions for every AWS service, so expect tens of megabytes, which matters for slim containers and Lambda layers. The real setup work is credentials: the resolution chain (env vars, ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.aws/config profiles, SSO, instance/task roles) is powerful and a classic source of it-works-on-my-machine bugs. Editor autocomplete requires installing boto3-stubs with the right service extras because the client factory is dynamic. Python 3.9 support ended in April 2026; you need 3.10+. Also note the resource API (boto3.resource) is feature-frozen; new work should use clients.

alternatives.name: aioboto3
alternatives.when: You need async AWS calls inside asyncio applications; community-maintained wrapper over aiobotocore

alternatives.name: awswrangler
alternatives.when: Pandas-centric data work against S3, Athena, Glue or Redshift with much less boilerplate

alternatives.name: s3fs
alternatives.when: You just want S3 to look like a filesystem for pandas, dask or fsspec-aware tools

guide.verdict: Mandatory and dependable if you use AWS from Python; the API is stable and Amazon ships releases almost daily. Just budget for the credentials learning curve, add boto3-stubs for sane autocomplete, and prefer clients over the frozen resource API.

apiStability.why: The 1.x line has been backwards compatible since general availability in 2015; changes are additive service updates. The one caveat: the resource API is feature-frozen, so its coverage will not grow.

docsQuality.why: The reference on docs.aws.amazon.com covers every operation because it is generated from service models, but that also makes it dry; realistic end-to-end examples are thin and you lean on guides and Stack Overflow.

maintenance.why: Maintained by AWS with near-daily releases tracking new service features, a published SDK maintenance policy, and pushes within a day of this review.

ecosystem.why: Everything AWS-adjacent in Python builds on it (moto for testing, boto3-stubs for types, awswrangler, aioboto3), though the essentials like type stubs and async are third-party rather than built in.

patterns.title: Create a client with explicit region
patterns.snippet:
import boto3

s3 = boto3.client("s3", region_name="us-east-1")

# or from a named profile
session = boto3.Session(profile_name="prod", region_name="eu-west-1")
s3 = session.client("s3")
patterns.note: Never hardcode keys in code; let the credential chain (env vars, profiles, IAM roles) supply them. Clients are thread-safe, sessions are not.

patterns.title: Upload and download S3 files
patterns.snippet:
import boto3

s3 = boto3.client("s3")
s3.upload_file("report.pdf", "my-bucket", "reports/report.pdf")
s3.download_file("my-bucket", "reports/report.pdf", "/tmp/report.pdf")
patterns.note: upload_file/download_file handle multipart transfers and retries automatically; prefer them over raw put_object for anything larger than a few MB.

patterns.title: Generate a presigned URL
patterns.snippet:
url = s3.generate_presigned_url(
    "get_object",
    Params={"Bucket": "my-bucket", "Key": "reports/report.pdf"},
    ExpiresIn=3600,
)
patterns.note: The URL is signed with the caller's credentials; if those are temporary (STS/role), the link dies when the credentials expire, whatever ExpiresIn says.

patterns.title: List all objects with a paginator
patterns.note: list_objects_v2 caps at 1000 keys per call; skipping the paginator and missing that cap is a classic silent-truncation bug.

patterns.title: Handle AWS errors by error code
patterns.note: Almost every service error is a ClientError; branch on the code string, not the exception type. head_object returns 404, get_object returns NoSuchKey.

patterns.title: Configure retries and timeouts
patterns.snippet:
from botocore.config import Config

cfg = Config(
    retries={"max_attempts": 10, "mode": "adaptive"},
    connect_timeout=5,
    read_timeout=60,
)
dynamodb = boto3.client("dynamodb", config=cfg)
patterns.note: Default is legacy retry mode; adaptive adds client-side rate limiting, which is what you want when you keep hitting Throttling errors.

patterns.title: DynamoDB put and get
patterns.snippet:
dynamodb = boto3.resource("dynamodb")
table = dynamodb.Table("users")

table.put_item(Item={"pk": "user#1", "name": "Ada", "score": 99})
resp = table.get_item(Key={"pk": "user#1"})
item = resp.get("Item")
patterns.note: The resource API is worth keeping for DynamoDB specifically because it converts Python types for you; the raw client makes you write {"S": "..."} type descriptors.

patterns.title: Assume an IAM role for cross-account access
patterns.snippet:
sts = boto3.client("sts")
creds = sts.assume_role(
    RoleArn="arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/Deploy",
    RoleSessionName="deploy-script",
)["Credentials"]

s3 = boto3.client(
    "s3",
    aws_access_key_id=creds["AccessKeyId"],
    aws_secret_access_key=creds["SecretAccessKey"],
    aws_session_token=creds["SessionToken"],
)
patterns.note: Temporary credentials expire (default 1 hour) and boto3 will not auto-refresh ones you pass manually; long-running jobs should re-assume or use a profile with role_arn.

patterns.title: Send and receive SQS messages
patterns.snippet:
sqs = boto3.client("sqs")
queue_url = sqs.get_queue_url(QueueName="jobs")["QueueUrl"]

sqs.send_message(QueueUrl=queue_url, MessageBody='{"job": 1}')

msgs = sqs.receive_message(
    QueueUrl=queue_url, MaxNumberOfMessages=10, WaitTimeSeconds=20
)
for m in msgs.get("Messages", []):
    process(m["Body"])
    sqs.delete_message(QueueUrl=queue_url, ReceiptHandle=m["ReceiptHandle"])
patterns.note: You must delete messages explicitly after processing or they reappear after the visibility timeout; WaitTimeSeconds=20 (long polling) cuts cost and empty responses.

patterns.title: Wait for a resource to reach a state
patterns.snippet:
ec2 = boto3.client("ec2")
resp = ec2.run_instances(ImageId="ami-123", InstanceType="t3.micro",
                         MinCount=1, MaxCount=1)
instance_id = resp["Instances"][0]["InstanceId"]

waiter = ec2.get_waiter("instance_running")
waiter.wait(InstanceIds=[instance_id])
patterns.note: Waiters poll with sane backoff and give up after a service-specific limit; tune via waiter.wait(..., WaiterConfig={"Delay": 15, "MaxAttempts": 40}).

patterns.title: Read a large S3 object without loading it all
patterns.note: resp["Body"] is a streaming object; calling .read() with no args pulls the whole file into memory, which is how Lambdas run out of RAM.

guide.whatIs: BullMQ is a Redis-backed job queue for Node.js: you add jobs to named queues and worker processes pick them up, with retries, delays, priorities, rate limiting, cron-style schedulers, and parent-child job flows. Operations run as atomic Lua scripts, which is why it survives crashes and concurrent workers without double-processing. It is the maintained successor to Bull, run by Taskforce.sh, with official ports for Python, Rust, Elixir, and PHP, and the v6 release (July 30, 2026) introduced pluggable backends beyond a single Redis client.
useIf: You already run Redis (or Valkey/Dragonfly) and need background jobs with retries, backoff, and scheduled or repeating work
You need orchestration: parent jobs that wait on children (flows), queue-level rate limits, per-worker concurrency
You use NestJS, where the official @nestjs/bullmq integration makes this the default queue
You are on the old Bull package and want the maintained successor with the same mental model
skipIf: You do not want to operate Redis: pg-boss gives you a competent queue inside the Postgres you already run
Your jobs are simple periodic tasks in one process: a cron library is far less machinery than queue plus worker plus Redis
You need groups, batches, or observables: those live in the paid BullMQ Pro package, not the open-source one
You deploy serverless: workers are long-lived processes holding blocking Redis connections, which does not fit Lambda-style runtimes without extra plumbing
You want boring and settled: v6 shipped days ago and changed the connection model, so most tutorials and AI answers still describe v5
guide.setupReality: npm install bullmq, plus a Redis 6.2+ instance you run yourself, so docker compose becomes part of local dev. Since v6 the Redis client is an optional peer dependency: you install ioredis, redis v5+, or @valkey/valkey-glide and hand BullMQ the connection. The two classic footguns: ioredis connections for workers need maxRetriesPerRequest: null, and completed or failed jobs stay in Redis forever unless you set removeOnComplete and removeOnFail. Types are good, but the config surface (job options, worker options, events) takes a day to internalize.

alternatives.name: pg-boss
alternatives.when: You already run Postgres and would rather not add Redis; SKIP LOCKED queues cover most job workloads

alternatives.name: bee-queue
alternatives.when: You want a minimal, fast Redis queue and can live without repeatable jobs and flows

alternatives.name: agenda
alternatives.when: MongoDB is your only datastore and job volume is modest; check its maintenance activity first

guide.verdict: The default job queue for Node when Redis is on the table: atomic, fast, and actively developed with commercial backing. Accept the cost of running Redis and the Pro paywall on some features, and pick v5 or v6 deliberately since v6 is brand new.

apiStability.why: The core Queue/Worker/FlowProducer API has carried over from v4 through v6, but majors arrive fast: v6 (July 2026) moved Redis clients to optional peer dependencies, and semantic-release means constant version churn.

docsQuality.why: docs.bullmq.io covers concepts, patterns, and an API reference, but open-source and Pro features are documented side by side, and some answers only exist in GitHub issues or the Taskforce blog.

maintenance.why: Commercially backed by Taskforce.sh, pushed the same day as this review (August 2026), 9.2k stars; the paid Pro tier funds full-time work on the open-source core.

ecosystem.why: 7.7M weekly downloads, official NestJS integration, bull-board and Taskforce UIs, Dragonfly compatibility, and ports to four other languages; smaller than Sidekiq-style incumbents elsewhere but the standard for Node.

patterns.title: Add a job and process it
patterns.note: Since v6 you install the Redis client yourself (ioredis here); worker connections need maxRetriesPerRequest: null or BullMQ rejects them.

patterns.title: Retry failed jobs with backoff
patterns.note: Jobs only retry when attempts > 1; after the last attempt the job lands in the failed set and sits there until you act or a cleanup policy removes it.

patterns.title: Schedule a job for later
patterns.snippet: await queue.add('reminder', { userId: 7 }, { delay: 60_000 });
patterns.note: Delay counts from add time. If no worker is running when the delay expires, the job just waits for the next worker to come up.

patterns.title: Run a job on a cron schedule
patterns.note: Job Schedulers replaced the older repeatable-jobs API; upserting by a fixed id means redeploys do not create duplicate schedules.

patterns.title: Listen for completion globally
patterns.note: QueueEvents uses Redis streams on its own blocking connection; worker.on('completed') only sees jobs handled by that one worker process.

patterns.title: Run a parent job after its children
patterns.note: The parent waits in a waiting-children state until every child completes; read child results in the parent via job.getChildrenValues().

patterns.title: Rate limit a queue
patterns.note: The limit applies to the queue as a whole, not per worker instance; per-group rate limiting is a BullMQ Pro feature.

patterns.title: Process many jobs in parallel
patterns.note: Concurrency shares one event loop, so it helps I/O-bound jobs only; CPU-bound work needs sandboxed processors or more worker processes.

patterns.title: Isolate heavy jobs in a child process
patterns.note: Passing a file path instead of a function runs jobs in a child process, so a crash or blocking loop cannot take down the worker; the job object inside is a proxy with a reduced API.

patterns.title: Stop finished jobs from filling Redis
patterns.note: Without these options finished jobs accumulate in Redis indefinitely; set them per add or once via the queue defaultJobOptions.

patterns.title: Shut a worker down cleanly
patterns.note: worker.close() waits for active jobs to finish; kill the process instead and those jobs get marked stalled and rerun after the stalled interval.

patterns.title: Deduplicate identical jobs
patterns.note: While a job with the same deduplication id exists, further adds are ignored; with a ttl it throttles, without one it holds until the job finishes.

guide.whatIs: Celery is a distributed task queue for Python: you decorate functions as tasks, call them with .delay(), and separate worker processes pick them up through a message broker (RabbitMQ and Redis are the feature-complete transports). It handles retries, periodic scheduling via celery beat, task workflows (chains, groups, chords), and scaling across machines, which is why it has been the default background-job system in the Django world for well over a decade.
useIf: You need background jobs that survive restarts and scale across multiple worker machines
You already run RabbitMQ or Redis and want mature retry, routing, and rate-limit controls on top
You need periodic jobs, task chains, or fan-out/fan-in workflows (groups and chords) beyond what a cron entry covers
You run Django or Flask, where the integration paths are well worn and heavily documented
skipIf: Your stack is asyncio-first: Celery workers are prefork process based, and native async task execution is not part of the story; arq fits an event-loop codebase better
You want simple: Celery means a broker, usually a result backend, worker processes, and a large configuration surface; RQ or Huey covers plain job queues with far less machinery
You deploy on Windows: the project explicitly does not support it and asks you not to file Windows issues
You have one server and modest job volume: a cron job or a database-backed queue avoids operating a broker at all
guide.setupReality: pip install celery is the easy part. The real setup is running a broker (RabbitMQ or Redis), adding a result backend if you ever read return values, keeping worker processes alive under systemd or a supervisor, and running celery beat as yet another process if you schedule anything. Configuration naming changed to lowercase forms in the 4.x era, so old Stack Overflow answers mix two styles. Local development means a broker plus a worker running next to your app, and reproducing bugs that only appear under the prefork pool is a skill of its own.

alternatives.name: rq
alternatives.when: You are on Redis anyway and want a job queue you can understand end to end in an afternoon.

alternatives.name: dramatiq
alternatives.when: You want Celery-style features with fewer knobs and reliability-focused defaults.

alternatives.name: huey
alternatives.when: You want a tiny queue with periodic tasks for small apps, including SQLite-backed setups.

alternatives.name: arq
alternatives.when: Your codebase is asyncio and you want async task execution on Redis instead of prefork workers.

guide.verdict: Still the heavyweight standard for Python background processing; the operational overhead is the fee for its maturity, workflows, and scaling. Pick it when you need those features, and pick RQ, Huey, or arq when you just need work off the request path.

apiStability.why: The task and canvas APIs have been steady across the 5.x line since 2020; the 4-to-5 CLI and config-naming changes still pollute old answers, and 5.7 will drop Python 3.9.

docsQuality.why: docs.celeryq.dev is deep: tutorials, a full configuration reference, and operations guides; the depth cuts both ways, since finding the one setting you need takes real digging.

maintenance.why: Pushed the day of this review with 5.6.x current, but it is a self-described minimal-funding project with nearly 800 open issues and PRs and no Windows support.

ecosystem.why: First-class Django and Flask paths, Flower for monitoring, experimental brokers beyond RabbitMQ/Redis, and protocol clients in Node, Go, and Rust listed by the project itself.

patterns.title: Define an app and a task
patterns.note: Calling add(2, 2) runs it inline like a normal function; only add.delay(2, 2) actually sends it to the queue.

patterns.title: Start a worker
patterns.snippet: celery -A tasks worker --loglevel=INFO --concurrency=4
patterns.note: In the 5.x CLI, -A comes before the worker subcommand; the old 'celery worker -A tasks' order from 4.x tutorials fails.

patterns.title: Wait for a task result
patterns.snippet:
app = Celery("tasks", broker="redis://localhost:6379/0",
             backend="redis://localhost:6379/1")

result = add.delay(4, 4)
print(result.ready())
print(result.get(timeout=10))
patterns.note: get() needs a configured result backend, and calling it inside another task is a documented deadlock trap.

patterns.title: Retry automatically on specific exceptions
patterns.snippet:
import requests

@app.task(autoretry_for=(requests.RequestException,),
          retry_backoff=True, max_retries=5)
def fetch(url):
    resp = requests.get(url, timeout=10)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.text
patterns.note: retry_backoff gives exponential delays with jitter applied by default, so retries do not stampede a recovering service.

patterns.title: Retry with control over the delay
patterns.note: bind=True makes self the task instance; self.retry raises to re-queue, so no code after it will run.

patterns.title: Schedule recurring jobs with beat
patterns.note: beat is a separate scheduler process; run exactly one instance or every job fires once per beat you started.

patterns.title: Compose tasks with chain, group, and chord
patterns.snippet:
