guide.verdict: The most practical way to run real models in a browser today, and excellent for embeddings, Whisper and classification. Be honest about physics: model downloads and experimental WebGPU mean it complements a server-side stack more often than it replaces one.

apiStability.why: The pipeline API has stayed consistent from v2 through v4 and mirrors the Python library on purpose; churn concentrates in device/dtype options and model-specific behavior rather than the core surface.

docsQuality.why: Hosted docs cover the API, WebGPU and quantization guides, and the README's task table shows exactly what is and is not supported; per-model quirks still send you to GitHub issues.

maintenance.why: Active Hugging Face project with recent pushes (late July 2026), though npm releases arrive in bursts; the latest package (4.2.0) shipped in April 2026.

ecosystem.why: Backed by the Hugging Face Hub with a dedicated transformers.js model tag, official example repos and templates; the ONNX conversion path via Optimum covers custom models.

patterns.title: Run a sentiment analysis pipeline
patterns.note: The first call downloads the model; construct pipelines once and reuse them, never per request.

patterns.title: Use a specific model from the Hub
patterns.note: Only models tagged transformers.js on the Hub ship the ONNX weights this library needs; arbitrary PyTorch repos will not load.

patterns.title: Run on GPU via WebGPU
patterns.note: WebGPU is still experimental in many browsers per the project's own warning; feature-detect navigator.gpu and fall back to WASM.

patterns.title: Shrink a model with quantization
patterns.note: Defaults differ by backend (q8 on WASM, fp32 on WebGPU); q4 cuts download and memory at some accuracy cost, and available dtypes vary per model.

patterns.title: Generate sentence embeddings
patterns.note: Without pooling and normalize you get raw token-level tensors, not comparable sentence vectors.

patterns.title: Transcribe audio with Whisper
patterns.note: Input audio must be 16kHz mono; in the browser decode with AudioContext({ sampleRate: 16000 }) before passing raw samples.

patterns.title: Chat-style text generation with messages
patterns.note: Passing a messages array applies the model's chat template automatically; stick to sub-1B models in browsers.

patterns.title: Serve models from your own origin
patterns.snippet:
import { env } from '@huggingface/transformers'

env.allowRemoteModels = false
env.localModelPath = '/models/'
env.backends.onnx.wasm.wasmPaths = '/wasm/'
patterns.note: The defaults fetch models from the Hub and WASM from a CDN at runtime; production apps should pin and self-host both.

patterns.title: Show model download progress
patterns.note: Models are tens to hundreds of MB on first load; a UI without a progress indicator looks frozen.

patterns.title: Keep inference off the main thread
patterns.note: WASM inference blocks whatever thread it runs on; anything beyond trivial models belongs in a worker to keep the page responsive.

guide.whatIs: Jest is an all-in-one JavaScript testing framework: test runner, assertion library, mocking system, coverage reporting, and snapshot testing in a single install. It runs test files in parallel worker processes with isolated module registries, so tests do not leak state into each other, and its watch mode re-runs only the tests related to files you just changed. It works out of the box for CommonJS Node projects and reaches everything else through Babel transforms.
useIf: You test React or React Native: both ecosystems treat Jest as the default and ship presets for it
You want mocking built in: jest.mock for modules, jest.fn for functions, and fake timers without adding sinon or proxyquire
You rely on snapshot testing for component output or serialized objects, which Jest popularized and still does best
You have a plain CommonJS Node project and want tests running with literally zero configuration
skipIf: Your project is built on Vite: Jest's own README says it is not fully supported with Vite's plugin system, while Vitest reuses your vite.config directly
You need native ESM without transforms: Jest's ESM support still sits behind the experimental --experimental-vm-modules flag and has rough edges around mocking
You want type errors caught while testing TypeScript: the default Babel path only strips types, so broken types pass silently unless you add ts-jest or run tsc separately
Startup and transform overhead bothers you: on large suites the per-worker module transform cost is noticeable compared with newer runners
guide.setupReality: npm install --save-dev jest and a test script is genuinely all a CommonJS project needs. The annoying parts arrive with modern syntax: ESM, JSX, or TypeScript each mean installing babel-jest plus @babel/preset-env (and preset-react or preset-typescript) and a babel.config.js, or going the ts-jest route instead. DOM testing needs the separate jest-environment-jsdom package plus testEnvironment: 'jsdom' in config, because it no longer ships in the box. Jest 30 needs Node ^18.14, ^20, ^22, or >=24 and TypeScript 5.4+ if you use its types. Expect to spend more time on the transform config than on your first hundred tests.

alternatives.name: vitest
alternatives.when: You use Vite or want native ESM and TypeScript with a Jest-compatible API and faster watch mode.

alternatives.name: mocha
alternatives.when: You want a minimal runner and prefer picking your own assertion and mocking libraries.

alternatives.name: ava
alternatives.when: You want concurrent tests in isolated processes with a small, opinionated API and no globals.

guide.verdict: Still the safest default for React codebases and plain Node projects, with the most battle-tested mocking and snapshot story in JavaScript. If you are starting a Vite or ESM-first project today, Vitest is the more natural fit and Jest is the one you configure around.

apiStability.why: The describe/test/expect and mocking APIs have barely changed in years; majors like Jest 30 mostly drop old Node versions and tighten defaults rather than rework the API.

docsQuality.why: jestjs.io covers getting started, every matcher, CLI flags, and configuration with examples, plus dedicated guides for webpack, TypeScript, and timer mocking.

maintenance.why: Actively developed under the OpenJS Foundation after leaving Meta, repo pushed August 2026 with 30.x shipping steadily, though the core team is small relative to the install base.

ecosystem.why: 46M weekly downloads, first-class presets from React Native and countless frameworks, and years of Stack Overflow answers; almost every JS tool documents a Jest integration.

patterns.title: Write and run a first test
patterns.note: Files matching *.test.js or living in __tests__/ are picked up automatically; no config file is required for CommonJS.

patterns.title: Test async code
patterns.note: Forgetting the await before expect(...).rejects makes the test pass before the promise settles.

patterns.title: Mock a callback with jest.fn
patterns.note: forEach passes (value, index, array), so toHaveBeenCalledWith needs all three arguments or it fails confusingly.

patterns.title: Mock an entire module
patterns.note: jest.mock calls are hoisted above imports automatically for CJS; under experimental ESM you must use jest.unstable_mockModule instead.

patterns.title: Spy on a method and restore it
patterns.note: Without restoreAllMocks (or restoreMocks: true in config) the spy leaks into every later test in the file.

patterns.title: Control setTimeout with fake timers
patterns.note: Modern fake timers also fake Date and queueMicrotask; use jest.useRealTimers() in afterEach if other tests need real time.

patterns.title: Snapshot a serializable value
patterns.note: Update stale snapshots with jest -u, but review the diff first; blindly updating turns snapshots into noise.

patterns.title: Share setup between tests
patterns.note: beforeAll runs once per file, not once per suite run; each parallel worker gets its own copy of module state.

patterns.title: Run one test over many cases
patterns.note: The template string variant test.each`...` reads better for named fields but breaks some editor test runners' go-to-test.

patterns.title: Run only what you are working on
patterns.snippet:
# one file
npx jest sum.test.js
# tests whose name matches
npx jest -t "adds 1"
# re-run on change, only affected tests
npx jest --watch
patterns.note: A committed test.only silently skips the rest of the file; ESLint's jest plugin has a rule to catch it.

patterns.title: Test DOM code with jsdom
patterns.note: jsdom is not bundled with Jest anymore; without the separate package this config errors at startup.

patterns.title: Collect coverage and enforce a floor
patterns.note: Without collectCoverageFrom, files no test ever imports are invisible to the report, inflating your numbers.

guide.whatIs: jsonwebtoken is Auth0's Node.js implementation of JSON Web Tokens (RFC 7519). You call jwt.sign() to create a signed token from a payload plus a secret or private key, and jwt.verify() to check the signature and standard claims like exp, aud, and iss on the way back in. It supports HMAC, RSA, RSA-PSS, and ECDSA algorithms, and it is the package nearly every Node auth tutorial reaches for, which is why it still moves 54M downloads a week.
useIf: You need to sign and verify JWTs in a plain Node.js service and want the API every tutorial and Stack Overflow answer uses
You verify tokens against a JWKS endpoint; the getKey callback pairs directly with jwks-rsa
You want claim validation (exp, nbf, aud, iss, sub, maxAge, clockTolerance) handled by options instead of hand-rolled checks
skipIf: You run on edge runtimes, Cloudflare Workers, Deno, or in the browser. This package needs Node's crypto module; jose runs everywhere
You want an actively developed library. There was no release at all between 9.0.2 in August 2023 and 9.0.3 in December 2025, and the repo has 206 open issues and PRs
You need EdDSA (Ed25519) signatures or JWE encrypted tokens; jsonwebtoken supports neither, jose supports both
Token verification sits on your hot path and throughput matters; fast-jwt exists for exactly that reason
guide.setupReality: npm install jsonwebtoken works everywhere Node runs, but it drags in ten dependencies including five lodash.* micro-packages and a full copy of semver, which is a lot for a token signer. The API is CommonJS with sync-or-callback style and no promises, so you either use the sync form or wrap it in util.promisify. TypeScript types live in the separate @types/jsonwebtoken package. Coming from v8, read the v9 migration notes: RSA keys under 2048 bits are rejected unless you explicitly opt out with allowInsecureKeySizes.

alternatives.name: jose
alternatives.when: When you need edge or browser support, EdDSA, JWE, or a modern promise-based API

alternatives.name: fast-jwt
alternatives.when: When token sign and verify throughput actually shows up in your profiles

guide.verdict: It works and half the Node auth code on the internet depends on it, but this is maintenance-mode software with a multi-year release gap. For new projects jose is the better default; pick jsonwebtoken mainly for consistency with an existing codebase.

apiStability.why: sign, verify, and decode have kept the same shape across v8 and v9; v9 mostly tightened security defaults like minimum RSA key sizes.

docsQuality.why: The README documents every sign and verify option with examples and lists all error types; there is no dedicated docs site but the surface is small enough not to need one.

maintenance.why: One release between August 2023 and December 2025, 206 open issues and PRs, and a stated TODO that X.509 certificate chains are not checked. Alive, but barely.

ecosystem.why: About 54M weekly downloads and near-universal presence in Node auth guides, express middleware, and boilerplates.

patterns.title: Sign a token with a shared secret (HS256)
patterns.snippet:
const jwt = require('jsonwebtoken');

const token = jwt.sign({ sub: 'user-123', role: 'admin' }, process.env.JWT_SECRET);
patterns.note: HS256 is the default algorithm; an iat (issued at) claim is added automatically unless you pass noTimestamp.

patterns.title: Sign a token that expires
patterns.note: A bare number means seconds but a numeric string like '120' means milliseconds; always include units in string values.

patterns.title: Sign with an RSA private key (RS256)
patterns.note: Since v9, RSA keys under 2048 bits throw unless you set allowInsecureKeySizes: true, which you should not.

patterns.title: Verify a token and read its payload
patterns.note: The README warns to treat the decoded payload like any other user input; verify checks the signature, not your business rules.

patterns.title: Pin the allowed algorithms on verify
patterns.note: Always pin algorithms when verifying; accepting whatever the token header claims is the classic JWT confusion attack.

patterns.title: Verify audience, issuer, and subject
patterns.note: clockTolerance (in seconds) absorbs small clock drift between servers when checking exp and nbf.

patterns.title: Distinguish an expired token from an invalid one
patterns.note: Expired tokens usually mean 'refresh', invalid tokens usually mean 'reject'; branching on err.name is how you tell them apart.

patterns.title: Peek into a token without verifying it
patterns.note: decode() does not check the signature at all; never make auth decisions from it, only routing decisions like picking a key by kid.

patterns.title: Verify against a remote JWKS endpoint
patterns.note: The getKey callback form only works with the async verify signature; the sync form cannot fetch keys.

patterns.title: Use verify with async/await
patterns.note: The library predates promises and never added them; promisify works because the callback is error-first.

guide.whatIs: langchain is the JavaScript/TypeScript framework for building LLM applications and agents. Version 1.x centers on createAgent: a tool-calling loop that takes a model (as a 'provider:model' string or an instance), a set of tools, and optional middleware, and runs the model against those tools until the task completes. It adds structured output, streaming, and thread-level memory, with LangGraph underneath for state and persistence, and one interface across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Ollama, and many other providers.
useIf: You swap or compare model providers and want one calling convention instead of rewriting against each vendor SDK
You need an agent loop with tools, conversation memory, and structured output and do not want to hand-build the loop, retries, and message plumbing
You expect to grow into LangGraph orchestration or LangSmith tracing, which plug into the same stack
skipIf: Your app is a couple of direct calls to one provider: the official SDK plus a little of your own code is fewer layers and much easier to debug
You have a 0.x LangChain codebase: 1.0 was a breaking rewrite around createAgent, old chain-style patterns are gone or moved, and migration is a project rather than a version bump
You ship size-sensitive frontend bundles: the package depends on zod, langsmith, and @langchain/langgraph before you add any provider package
You have low tolerance for churn: the core abstractions have been rethought more than once, and online examples for 0.x will actively mislead you
guide.setupReality: You install langchain plus @langchain/core (a peer dependency) plus one provider package like @langchain/openai, and the docs quickstart assumes Node 22+. The classic install trap is peer-dependency version mismatch between @langchain/core and provider packages after a partial upgrade; align them or you get confusing type and runtime errors. Provider API keys come from environment variables. Expect to spend time orienting in docs that span LangChain, LangGraph, and LangSmith, and to distrust any tutorial written before the 1.0 rewrite.

alternatives.name: ai
alternatives.when: You want a leaner TypeScript SDK with first-class streaming UI hooks, especially in Next.js

alternatives.name: @langchain/langgraph
alternatives.when: You need custom multi-step orchestration beyond what the createAgent loop offers

alternatives.name: llamaindex
alternatives.when: Your app is primarily retrieval over your own documents rather than a general agent

guide.verdict: v1 finally gives LangChain.js a focused core: createAgent is a capable agent loop with real provider breadth. If your app is a few direct model calls, a provider SDK and fifty lines of your own code remain the simpler, more debuggable choice.

apiStability.why: The 0.x line saw repeated deprecations and the 1.0 release rewrote the core API around createAgent. 1.x has been consistent so far, but it is young and the project's history is one of moving abstractions.

docsQuality.why: docs.langchain.com is thorough, with per-provider runnable examples for agents, streaming, and memory. The catch is content spread across LangChain, LangGraph, and LangSmith, and a web full of stale 0.x tutorials.

maintenance.why: Developed by LangChain, Inc. with near-daily pushes; the repo was updated the day of this review and 1.x has moved from 1.0 to 1.5 in a matter of months.

ecosystem.why: Large integration catalog of model providers, vector stores, and tools, plus LangGraph and LangSmith. Smaller than the Python ecosystem, and some community integrations lag core releases.

patterns.title: Create and invoke a basic agent
patterns.note: The 'provider:model' string needs the matching provider package installed and its API key set as an env var.

patterns.title: Define a tool with a zod schema
patterns.note: The description is what the model reads to decide when to call the tool; vague descriptions produce bad tool choice.

patterns.title: Set a system prompt on the agent
patterns.note: systemPrompt is a plain string; for dynamic prompts based on state you reach for middleware instead.

patterns.title: Get validated structured output
patterns.note: The parsed object lives on result.structuredResponse, not in the message list.

patterns.title: Stream tokens as they generate
patterns.note: streamMode 'messages' yields token chunks; 'values' yields the full state after each step, which is much chattier.

patterns.title: Keep conversation history across turns
patterns.note: MemorySaver is in-process only; use a persistent checkpointer in production or history dies with the process.

patterns.title: Read the final text reply from a result
patterns.note: result.messages contains the whole run including tool calls and tool results, not just the final answer.

patterns.title: Call a chat model without an agent
patterns.note: For a single completion with no tools, calling the model directly skips the whole agent loop and its overhead.

patterns.title: Build a reusable prompt template chain
patterns.note: Templates live in @langchain/core; single curly braces are template variables, so escape literal braces by doubling them.

guide.whatIs: LangChain is the most widely used Python framework for building LLM applications and agents (this page covers the PyPI package named langchain; there is a separate npm package with the same name for JavaScript). Since the 1.0 rewrite it centers on one idea: create_agent, a production-ready agent loop built on the LangGraph runtime, plus init_chat_model so you can address OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and dozens of other providers through one interface. The old 0.x chains and AgentExecutor now live in separate legacy packages.
useIf: You want to swap model providers (or run several) without rewriting call sites; the provider abstraction is the core product
You are building a tool-calling agent and want the loop, message state, and structured output handled for you instead of hand-rolling a while loop
You need its integration catalog: hundreds of maintained packages for vector stores, retrievers, and tools that would each be bespoke glue code otherwise
You plan to grow into LangGraph for multi-step workflows; create_agent already returns a LangGraph graph, so the upgrade path is native
skipIf: You call one provider with straightforward prompts: the official openai or anthropic SDK is fewer layers, and every layer here is one more place to debug when output looks wrong

You maintain 0.x code: the 1.0 rewrite moved chains, LLMChain, and AgentExecutor out to langchain-classic, and most tutorials, blog posts, and Stack Overflow answers still show pre-1.0 APIs that no longer import
You want a small dependency footprint: the base install pulls langchain-core, langgraph, and pydantic, and every provider is yet another package on top

Deep debugging matters more than speed of assembly: tracing a bad answer through middleware, graph nodes, and message transforms is real work, and the first-party observability tool (LangSmith) is a commercial product
guide.setupReality: pip install langchain brings in langchain-core and langgraph, but no model provider: you also need langchain-openai, langchain-anthropic, or the matching extra like langchain[openai], plus the provider API key in your environment. The sharpest edge is version skew. Pre-1.0 examples dominate search results and fail on import in 1.x, and the docs are split between docs.langchain.com and a separate reference site, so expect to check which era a snippet comes from before trusting it. Pinning versions matters; minor releases arrive frequently.

alternatives.name: openai
alternatives.when: One provider, direct calls, no framework; the SDK plus a small hand-written loop covers many agent use cases

alternatives.name: pydantic-ai
alternatives.when: You want a typed, Pydantic-first agent framework with a smaller surface area

alternatives.name: llama-index
alternatives.when: Your app is mostly retrieval over documents; its indexing and query pipeline is more focused for RAG

alternatives.name: langgraph
alternatives.when: You want explicit graph-level control of an agent workflow and can skip the higher-level conveniences

guide.verdict: The 1.x rewrite is a real improvement: one blessed agent abstraction on a solid runtime, with the largest integration catalog in the Python LLM space. Pay the abstraction tax only if you need provider portability or that catalog; for a single provider and simple calls, the plain SDK is less to learn and less to debug.

apiStability.why: The project reorganized repeatedly through 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3, and the 1.0 release retired chains and AgentExecutor to legacy packages; 1.x comes with a stability promise, but that promise is young and the churn burned many codebases

docsQuality.why: The current docs at docs.langchain.com are thorough with runnable examples, but content is split across a docs site, a reference site, and an academy, and the internet is full of outdated pre-1.0 examples that look official

maintenance.why: Pushed the day of this review, large full-time team at LangChain the company, rapid release cadence across the core, provider, and langgraph packages

ecosystem.why: The largest LLM framework ecosystem in Python: hundreds of provider and integration packages, LangGraph and LangSmith around it, and enough adoption that most vendors ship a langchain-x package themselves

patterns.title: One interface for any provider
patterns.snippet:
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

model = init_chat_model("openai:gpt-4o", temperature=0)
result = model.invoke("Say hi in one word")
print(result.content)
patterns.note: The provider prefix (openai:, anthropic:, ollama:) selects which integration package to load; that package must be installed separately or you get an ImportError at runtime, not install time.

patterns.title: Tool-calling agent in a few lines
patterns.snippet:
from langchain.agents import create_agent

agent = create_agent(
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5",
    tools=[get_weather],
    system_prompt="You are a terse assistant.",
)
result = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in Pune?"}]})
print(result["messages"][-1].content)
patterns.note: create_agent replaced 0.x AgentExecutor and returns a compiled LangGraph graph; input and output are dicts with a messages list, not a plain string.

patterns.title: Define a tool with the decorator
patterns.note: The docstring is not decoration: it is the description the model reads to decide when to call the tool. A vague docstring produces an agent that ignores or misuses the tool.

patterns.title: Get a Pydantic object back from an agent
patterns.snippet:
from pydantic import BaseModel
from langchain.agents import create_agent

class Verdict(BaseModel):
    rating: int
    summary: str

agent = create_agent(model="openai:gpt-4o", tools=[], response_format=Verdict)
result = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Rate this printer: ..."}]})
print(result["structured_response"].rating)
patterns.note: The parsed object arrives under the structured_response key, separate from messages. Validation failures surface as retries or errors depending on strategy, so keep schemas simple.

patterns.title: Multi-turn conversation with message objects
patterns.snippet:
from langchain.messages import HumanMessage, SystemMessage

messages = [
    SystemMessage("You answer in Hindi."),
    HumanMessage("What is a copier drum?"),
]
reply = model.invoke(messages)
messages.append(reply)
patterns.note: In 1.x these classes are importable from langchain.messages directly; older code imports them from langchain_core.messages, which still works but reads as pre-1.0 style.

patterns.title: Stream tokens from a model
patterns.snippet:
for chunk in model.stream("Explain RESP3 in two sentences"):
    print(chunk.text, end="", flush=True)
patterns.note: Chunks are AIMessageChunk objects, not strings. With reasoning models some chunks carry non-text content blocks, so chunk.text is safer than assuming chunk.content is a string.

patterns.title: Stream agent progress step by step
patterns.note: stream_mode matters: values yields full state each step, updates yields deltas, and messages yields token-level chunks. Picking the wrong mode is the usual reason streaming output looks duplicated or empty.

patterns.title: Give an agent conversation memory
patterns.snippet:
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

agent = create_agent(model="openai:gpt-4o", tools=[], checkpointer=InMemorySaver())
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-42"}}
agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "I am Keyoor"}]}, config)
agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Who am I?"}]}, config)
patterns.note: Memory is per thread_id and InMemorySaver evaporates on restart; production needs a persistent checkpointer such as the Postgres one from the langgraph ecosystem.

patterns.title: Bind tools without the agent loop
patterns.snippet:
model_with_tools = model.bind_tools([get_weather])
response = model_with_tools.invoke("Weather in Pune?")
for call in response.tool_calls:
    print(call["name"], call["args"])
patterns.note: bind_tools only makes the model emit tool calls; nothing executes them. You own the loop of running tools and feeding ToolMessage results back, which is exactly what create_agent automates.

patterns.title: Prompt template piped to a model
patterns.snippet:
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template("Translate to {lang}: {text}")
chain = prompt | model | StrOutputParser()
print(chain.invoke({"lang": "German", "text": "good morning"}))
patterns.note: The pipe-operator (LCEL) style still works through langchain-core, but 1.x docs push agents instead; treat this as the tool for fixed transformations, not decision-making flows.

patterns.title: Middleware to keep context under control
patterns.snippet:
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import SummarizationMiddleware

agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-4o",
    tools=[get_weather],
    middleware=[SummarizationMiddleware(model="openai:gpt-4o-mini")],
)
patterns.note: Middleware is new in 1.x and the hooks run inside the graph, so a misbehaving middleware shows up as confusing agent behavior; add them one at a time and test.

guide.whatIs: An open source AI gateway that gives you one OpenAI-format interface to 100+ LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, Azure, and more). You use it two ways: as a Python SDK where litellm.completion() replaces per-provider SDKs, or as a self-hosted proxy server that your whole org points OpenAI clients at, adding virtual keys, spend tracking, load balancing, guardrails, and an admin dashboard. Provider errors are mapped to OpenAI-style exceptions so retry and fallback logic is written once.
useIf: You call two or more LLM providers and want one request/response format instead of juggling per-provider SDKs and auth patterns
You need fallbacks, retries, and load balancing across model deployments, which the Router handles for you
A platform team wants a central gateway with virtual keys, per-team budgets, and spend tracking rather than API keys scattered across services
You want to switch models via a config or model string without touching application code
skipIf: You only call one provider; the official SDK is thinner, better typed, and gets new features (new endpoints, betas) before the translation layer does
You want a small dependency footprint; litellm is a large package that moves extremely fast, with releases landing near-daily, so unpinned installs drift and pinned ones go stale in weeks
You rely on provider-specific capabilities at the edges; the unified interface papers over real differences, and non-portable params either pass through untyped or get dropped
You need an agent framework; litellm is a call layer and gateway, not chains, memory, or tool orchestration
guide.setupReality: pip install litellm, export your provider API keys as env vars, and completion(model="provider/model") works in minutes. The proxy is where setup gets real: pip install 'litellm[proxy]' pulls a much bigger dependency tree, the quick start (litellm --model gpt-4o) is one command, but a production gateway means writing a config.yaml, standing up Postgres for virtual keys and spend tracking, and running it in Docker. Release velocity is the recurring annoyance: pin your version, read changelogs before bumping, and expect the occasional regression in less-used providers.

alternatives.name: openai
alternatives.when: You only talk to OpenAI (or OpenAI-compatible endpoints) and want the first-party SDK

alternatives.name: anthropic
alternatives.when: You only call Claude and want first-party types, streaming helpers, and day-one feature support

alternatives.name: langchain
alternatives.when: You want a full framework (chains, agents, retrieval) rather than just a unified call layer

guide.verdict: The pragmatic choice the moment you talk to more than one provider or need a gateway with keys, budgets, and fallbacks; adoption and maintenance pace back that up. For a single-provider app it is more machinery than the problem needs.

apiStability.why: completion() has kept its OpenAI-shaped contract across years of 1.x releases, but the surface area is enormous and near-daily releases mean behavior in less-traveled providers and proxy features shifts more often than the core.

docsQuality.why: docs.litellm.ai is broad, with per-provider pages, a proxy end-to-end tutorial, and published benchmarks; depth is uneven across the 100+ providers and some pages lag the code given the release pace.

maintenance.why: Pushed to within the hour of this review, 55k+ stars, backed by a YC W23 company with an enterprise tier funding full-time development.

ecosystem.why: The README lists Netflix, Stripe, and OpenHands among OSS adopters, and it plugs into A2A agents, MCP tools, and the major agent SDKs; it is the default multi-provider layer in much of the Python LLM stack.

patterns.title: Call any provider in OpenAI format
patterns.snippet:
import os
from litellm import completion

os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-..."

response = completion(
    model="anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
patterns.note: The model string is "provider/model"; auth comes from the provider's standard env var, so nothing else changes when you swap providers.

patterns.title: Stream tokens as they arrive
patterns.note: delta.content is None on some chunks (role headers, finish chunks), so guard before concatenating.

patterns.title: Async calls with acompletion
patterns.snippet:
import asyncio
from litellm import acompletion

async def main():
    response = await acompletion(
        model="gemini/gemini-2.5-flash",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}],
    )
    print(response.choices[0].message.content)

asyncio.run(main())
patterns.note: acompletion mirrors completion exactly; combine with asyncio.gather for concurrent calls instead of threads.

patterns.title: Retries and timeouts on a call
patterns.snippet:
from litellm import completion

response = completion(
    model="openai/gpt-4o",
    messages=msgs,
    timeout=30,
    num_retries=2,
)
patterns.note: Because provider errors are mapped to OpenAI-style exception types, retry behavior is consistent no matter which provider actually failed.

patterns.title: Fall back to another provider
patterns.snippet:
from litellm import completion

response = completion(
    model="openai/gpt-4o",
    messages=msgs,
    fallbacks=["anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514", "gemini/gemini-2.5-flash"],
)
patterns.note: Fallbacks trigger on errors from the primary model; each fallback model needs its own provider key set in the environment.

patterns.title: Load balance across deployments
patterns.snippet:
from litellm import Router

router = Router(model_list=[
    {"model_name": "gpt-4o", "litellm_params": {"model": "azure/gpt-4o-eu", "api_key": key1, "api_base": base1}},
    {"model_name": "gpt-4o", "litellm_params": {"model": "openai/gpt-4o"}},
])

response = router.completion(model="gpt-4o", messages=msgs)
patterns.note: Deployments sharing a model_name form a pool; the Router spreads load and cools down deployments that error, which is how you survive per-key rate limits.

patterns.title: Run the proxy (AI gateway)
patterns.snippet:
pip install 'litellm[proxy]'
litellm --model gpt-4o
# then point any OpenAI client at it:
# client = openai.OpenAI(api_key="anything", base_url="http://0.0.0.0:4000")
patterns.note: The one-liner is for trying it out; virtual keys, budgets, and spend tracking require a config.yaml plus a Postgres database.

patterns.title: Compute the cost of a response
patterns.snippet:
from litellm import completion, completion_cost

response = completion(model="openai/gpt-4o", messages=msgs)
usd = completion_cost(completion_response=response)
print(f"${usd:.6f}")
patterns.note: Pricing comes from a bundled model-price map; brand-new models may be missing until you upgrade litellm.

patterns.title: Embeddings through the same interface
patterns.snippet:
from litellm import embedding

result = embedding(
    model="text-embedding-3-small",
    input=["good morning", "good night"],
)
vectors = [d["embedding"] for d in result.data]
patterns.note: Same provider-prefix convention as completion; response shape follows the OpenAI embeddings format regardless of provider.

patterns.title: Catch provider errors uniformly
patterns.note: Every provider's errors are mapped onto OpenAI-style exception classes, so one except block covers all backends.

patterns.title: Drop params a provider does not support
patterns.snippet:
import litellm

litellm.drop_params = True

# now e.g. passing frequency_penalty to a provider
# that lacks it is dropped instead of raising
patterns.note: Convenient for portable code, but it fails silently by design; leave it off in tests so you notice which knobs a provider actually ignores.

guide.whatIs: LlamaIndex is a Python framework for building LLM applications over your own data, with retrieval-augmented generation as its core competency. It provides data loaders, chunking, embeddings, vector indexes, retrievers, query and chat engines, and agent workflows behind a few high-level classes; the five-line SimpleDirectoryReader-to-VectorStoreIndex path is the canonical demo. The llama-index package on PyPI is a starter bundle: llama-index-core plus OpenAI LLM and embedding defaults. Everything else (other LLMs, embedding models, vector stores) is a separate llama-index-* integration package from a catalog of 300+.
useIf: Your app is fundamentally retrieval over documents: internal search, chat over PDFs, knowledge assistants
You want to swap LLMs, embedding models, and vector stores behind one interface instead of committing to a single vendor's SDK
You need ready-made ingestion machinery: readers for many formats, sentence-aware chunking, and metadata handling
You are prototyping RAG and want the five-line index-and-query path working before you customize retrievers and chunking
skipIf: You are just calling one LLM API with prompts; the provider SDK plus a few functions is less machinery than adopting a framework
You need API stability: the package is still 0.x, breaking changes land between minor releases, and 2024-era tutorial code frequently no longer imports

Dependency weight bothers you: the starter bundle pulls nltk and OpenAI integrations whether you use them or not, and a real app accumulates a dozen llama-index-* packages that must stay version-compatible with core
Your workload is agent orchestration more than retrieval; LangGraph or a hand-rolled state machine can fit better than retrofitting query engines
guide.setupReality: pip install llama-index gets you the starter bundle wired to OpenAI, so the quickstart only works after export OPENAI_API_KEY. Going beyond the defaults means finding the right integration on LlamaHub (llama-index-llms-ollama, llama-index-vector-stores-chroma, and so on) and pip-installing each one; import paths mirror package names, which helps. Expect churn: pre-1.0 versioning means you pin versions and read changelogs on every upgrade, and the README itself warns that the docs are more current than the README.

alternatives.name: langchain
alternatives.when: You want the larger ecosystem and LangGraph-style agent orchestration around your retrieval

alternatives.name: haystack-ai
alternatives.when: You want explicit, typed pipeline graphs for production RAG and search

alternatives.name: txtai
alternatives.when: You want a lighter all-in-one embeddings database with optional LLM plumbing

guide.verdict: The most focused RAG framework in Python: if the problem is answering questions over your documents, its abstractions earn their keep. Pin versions and budget for upgrade churn until it reaches 1.0.

apiStability.why: Still 0.x after years: the 0.10 era split the codebase into per-integration packages with new import paths, and breaking changes continue to land in minor releases.

docsQuality.why: developers.llamaindex.ai is extensive with runnable examples for nearly every module, but the API moves faster than community content, so most external snippets target dead APIs.

maintenance.why: Backed by the LlamaIndex company, pushed daily across the integration monorepo, with very frequent releases (0.14.23 current at review time).

ecosystem.why: 300+ integration packages for LLMs, embeddings, and vector stores plus LlamaHub and the LlamaParse platform; overall mindshare still trails LangChain (about 1.7M vs 64M weekly downloads).

patterns.title: Index a folder and ask a question
patterns.snippet:
from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, SimpleDirectoryReader

documents = SimpleDirectoryReader("data").load_data()
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents)
query_engine = index.as_query_engine()
print(query_engine.query("What does the contract say about termination?"))
patterns.note: Defaults to OpenAI for both LLM and embeddings; fails immediately without OPENAI_API_KEY set.

patterns.title: Use a local or non-OpenAI LLM
patterns.snippet:
from llama_index.core import Settings
from llama_index.llms.ollama import Ollama

Settings.llm = Ollama(model="llama3.1", request_timeout=360.0)
patterns.note: Requires pip install llama-index-llms-ollama; Settings is a global that all components created afterwards read.

patterns.title: Use local embeddings
patterns.snippet:
from llama_index.core import Settings
from llama_index.embeddings.huggingface import HuggingFaceEmbedding

Settings.embed_model = HuggingFaceEmbedding(
    model_name="BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5"
)
patterns.note: Requires pip install llama-index-embeddings-huggingface; changing the embed model invalidates existing indexes, so re-embed everything.

patterns.title: Persist an index to disk and reload it
patterns.snippet:
index.storage_context.persist(persist_dir="./storage")

from llama_index.core import StorageContext, load_index_from_storage

storage_context = StorageContext.from_defaults(persist_dir="./storage")
index = load_index_from_storage(storage_context)
patterns.note: Default storage is in-memory and dies with the process; disk persistence writes JSON, fine for small corpora only.

patterns.title: Back the index with a real vector store
patterns.snippet:
import chromadb
from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, StorageContext
from llama_index.vector_stores.chroma import ChromaVectorStore

client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_db")
collection = client.get_or_create_collection("docs")
vector_store = ChromaVectorStore(chroma_collection=collection)
storage_context = StorageContext.from_defaults(vector_store=vector_store)
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents, storage_context=storage_context)
patterns.note: Needs pip install llama-index-vector-stores-chroma chromadb; the same StorageContext pattern applies to every vector store integration.

patterns.title: Control chunk size and overlap
patterns.snippet:
from llama_index.core.node_parser import SentenceSplitter

splitter = SentenceSplitter(chunk_size=512, chunk_overlap=50)
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents, transformations=[splitter])
patterns.note: Retrieval quality is usually more sensitive to chunking than to which LLM you picked; tune this first.

patterns.title: Retrieve more context per query
patterns.snippet:
query_engine = index.as_query_engine(
    similarity_top_k=8,
    response_mode="compact",
)
patterns.note: The default top_k of 2 is often too few for real corpora; compact mode packs retrieved chunks into fewer LLM calls.

patterns.title: Chat engine with conversation history
patterns.snippet:
chat_engine = index.as_chat_engine(chat_mode="condense_plus_context")
response = chat_engine.chat("What is the notice period?")
follow_up = chat_engine.chat("And who does it apply to?")
patterns.note: as_query_engine is stateless; chat engines keep history and rewrite follow-ups into standalone retrieval queries.

patterns.title: Stream the answer token by token
patterns.snippet:
query_engine = index.as_query_engine(streaming=True)
response = query_engine.query("Summarize the report")
for token in response.response_gen:
    print(token, end="")
patterns.note: Streaming covers the synthesis step only; retrieval still completes before the first token arrives.

patterns.title: See which chunks produced the answer
patterns.snippet:
response = query_engine.query("What changed in Q3?")
for node in response.source_nodes:
    print(node.score, node.metadata.get("file_name"))
    print(node.text[:200])
patterns.note: Check source_nodes whenever answers look wrong; bad answers are usually bad retrieval, not a bad LLM.

patterns.title: Agent that calls Python functions as tools
patterns.snippet:
import asyncio
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import FunctionAgent
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI

def multiply(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Multiply two numbers."""
    return a * b

agent = FunctionAgent(tools=[multiply], llm=OpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini"))
result = asyncio.run(agent.run("What is 7 times 8?"))
patterns.note: Agent runs are async, so wrap them in asyncio.run outside notebooks; function docstrings become the tool descriptions.

patterns.title: Install only what you use
patterns.snippet:
pip install llama-index-core \
  llama-index-llms-openai \
  llama-index-embeddings-huggingface
patterns.note: Skip the llama-index starter bundle in production so you control exactly which integrations and transitive deps ship.

guide.whatIs: Lodash is a grab-bag of utility functions for arrays, objects, strings, and functions: debounce, cloneDeep, groupBy, merge, get, and about 300 more. It sits in your dependency tree as the standard library JavaScript never shipped. It has been on major version 4 since 2016 and, per the OpenJS Foundation announcement in its own README, is now moving to a Feature-Complete maturity stage: stable and maintained, but no new features are coming.
useIf: You need battle-tested implementations of debounce, throttle, or deep clone and do not want to hand-roll edge cases like leading/trailing calls or circular references
You work in a large codebase that already uses it everywhere; consistency beats purity here
You need deep object operations natives still do not cover well: merge with nested defaults, groupBy/keyBy, orderBy with multiple keys, isEqual structural comparison
You support older runtimes and want utilities that do not assume the newest ECMAScript features
skipIf: You are starting a new project in 2026: modern JS covers a lot of lodash (flat, Object.entries, structuredClone, Array.prototype.at, optional chaining replaces most _.get calls), and es-toolkit or remeda give you the rest smaller and tree-shakeable

Bundle size matters and your team imports the whole package: the main lodash package is CommonJS and does not tree-shake, so 'import _ from lodash' ships roughly 70 KB minified for the two functions you actually use
You want a library that will grow with the language: lodash is explicitly feature-complete, so new proposals and patterns will never land in it
You only need one function: lodash.debounce-style per-method packages exist but are frozen at old versions; copying 20 lines or using a focused package is cleaner
guide.setupReality: npm install lodash and it just works, no peer dependencies, no config, runs anywhere. The annoyance is bundling: the default package is CommonJS, so bundlers cannot tree-shake it and you must either cherry-pick imports (import debounce from 'lodash/debounce'), switch to lodash-es, or add babel-plugin-lodash. TypeScript types live in a separate @types/lodash install. Teams routinely discover the full library in their bundle months later.

alternatives.name: es-toolkit
alternatives.when: New code that wants the same utility names, smaller and faster, with native ESM and tree-shaking

alternatives.name: remeda
alternatives.when: TypeScript-first projects that want data-last pipe-friendly utilities with strong type inference

alternatives.name: lodash-es
alternatives.when: You want lodash exactly as-is but as ES modules so your bundler can tree-shake it

guide.verdict: Still the safest set of utility implementations ever shipped and fine to keep in existing codebases, but for new projects the language plus es-toolkit covers almost everything at a fraction of the weight. Feature-complete status means this is maintenance mode by design, not neglect.

apiStability.why: Major version 4 since 2016 and now formally feature-complete; the API you learned a decade ago still works unchanged.

docsQuality.why: lodash.com/docs documents every method with examples and is easy to search, but guidance on modern usage (ESM, tree-shaking, when natives suffice) is thin and the FP guide lives off in a wiki.

maintenance.why: There was a multi-year release gap after 4.17.21, and the project is now funded via the Sovereign Tech Agency in a declared Feature-Complete stage: security and stability fixes yes, new development no. Governance is being rebooted with a new TSC per the README.

ecosystem.why: 166M weekly downloads, per-method mirror packages, lodash-es, babel and webpack plugins, and a decade of Stack Overflow answers; nearly every JS tool understands it.

patterns.title: Debounce a search input
patterns.note: Create the debounced function once, not inside a render/handler, or every call gets a fresh timer and nothing debounces.

patterns.title: Throttle a scroll handler
patterns.note: Default is leading and trailing both true; set trailing: false if a final late call after the user stops scrolling would be wrong.

patterns.title: Deep clone an object
patterns.note: Native structuredClone covers most cases now but throws on functions and DOM nodes; cloneDeep copies functions by reference instead of throwing.

patterns.title: Read a nested path with a default
patterns.note: For static paths use optional chaining (user?.address?.city ?? 'unknown'); get is only worth it when the path is built at runtime.

patterns.title: Group an array of objects by a field
patterns.note: Native Object.groupBy exists in Node 21+ and modern browsers; lodash groupBy is the drop-in for anything older.

patterns.title: Turn an array into a lookup map
patterns.note: Later duplicates overwrite earlier ones silently; use groupBy if keys can repeat and you need all of them.

patterns.title: Deep merge config with defaults
patterns.snippet:
import merge from 'lodash/merge';

const config = merge({}, defaults, fileConfig, cliOverrides);
patterns.note: merge mutates its first argument; always pass {} first. Arrays are merged index-by-index, which surprises almost everyone.

patterns.title: Structural equality check
patterns.note: Handles nested objects, arrays, dates, and regexes; it is O(n) over the whole structure, so avoid it in hot paths on large objects.

patterns.title: Split an array into batches
patterns.note: The last chunk is whatever remains and can be shorter than the batch size.

patterns.title: Remove duplicates by a field
patterns.note: First occurrence wins; sort first if you want the newest record kept.

patterns.title: Whitelist or drop object fields
patterns.note: Prefer pick for API responses: an allowlist stays safe when new sensitive fields are added later, omit does not.

patterns.title: Sort by multiple keys with direction
patterns.snippet:
import orderBy from 'lodash/orderBy';

const sorted = orderBy(users, ['role', 'createdAt'], ['asc', 'desc']);
patterns.note: Returns a new array (sortBy/orderBy never mutate), and the sort is stable.

guide.whatIs: Matplotlib is Python's foundational plotting library for static, animated, and interactive visualizations. It renders publication-quality figures to PNG, SVG, PDF, and interactive GUI windows, and runs anywhere Python does: scripts, IPython, Jupyter, web servers, and desktop toolkits. Nearly every chart you have seen from a Python codebase touches it somewhere, because pandas .plot(), seaborn, and many other tools are built directly on its Figure and Axes objects.
useIf: You need publication-quality figures with control over every tick, label, font, and margin, exported to PNG, SVG, or PDF
You already use pandas or seaborn and want to customize the figures they produce, since both hand you matplotlib objects
You need plots generated headlessly on a server or in CI, where the Agg backend writes image files with no display attached
You want animations or embedded plots inside Tk, Qt, or other GUI applications
skipIf: You are building browser dashboards with hover tooltips, zooming, and linked views: Plotly or Bokeh produce interactive HTML natively, matplotlib does not
You mainly do quick statistical exploration: seaborn gets you a better-looking result in a third of the code, on top of the same engine
You want one obvious way to do things: the pyplot state machine and the object-oriented API coexist everywhere in tutorials, and mixing them is the top source of beginner confusion
You need to stream high-frequency live data; redrawing matplotlib figures at speed is possible but fights the library the whole way
guide.setupReality: pip install matplotlib pulls numpy, pillow, fonttools, and friends, but prebuilt wheels cover the common platforms so compiles are rare. The real setup pain is backends: on a headless server the default may try to open a GUI and fail, so you set the Agg backend; in Jupyter you occasionally fight magics and inline renderers; on a bare Linux install, Tk may simply be missing. After that it is the two-API problem: examples online mix plt.plot state-machine calls with fig/ax object calls, and figures leak memory in long-running processes unless you plt.close() them. Current releases require Python 3.11 or newer.

alternatives.name: plotly
alternatives.when: You want interactive charts with tooltips and zoom that drop into a web page or Dash app.

alternatives.name: seaborn
alternatives.when: You want attractive statistical plots from DataFrames with far less code, still on matplotlib underneath.

alternatives.name: altair
alternatives.when: You prefer a declarative grammar-of-graphics API and your data fits comfortably in memory.

guide.verdict: The workhorse of Python plotting: unmatched control, output quality, and staying power, with an API that shows its age and a learning curve bent by two coexisting styles. Learn the object-oriented interface once and it will outlast every dashboard fad.

apiStability.why: Twenty years of careful backward compatibility under an explicit EffVer versioning scheme; code from old tutorials usually still runs, with deprecations phased in over multiple releases.

docsQuality.why: matplotlib.org has extensive tutorials, a full API reference, and a large example gallery, but the sheer volume plus the two-API split makes finding the current recommended way harder than it should be.

maintenance.why: NumFOCUS-sponsored with a large contributor base, CI across multiple platforms, and the repo pushed August 2026; 3.11.x patch releases continue steadily.

ecosystem.why: About 58M weekly downloads and the render layer for pandas, seaborn, and much of scientific Python; third-party styles, colormaps, and backend integrations are abundant.

patterns.title: Basic line plot, object-oriented style
patterns.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, np.sin(x), label="sin")
ax.plot(x, np.cos(x), label="cos")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
patterns.note: Prefer fig, ax = plt.subplots() over bare plt.plot from the start; every serious customization later needs the ax object anyway.

patterns.title: Save a figure to file
patterns.snippet:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.plot(x, y)
fig.savefig("chart.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
fig.savefig("chart.svg", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)
patterns.note: Call savefig before plt.show(), not after; show can clear the figure and you end up saving a blank image.

patterns.title: Multiple panels in one figure
patterns.snippet:
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 8), sharex=True)
axs[0, 0].plot(x, y1)
axs[0, 1].scatter(x, y2, s=8)
axs[1, 0].hist(y1, bins=30)
axs[1, 1].bar(["a", "b", "c"], [3, 1, 2])
fig.tight_layout()
patterns.note: axs is a 2D numpy array here; with a single row or column it is 1D, which changes the indexing and trips people up.

patterns.title: Label axes, title, and legend
patterns.snippet:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y, label="revenue")
ax.set_xlabel("Month")
ax.set_ylabel("USD (thousands)")
ax.set_title("Monthly revenue")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=False)
patterns.note: On Axes objects the methods are set_xlabel and set_title; the shorter plt.xlabel names only exist on the pyplot state machine.

patterns.title: Scatter with color mapping and colorbar
patterns.snippet:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sc = ax.scatter(x, y, c=values, cmap="viridis", s=20)
fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, label="temperature")
patterns.note: The colorbar needs the mappable returned by scatter; calling fig.colorbar() without it is the classic error here.

patterns.title: Bar chart with readable labels
patterns.snippet:
labels = ["alpha", "beta", "gamma", "delta"]
counts = [12, 31, 7, 24]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
bars = ax.bar(labels, counts)
ax.bar_label(bars, padding=3)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45)
patterns.note: ax.bar_label writes the value above each bar; for many categories consider ax.barh, which keeps labels horizontal and legible.

patterns.title: Histogram of a distribution
patterns.snippet:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(data, bins=40, edgecolor="white", alpha=0.8)
ax.axvline(data.mean(), color="red", linestyle="--", label="mean")
ax.legend()
patterns.note: The default of 10 bins hides structure in most real datasets; pass an integer, a sequence of edges, or bins="auto".

patterns.title: Plot a time series with readable dates
patterns.snippet:
import matplotlib.dates as mdates

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(dates, values)
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator())
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b %Y"))
fig.autofmt_xdate()
patterns.note: Pass real datetime or numpy datetime64 values, not strings; strings plot as unordered categories and the axis becomes nonsense.

patterns.title: Render on a server with no display
patterns.snippet:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # before importing pyplot
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(range(10))
fig.savefig("/tmp/out.png")
plt.close(fig)
patterns.note: The backend must be set before pyplot is first imported; the MPLBACKEND=Agg environment variable does the same without code changes.

patterns.title: Apply a built-in style sheet
patterns.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.style.use("ggplot")
print(plt.style.available)  # list all styles

with plt.style.context("dark_background"):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(x, y)
patterns.note: plt.style.use is global for the process; the context manager form scopes a style to one figure without leaking.

patterns.title: Two y-axes on one plot
patterns.snippet:
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots()
ax1.plot(x, revenue, color="tab:blue")
ax1.set_ylabel("revenue", color="tab:blue")

ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.plot(x, users, color="tab:orange")
ax2.set_ylabel("users", color="tab:orange")
patterns.note: Legends do not merge across twins automatically; collect handles from both axes and call ax1.legend(h1 + h2, l1 + l2).

patterns.title: Annotate a specific data point
patterns.snippet:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y)
ax.annotate(
    "launch day",
    xy=(x[42], y[42]),
    xytext=(x[42] + 1, y[42] + 10),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"),
)
patterns.note: xy is the point the arrow targets and xytext is where the label sits; in data coordinates by default, switchable via textcoords.

guide.whatIs: The official TypeScript SDK for the Model Context Protocol, the standard that lets AI applications (Claude, Cursor, VS Code, and most agent frameworks) talk to external tools, resources, and prompts through a common wire format. You use it to build MCP servers that expose your tools to any MCP client, or MCP clients that consume them, over stdio or Streamable HTTP. Important context: this package is the v1 line. The project's main branch is now v2, which splits the SDK into @modelcontextprotocol/server and @modelcontextprotocol/client, targeting the 2026-07-28 spec.
useIf: You maintain an existing MCP server or client built on the 1.x API and need continued bug and security fixes, which the team has committed to for at least 6 months after the v2 release
You depend on tooling, templates, or hosting platforms that still expect the single @modelcontextprotocol/sdk package and its 1.x import paths
You want the reference implementation of the protocol in TypeScript, with both server and client sides, stdio and Streamable HTTP transports, and OAuth helpers in one package
You are pinned to Zod-shaped tool schemas that 1.x uses directly (v2 moved to Standard Schema, which accepts Zod v4, Valibot, or ArkType)
skipIf: You are starting a new project today: the maintainers call v2 the stable release line, and it ships as separate @modelcontextprotocol/server and @modelcontextprotocol/client packages implementing the 2026-07-28 spec; building new work on 1.x buys you a migration
You want a lean dependency tree: the 1.x package pulls in express, hono, ajv, jose, cors, and more even if you only build a stdio server
Your stack is Python: the official mcp package (and FastMCP, now part of it) is the native path, not this SDK behind a subprocess
You expect a settled API: the MCP spec itself still revs roughly twice a year, and SDK majors track spec releases, so churn is structural, not incidental
guide.setupReality: npm install @modelcontextprotocol/sdk zod and you can have a stdio server running in 20 lines; Node 18+ required and zod (v3.25+ or v4) is a peer dependency you install yourself. The annoyances: all imports use explicit .js subpaths (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/mcp.js) which trips up TypeScript configs without moduleResolution node16/bundler; the package drags in a large dependency set including express and hono whether you use HTTP or not; Streamable HTTP session management (session IDs, resumability, DNS-rebinding protection) is your code to wire; and with v2 now published, a growing share of docs, examples, and blog posts show APIs that do not exist in 1.x.

alternatives.name: @modelcontextprotocol/server
alternatives.when: New MCP servers should start here: the v2 stable line for the 2026-07-28 spec, with Standard Schema support

alternatives.name: fastmcp
alternatives.when: You want a higher-level TypeScript framework with sessions, auth, and CLI testing conveniences on top of MCP

alternatives.name: mcp
alternatives.when: Your tools live in Python; this is the official Python SDK with the FastMCP decorator API built in

guide.verdict: The canonical way TypeScript speaks MCP, maintained by the protocol's own team, but the package is now the previous generation. Keep it for existing 1.x servers; start anything new on the v2 split packages.

apiStability.why: 1.x accumulated deprecations (tool() vs registerTool, SSE vs Streamable HTTP) and the jump to v2 is a package split with a new schema layer; the SDK majors track a spec that still changes twice a year.

docsQuality.why: A dedicated docs site with step-by-step first-server and first-client tutorials, an API reference, troubleshooting page, and runnable self-verifying examples; the v1/v2 split means you must constantly check which generation a page describes.

maintenance.why: Backed by the MCP steering group with Anthropic involvement, pushed to daily, and an explicit support policy: v1.x gets bug and security fixes for at least 6 months after v2's release.

ecosystem.why: MCP is the de facto tool protocol for AI apps; 54M weekly downloads, and every major client (Claude, VS Code, Cursor) plus thousands of published servers interoperate with servers built on this SDK.

patterns.title: Minimal stdio MCP server (1.x API)
patterns.note: In 1.x, inputSchema is a plain object of Zod fields (a raw shape), not z.object(...); v2 takes a full Standard Schema object instead.

patterns.title: Tool that returns structured content
patterns.note: When outputSchema is declared, you must return structuredContent that validates against it; keep the text content as a JSON mirror for older clients.

patterns.title: Expose a resource with a URI template
patterns.note: Resources are for data the client chooses to read; if the model should decide to fetch it during a conversation, make it a tool instead.

patterns.title: Reusable prompt template
patterns.note: Prompts surface as user-invoked commands (slash commands in many clients), not as things the model calls on its own.

patterns.title: Stateless Streamable HTTP server with Express
patterns.note: sessionIdGenerator: undefined disables sessions entirely; create a new server and transport per request or concurrent clients will collide.

patterns.title: Session-aware Streamable HTTP (multi-request clients)
patterns.note: You own the session store and its cleanup; also enable enableDnsRebindingProtection and allowedHosts for locally exposed servers.

patterns.title: Client: spawn a stdio server and call a tool
patterns.note: StdioClientTransport spawns the server as a child process; the server must never write logs to stdout or it corrupts the JSON-RPC stream (use stderr).

patterns.title: Client: connect to a remote server over Streamable HTTP
patterns.note: Streamable HTTP replaced the older SSE transport; for servers that still speak SSE only, 1.x keeps SSEClientTransport as a deprecated fallback.

patterns.title: Return a tool error the model can read
patterns.note: Throwing raises a protocol-level error; returning isError: true keeps the failure inside the tool result so the model can recover from it.

patterns.title: Enable, disable, and update tools after connect
patterns.note: registerTool returns a handle; enable/disable/update automatically send tools/listChanged so connected clients refresh.

patterns.title: Send log messages to the client
patterns.note: Declare the logging capability at construction; console.log is not an option on stdio transports because stdout carries the protocol.

guide.whatIs: The official MongoDB driver for Node.js, maintained by MongoDB Inc. It is the low-level client: you get a connection pool, typed CRUD methods on collections, aggregation pipelines, transactions, change streams, and BSON handling, with first-class TypeScript generics for your document shapes. There is no schema layer, no validation, no model classes; documents go in and come out as plain objects with BSON types like ObjectId and Decimal128. Every higher-level MongoDB tool in the Node ecosystem (Mongoose included) sits on top of this driver, so learning its API pays off even if you add an ODM later.
useIf: You want direct control over queries, indexes, and aggregation pipelines without an ODM translating for you
You already validate data at the application boundary (zod, JSON Schema, or MongoDB server-side validation) and do not need Mongoose's schema layer
You need driver-level features quickly: change streams, transactions, client-side field level encryption, or the newest server capabilities land here first
You care about dependency weight: the driver has three runtime deps, all MongoDB-owned
skipIf: Your team relies on schemas, middleware hooks, and populate(); rebuilding those on the raw driver is real work and Mongoose already does it
You are on an older Node: v7 of the driver requires Node >=20.19.0, and recent majors keep raising the floor
You dislike frequent major versions: the driver has shipped several majors in recent years (v7 has its own upgrade guide) and each one deprecates or removes API surface
Your data is fundamentally relational with many joins and constraints; a SQL database with an ORM will fight you less than $lookup pipelines
You need to file bugs in GitHub Issues; the project tracks everything in MongoDB's JIRA, which adds friction
guide.setupReality: npm install mongodb is clean: three dependencies and no native builds by default. The catch is the optional peer dependency list (kerberos, mongodb-client-encryption, @mongodb-js/zstd, snappy, socks, gcp-metadata, aws credential providers); npm prints noisy warnings for features you may never use, and the moment you do need Kerberos auth or field-level encryption you are compiling native modules. Budget time for connection-string tuning too: pool sizes, serverSelectionTimeoutMS, and TLS options are where most production incidents hide. Node >=20.19.0 is enforced for v7.

alternatives.name: mongoose
alternatives.when: You want schemas, validation, middleware, and populate() on top of MongoDB and accept the abstraction cost

alternatives.name: prisma
alternatives.when: You want a typed data layer with schema migrations across databases; its MongoDB support covers common CRUD but not the full aggregation surface

alternatives.name: postgres
alternatives.when: Your data is relational; this driver plus PostgreSQL is a simpler long-term bet than modelling relations in MongoDB

guide.verdict: If you use MongoDB from Node, this driver is not optional, the only question is whether you put Mongoose on top. Use it bare when you want control and few dependencies; add an ODM when your team wants schemas and hooks.

apiStability.why: Follows semver strictly and documents every breaking change with per-major upgrade guides, but majors arrive often (v7 is current, released within the last year of majors v5/v6) and each one raises the Node floor or removes callbacks-era API.

docsQuality.why: The official docs site covers fundamentals, usage examples, and an API reference, plus MongoDB University courses; quality is high but content is spread across docs, API site, and upgrade notes in the repo.

maintenance.why: Corporate-backed team with daily activity (pushed 2026-08-03), only 31 open GitHub issues because triage happens in JIRA, signed releases with npm provenance, and a published semver policy.

ecosystem.why: 14.8M weekly downloads and it underpins Mongoose and most MongoDB tooling in Node; the ecosystem is deep but MongoDB-shaped, so it is smaller than the SQL world's collective tooling.

patterns.title: Connect and reuse one client
patterns.note: Create one MongoClient per process and reuse it; it manages a pool internally, so per-request clients exhaust connections.

patterns.title: Type documents with generics
patterns.note: Types are compile-time only; the driver does zero runtime validation of what you insert.

patterns.title: Insert one and many
patterns.note: ordered: false keeps inserting past duplicate-key errors instead of stopping at the first failure.

patterns.title: Query with filter, projection, sort
patterns.snippet:
const recent = await users
  .find({ createdAt: { $gte: new Date('2026-01-01') } })
  .project({ email: 1 })
  .sort({ createdAt: -1 })
  .limit(20)
  .toArray()
patterns.note: find() returns a lazy cursor; nothing hits the server until toArray(), for-await, or next().

patterns.title: Look up by _id
patterns.snippet:
import { ObjectId } from 'mongodb'

const user = await users.findOne({ _id: new ObjectId(idString) })
patterns.note: String ids never match ObjectId fields; forgetting the wrapper is the classic silent empty-result bug.

patterns.title: Update with $set and upsert
patterns.snippet:
await users.updateOne(
  { email: 'a@b.com' },
  { $set: { plan: 'pro' }, $setOnInsert: { createdAt: new Date() } },
  { upsert: true },
)
patterns.note: Passing a plain object without update operators throws; replaceOne is the API for full-document replacement.

patterns.title: Atomically update and return the doc
patterns.note: Since v6 this returns the document directly (or null); older code expecting result.value breaks.

patterns.title: Run an aggregation pipeline
patterns.snippet:
const totals = await orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: 'paid' } },
  { $group: { _id: '$userId', total: { $sum: '$amount' } } },
  { $sort: { total: -1 } },
  { $limit: 10 },
]).toArray()
patterns.note: Put $match first so indexes apply; stages after $group run on unindexed in-memory data.

patterns.title: Create indexes at startup
patterns.snippet:
await users.createIndex({ email: 1 }, { unique: true })
await orders.createIndex({ userId: 1, createdAt: -1 })
patterns.note: createIndex is a no-op if the identical index exists, so calling it on boot is safe and common.

patterns.title: Multi-document transaction
patterns.note: Every operation inside must pass { session } or it silently runs outside the transaction; requires a replica set.

patterns.title: React to live data changes
patterns.note: Change streams need a replica set or Atlas; on a standalone mongod watch() errors immediately.

patterns.title: Batch mixed writes
patterns.snippet:
await users.bulkWrite([
  { insertOne: { document: { email: 'x@y.com', createdAt: new Date() } } },
  { updateOne: { filter: { email: 'a@b.com' }, update: { $set: { plan: 'free' } } } },
  { deleteOne: { filter: { email: 'old@z.com' } } },
])
patterns.note: One round trip for many writes; with ordered: false the server executes what it can and reports all errors together.

guide.whatIs: The standard MongoDB object modeling layer (ODM) for Node.js, built on top of the official MongoDB driver. You define schemas that add structure to schemaless collections: types, validators, defaults, getters and setters, indexes, middleware hooks, instance methods, and populate for pseudo-joins between collections. Documents you load become full model instances with save(), change tracking, and validation. It supports Node.js with alpha-level Deno support, and Mongoose 9.0 shipped in November 2025.
useIf: You are on MongoDB with Node.js and want schema validation, casting, and defaults enforced at the application layer
You use lifecycle hooks (pre-save, pre-find), virtuals, and populate rather than hand-writing that plumbing over the raw driver
Your team benefits from the plugin ecosystem (pagination, soft delete, autopopulate) and a well-trodden path with years of Stack Overflow answers
You want one place where document shape, indexes, and business rules for a collection live together
skipIf: You are TypeScript-first; you end up describing every model twice (interface plus schema) and keeping them in sync by hand, unless you add another layer like Typegoose
You might not stay on MongoDB; Prisma and other multi-database ORMs keep the exit door open, Mongoose does not
You need raw driver throughput; hydrating full Mongoose documents has real overhead, and teams end up sprinkling .lean() on most read paths anyway
You dislike the magic: command buffering that hides a dead connection until timeouts fire, automatic collection-name pluralization, and hook-driven side effects all surprise people in production
guide.setupReality: npm install mongoose, no native builds, works everywhere Node does. The friction is conceptual, not install-time. The default connection is a singleton: models registered via mongoose.model() are bound to it, and if you use createConnection() you must register models on that connection or saves silently target a connection that was never opened (the README calls this out explicitly). Command buffering means your app boots fine with a wrong URI and only fails later with timeouts. Collection names are auto-pluralized (model Ticket writes to tickets). Majors arrive regularly, 9.0 in November 2025, each with a documented list of backwards breaking changes you actually need to read before upgrading.

alternatives.name: mongodb
alternatives.when: You want the official driver with no ODM layer: full control, no schema magic, best performance

alternatives.name: prisma
alternatives.when: You want generated TypeScript types from one schema file and the option to move between databases later

alternatives.name: @typegoose/typegoose
alternatives.when: You are committed to Mongoose but want class-based models so TypeScript types and schemas stay as one definition

guide.verdict: Still the default ODM for MongoDB plus Node and dependable at that job, with very active maintenance. If your project is TypeScript-heavy or your database choice is not settled, evaluate Prisma before committing.

apiStability.why: The core schema-model-query API has been recognizable for a decade, but majors land roughly yearly (9.0 in November 2025) and each ships a real backwards-breaking-changes list; callback APIs were removed entirely in v7.

docsQuality.why: mongoosejs.com pairs topic guides with generated API docs and a migration guide per major; middleware ordering and connection edge cases are documented but still routinely send people to Stack Overflow.

maintenance.why: Pushed to within hours of this review, 400+ contributors, backed by Automattic with commercial support via Tidelift; issues get triaged fast.

ecosystem.why: Hundreds of community plugins on the official plugin search site plus session stores, seeders, and test runners like mongodb-memory-server; smaller than the SQL ORM world but deep for MongoDB.

patterns.title: Connect to MongoDB
patterns.snippet:
const mongoose = require("mongoose");

await mongoose.connect("mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/my_database");
patterns.note: Commands are buffered until the connection opens, so a bad URI does not fail at startup; it fails later as operation timeouts. Use 127.0.0.1 instead of localhost if local connects hang.

patterns.title: Define a schema and model
patterns.note: The model name is singular; Mongoose pluralizes it for the collection, so model("Ticket", ...) reads and writes the tickets collection.

patterns.title: Create and save a document
patterns.note: Validation runs on save/create by default; a failed validator rejects the promise with a ValidationError listing every bad path.

patterns.title: Find with filters, sort, and limit
patterns.note: Queries are thenables, not promises; awaiting works, but calling .then() twice re-executes the query.

patterns.title: Fast read-only queries with lean()
patterns.snippet: const rows = await BlogPost.find({ published: true }).lean();
patterns.note: lean() returns plain JS objects instead of Mongoose documents: much faster and lighter, but no getters, virtuals, defaults, or save().

patterns.title: Atomic find-and-update
patterns.note: Without new: true you get the pre-update document back; update validators only run when you pass runValidators, and they see the update, not the whole doc.

patterns.title: Populate referenced documents
patterns.note: populate is extra queries under the hood, not a server-side join; populating in a loop over N docs is a classic N+1 problem.

patterns.title: Pre and post middleware
patterns.note: In document middleware `this` is the document; in query middleware (find, updateOne by default) `this` is the query object. Getting that wrong is the top middleware bug.

patterns.title: Embedded subdocuments
patterns.note: Subdocuments get their own validators, defaults, and middleware, but they only persist when the parent document is saved.

patterns.title: Multi-document transaction
patterns.note: Transactions require a replica set or mongos; they throw on a plain standalone mongod, which is exactly what most local dev setups run.

patterns.title: Schema field literally named type
patterns.note: A bare `type: String` inside a nested object makes Mongoose treat the whole parent as a String path; wrap it as { type: String } to get a real nested field.

patterns.title: Models on a separate connection
patterns.note: Register the model on the connection (conn.model), not mongoose.model; otherwise it binds to the default connection that may never have been opened.

guide.whatIs: mypy is the original static type checker for Python and the reference implementation of PEP 484 type hints. You annotate your code, run mypy over it, and it reports type errors without executing anything: passing a str where an int is expected, forgetting a None check, breaking a Protocol. It is built for gradual typing, so you can annotate one module at a time and leave the rest dynamic. It ships with a daemon (dmypy) for fast incremental re-checks on large codebases, error codes you can suppress individually, and it is itself compiled with mypyc, which the project says makes it about 4x faster than running interpreted. It lives under the python GitHub org and effectively defines how Python typing behaves in practice.
