You want typed environment and settings parsing via the companion pydantic-settings package
skipIf: You just need lightweight typed classes with no external-data parsing; dataclasses or attrs do that with less magic and no compiled dependency
You are on a hot pure-serialization path where every microsecond counts; msgspec benchmarks faster for plain encode/decode work
Your codebase is full of Pydantic v1 idioms; v2 renamed most of the API (.dict() to model_dump(), @validator to @field_validator) and migrating a large app is real work, not a find-and-replace
You expect validation on mutation: models do not revalidate on attribute assignment unless you enable validate_assignment, so a validated object can silently drift invalid
guide.setupReality: pip install pydantic pulls prebuilt pydantic-core wheels for every common platform, so installation is painless; only unusual targets ever compile Rust. The real setup cost is conceptual: learning the v2 spelling (model_validate, model_dump, Field, ConfigDict) when a decade of StackOverflow answers teach v1, remembering that BaseSettings moved to the separate pydantic-settings package, and that email validation needs the pydantic[email] extra. Python 3.9+ is required.

alternatives.name: msgspec
alternatives.when: Raw JSON encode/decode speed matters more than validator features

alternatives.name: attrs
alternatives.when: You want plain typed classes without runtime coercion or a compiled core

alternatives.name: marshmallow
alternatives.when: You prefer schema classes kept separate from your domain objects

guide.verdict: The de facto standard for data validation in Python and a safe dependency: fast, thoroughly documented, and everywhere. Learn the v2 idioms first and ignore tutorials written before 2023.

apiStability.why: The v2 API has been stable since 2023 and v1 compatibility ships inside the package (from pydantic import v1), but the v1 to v2 break was large and outdated examples still circulate widely.

docsQuality.why: docs.pydantic.dev has a full concepts guide, API reference, migration guide, and an llms.txt; validation errors link to documented error codes.

maintenance.why: Developed by a funded company (Pydantic Inc.) with a full-time team, daily pushes, and frequent patch releases; 2.13.4 current at review time.

ecosystem.why: FastAPI, the OpenAI SDK, LangChain, and thousands of other packages build on it; pydantic-settings and pydantic-extra-types extend the core, and roughly 274M weekly downloads speak for adoption.

patterns.title: Define and instantiate a model
patterns.snippet:
from datetime import datetime
from pydantic import BaseModel

class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str = 'John Doe'
    signup_ts: datetime | None = None
    friends: list[int] = []

user = User(id='123', friends=[1, '2'])  # coerced to ints
patterns.note: Mutable defaults like [] are safe here; Pydantic copies them per instance, unlike plain dataclasses.

patterns.title: Validate a dict or raw JSON
patterns.snippet:
user = User.model_validate({'id': 123, 'name': 'Ana'})
user = User.model_validate_json('{"id": 123, "name": "Ana"}')
patterns.note: model_validate_json parses JSON inside the Rust core; it beats json.loads followed by model_validate.

patterns.title: Dump a model to dict or JSON
patterns.snippet:
user.model_dump()                      # dict
user.model_dump_json()                 # JSON string
user.model_dump(exclude_none=True, by_alias=True)
patterns.note: The v1 names .dict() and .json() are gone in v2; model_dump_json returns str, not bytes.

patterns.title: Constrain fields with Field
patterns.snippet:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Product(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=100)
    price: float = Field(gt=0)
    sku: str = Field(pattern=r'^[A-Z]{3}-\d{4}$')
patterns.note: Constraints run at validation time only; later attribute assignment skips them unless validate_assignment is enabled.

patterns.title: Add a custom field validator
patterns.note: Return the (possibly transformed) value; a raised ValueError becomes a ValidationError with the field's location.

patterns.title: Validate across fields
patterns.note: mode='after' receives the constructed model; mode='before' receives the raw input dict instead.

patterns.title: Nest models
patterns.note: Nested dicts validate recursively, and errors carry the full path, like addresses.0.city.

patterns.title: Load settings from environment variables
patterns.snippet:
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    database_url: str
    debug: bool = False

settings = Settings()  # reads DATABASE_URL and DEBUG from the env
patterns.note: BaseSettings lives in the separate pydantic-settings package since v2; importing it from pydantic raises.

patterns.title: Discriminated unions
patterns.note: The discriminator keeps union validation fast and error messages readable; without it every branch gets tried.

patterns.title: Validate non-model types with TypeAdapter
patterns.snippet:
from pydantic import TypeAdapter

adapter = TypeAdapter(list[dict[str, int]])
data = adapter.validate_python([{'a': '1'}])
schema = adapter.json_schema()
patterns.note: Build the adapter once at module level, not per call; construction is the expensive part.

patterns.title: Emit JSON Schema
patterns.snippet: schema = User.model_json_schema()
patterns.note: This is the same output FastAPI uses for OpenAPI and what you hand to LLM tool-calling APIs.

patterns.title: Turn off type coercion
patterns.snippet:
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class StrictUser(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)
    id: int  # '123' now fails instead of coercing
patterns.note: Default lax mode coerces '123' to 123; strict mode rejects it, and you can also set strict per field via Field(strict=True).

guide.whatIs: PyJWT is the standard Python implementation of JSON Web Tokens (RFC 7519). It encodes and decodes the compact signed-token format, verifying signatures and registered claims like exp, aud, and iss. It is a focused signing and verification library, not an auth framework: sessions, OAuth flows, and user models are your problem. Symmetric HS256 works out of the box; RSA and ECDSA algorithms need the optional cryptography dependency.
useIf: You issue or verify JWTs in a Python API and want the boring, widely audited default that most frameworks build on
You verify RS256/ES256 tokens against a JWKS endpoint (Auth0, Cognito, Entra ID); PyJWKClient handles key fetching and caching
You want a light dependency: the base install is pure Python, and cryptography is only pulled in when you opt into asymmetric algorithms
skipIf: You need JWE (encrypted tokens) or the wider JOSE suite; PyJWT does signed tokens only, so use joserfc or Authlib for the rest
You actually want login sessions or OAuth, not raw tokens; a framework-level auth library handles claims, refresh, and rotation with fewer footguns
You expect the library to stop JWT misuse by itself; it makes the safe path available, but skipping audience checks or shipping a weak secret is still on you
guide.setupReality: pip install pyjwt covers HS256 end to end. The classic trip-ups: RS256 and friends raise at runtime until you install the pyjwt[crypto] extra, jwt.decode in 2.x demands an explicit algorithms list (code ported from the 1.x era breaks right there), and there is an unrelated package literally named jwt on PyPI that also imports as jwt, so one typo in requirements gets you a different library with a colliding module name.

alternatives.name: joserfc
alternatives.when: Full JOSE support including JWE, when signed-only tokens stop being enough

alternatives.name: authlib
alternatives.when: OAuth and OIDC client/server flows with JOSE built in

alternatives.name: python-jose
alternatives.when: A JOSE-shaped API some older stacks standardized on; check its maintenance status before adopting

guide.verdict: The correct default for signing and verifying JWTs in Python. The moment you need encryption, key management, or login flows, step up to joserfc or Authlib instead of bolting extras onto PyJWT.

apiStability.why: The 2.x API has been stable for years; the notable breaking change was the 1.x to 2.x tightening (string output from encode, mandatory algorithms on decode), which was a security improvement.

docsQuality.why: readthedocs covers usage, algorithm options, and JWKS with runnable examples; it is short, but so is the library surface, and the README quickstart is enough for the common case.

maintenance.why: Steady releases under jpadilla with pushes as recent as 2026-08-03, plus a CI badge and codecov; it is a small-maintainer project rather than a company-backed one, hence not a 5.

ecosystem.why: At roughly 166M weekly downloads it is the assumed JWT layer across Python web frameworks and auth providers' Python examples.

patterns.title: Sign a token with HS256
patterns.snippet:
import jwt

token = jwt.encode({"sub": "user-123"}, "secret", algorithm="HS256")
# 'eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...'
patterns.note: encode returns a str in 2.x (it was bytes in 1.x); use a long random secret, not a password.

patterns.title: Decode and verify a token
patterns.snippet:
import jwt

payload = jwt.decode(token, "secret", algorithms=["HS256"])
patterns.note: algorithms is mandatory in 2.x and must be a fixed allowlist; never derive it from the token header, that is the classic algorithm-confusion attack.

patterns.title: Issue and check expiring tokens
patterns.snippet:
import jwt
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
token = jwt.encode(
    {"sub": "user-123", "iat": now, "exp": now + timedelta(minutes=15)},
    "secret",
    algorithm="HS256",
)

try:
    jwt.decode(token, "secret", algorithms=["HS256"])
except jwt.ExpiredSignatureError:
    ...  # force re-auth
patterns.note: datetime objects are converted to epoch seconds for you; exp is only enforced if the claim is present in the token.

patterns.title: Verify audience and issuer
patterns.snippet:
payload = jwt.decode(
    token,
    "secret",
    algorithms=["HS256"],
    audience="my-api",
    issuer="https://auth.example.com",
)
patterns.note: If the token carries an aud claim and you pass no audience, decode raises InvalidAudienceError rather than silently passing.

patterns.title: Sign and verify with RS256
patterns.snippet:
import jwt

with open("private.pem") as f:
    private_key = f.read()
with open("public.pem") as f:
    public_key = f.read()

token = jwt.encode({"sub": "user-123"}, private_key, algorithm="RS256")
payload = jwt.decode(token, public_key, algorithms=["RS256"])
patterns.note: Requires pip install pyjwt[crypto]; without the extra you get an ImportError-flavored error only when an RSA algorithm is first used.

patterns.title: Verify against a JWKS endpoint (OIDC)
patterns.snippet:
import jwt
from jwt import PyJWKClient

jwks_client = PyJWKClient("https://example.auth0.com/.well-known/jwks.json")

signing_key = jwks_client.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token)
payload = jwt.decode(
    token,
    signing_key.key,
    algorithms=["RS256"],
    audience="my-api",
)
patterns.note: Construct PyJWKClient once at module or app scope; it caches keys, and rebuilding it per request refetches the JWKS every time.

patterns.title: Tolerate clock skew
patterns.snippet:
payload = jwt.decode(
    token,
    "secret",
    algorithms=["HS256"],
    leeway=10,  # seconds
)
patterns.note: leeway applies to exp, nbf, and iat checks; a few seconds covers real-world clock drift between servers.

patterns.title: Require specific claims to exist
patterns.snippet:
payload = jwt.decode(
    token,
    "secret",
    algorithms=["HS256"],
    options={"require": ["exp", "sub"]},
)
patterns.note: require only checks presence, not validity; a token with exp still needs the normal expiry check, which decode does anyway.

patterns.title: Read the header to pick a key
patterns.snippet:
import jwt

header = jwt.get_unverified_header(token)
key = key_store[header["kid"]]
payload = jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=["RS256"])
patterns.note: The header is attacker-controlled until the signature is verified; use it only for key lookup, never for trust decisions.

patterns.title: Catch token errors broadly
patterns.note: InvalidTokenError is the base class for the whole family (signature, audience, issuer, decode errors), so order the except blocks specific-first.

guide.whatIs: pytest is the de facto standard test framework for Python. You write plain functions with plain assert statements, and pytest rewrites those asserts so failures show the actual values on each side instead of a bare AssertionError. Around that core it adds auto-discovery of test files, fixtures (dependency-injected setup/teardown resources declared once and requested by argument name), parametrization for running one test across many inputs, and a hook-based plugin architecture with over 1300 external plugins. It also runs existing unittest suites out of the box, so adoption in a legacy codebase does not require a rewrite. Current major is 9, requiring Python 3.10+ or PyPy3.
useIf: You want readable tests: plain assert with detailed failure introspection instead of memorizing self.assertEqual and friends
Your tests share expensive resources (databases, temp dirs, servers); fixtures with scopes and yield-based teardown handle this far better than setUp/tearDown
You need to run one test across many inputs; @pytest.mark.parametrize turns a table of cases into individually reported tests
You have an existing unittest suite; pytest runs it unchanged, so you can adopt incrementally
You want ecosystem depth: coverage, parallel execution (pytest-xdist), async support, and framework integrations all exist as maintained plugins
skipIf: Your organization mandates stdlib-only tooling; unittest ships with Python and pytest's assertion rewriting and fixture injection are extra machinery and magic to audit
You dislike implicit behavior: fixtures are injected by matching parameter names against conftest.py hierarchies, and in large codebases tracing where a fixture comes from is genuinely annoying
You are pinned to an old interpreter; pytest 9 requires Python 3.10+, and older interpreter versions cap you at older pytest lines
Your suite leans on many third-party plugins; pytest majors deprecate and remove hooks on a cycle, and every major release strands some unmaintained plugins until you replace them
Non-programmers write your acceptance tests; keyword-driven tools like robotframework fit that workflow better than Python test functions
guide.setupReality: pip install pytest is quick and pulls only small pure-Python dependencies (iniconfig, packaging, pluggy, pygments, plus colorama on Windows). The annoyances are configuration and discovery, not installation: config can live in pytest.ini, pyproject.toml, tox.ini, or setup.cfg and figuring out which one wins takes a docs trip; rootdir and import-mode discovery rules surprise people with duplicate-basename test files or missing __init__.py packages; and assertion rewriting occasionally confuses tools that import test modules directly. Plan a plugin compatibility check before every major upgrade, since removed hooks break older plugins.

alternatives.name: hypothesis
alternatives.when: You want property-based testing that generates inputs and shrinks failures, alongside or inside pytest

alternatives.name: nose2
alternatives.when: You are maintaining a legacy nose-style suite and need a minimal unittest-based runner

alternatives.name: robotframework
alternatives.when: Non-developers write keyword-driven acceptance tests rather than Python code

guide.verdict: The right default for testing Python, full stop; 265M weekly downloads and the plugin ecosystem back that up. The only real debate is stdlib purists choosing unittest, and even they usually end up running it under pytest.

apiStability.why: Core usage (assert, fixtures, parametrize) has been stable for many years and deprecations are warned about across releases before removal; majors like 8 and 9 do remove long-deprecated hooks, which periodically breaks older plugins.

docsQuality.why: docs.pytest.org has getting-started, how-to guides, explanation pages, and a full reference including a generated list of 1300+ plugins; failure output itself is documented and the changelog is thorough.

maintenance.why: Active since 2004, pushed 2026-08-03, with a maintainer team, Open Collective and Tidelift funding, a security advisory process, and a steady release cadence on the 9.x line.

ecosystem.why: 265M weekly downloads, 1300+ external plugins per the README, and first-class integration points in virtually every Python framework and CI system.

patterns.title: Write and run a first test
patterns.snippet:
# content of test_sample.py
def inc(x):
    return x + 1

def test_answer():
    assert inc(3) == 4

# run:  pytest            (discovers test_*.py files)
# or:   pytest test_sample.py -v
patterns.note: Files must match test_*.py or *_test.py and functions must start with test_ or discovery skips them silently.

patterns.title: Share setup with a fixture
patterns.note: Code after yield is the teardown; requesting the fixture is just naming an argument, there is no import of it.

patterns.title: Run one test over many inputs
patterns.note: Each tuple becomes a separately reported test; stack parametrize decorators to get the full cross product.

patterns.title: Assert that code raises an exception
patterns.snippet:
import pytest

def test_divide_by_zero():
    with pytest.raises(ZeroDivisionError):
        1 / 0

def test_error_message():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match='invalid literal'):
        int('not a number')
patterns.note: match is a regex search against the exception string, not an exact-equality check.

patterns.title: Use a temporary directory
patterns.snippet:
def test_write_config(tmp_path):
    cfg = tmp_path / 'config.toml'
    cfg.write_text('[app]\nname = "demo"\n')
    assert cfg.read_text().startswith('[app]')
patterns.note: tmp_path is a built-in fixture yielding a fresh pathlib.Path per test; prefer it over the older tmpdir (py.path) fixture.

patterns.title: Patch environment and attributes safely
patterns.snippet:
def test_reads_env(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv('API_KEY', 'test-key')
    monkeypatch.setattr('myapp.client.timeout', 1)
    assert myapp.client.build_headers()['Authorization'] == 'Bearer test-key'
patterns.note: All monkeypatch changes are undone automatically after the test; no try/finally cleanup needed.

patterns.title: Skip tests or mark expected failures
patterns.note: An xfail test that unexpectedly passes reports as XPASS; add strict=True to turn that into a failure so fixes get noticed.

patterns.title: Share fixtures across files with conftest.py
patterns.note: conftest.py fixtures are visible to all tests in that directory and below; scope='session' builds the fixture once per run.

patterns.title: Run a subset of the suite
patterns.snippet:
pytest tests/test_api.py::test_login      # one test by node id
pytest -k 'login and not slow'            # match test names by expression
pytest -m integration                     # only tests marked @pytest.mark.integration
pytest --lf                               # only tests that failed last run
patterns.note: Custom marks must be registered in config (markers = ...) or pytest warns and, under strict markers, errors.

patterns.title: Compare floats without brittle equality
patterns.snippet:
import pytest

def test_math():
    assert 0.1 + 0.2 == pytest.approx(0.3)
    assert [0.1 + 0.2, 1.0] == pytest.approx([0.3, 1.0])
patterns.note: approx works on scalars, sequences, and dicts, with rel/abs tolerance arguments when the defaults are too tight.

patterns.title: Assert on printed output
patterns.note: readouterr() drains the buffer; call it once and keep the result, a second call returns empty output.

patterns.title: Run an existing unittest suite under pytest
patterns.snippet:
# no changes needed to the legacy suite
pytest tests/legacy/

# unittest classes gain pytest features gradually:
import unittest

class TestLegacy(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_old_style(self):
        self.assertEqual(1 + 1, 2)
patterns.note: unittest tests run as-is, but pytest fixtures cannot be injected into TestCase methods; migrate classes to plain functions to use them.

guide.whatIs: python-dotenv reads key-value pairs from a .env file and loads them into os.environ, so an app configured by environment variables (12-factor style) runs locally without you exporting a dozen variables by hand. That is the whole job: load_dotenv() for the common case, dotenv_values() when you want a dict without touching the environment, a small CLI (dotenv set/list/run), and a bash-like file format with quoting, multiline values, and ${VAR} interpolation.
useIf: Your app reads config from os.environ and you want local development to pick values up from a .env file automatically
You need layered config: merging .env.shared, .env.secret, and the real environment via dotenv_values() dicts
You want a dependency with zero required transitive packages that does exactly one thing
You use dotenv run to inject variables into any command without touching your shell profile
skipIf: You are configuring production on a real platform: Docker, systemd, Kubernetes, and every PaaS already inject environment variables, and a .env file there is just an unencrypted secrets file on disk
You want types and validation: pydantic-settings reads .env files and gives you typed, validated settings objects instead of raw strings
Your framework already loads .env: the Flask CLI and uvicorn --env-file do it for you, so calling load_dotenv() yourself can duplicate or conflict with that
You need actual secrets management: this is plaintext on disk, not a substitute for Vault, SOPS, or your cloud secret manager
guide.setupReality: pip install python-dotenv and call load_dotenv() before anything reads os.environ, which in practice means the first lines of your entrypoint; modules that read env vars at import time will beat a late call and see nothing. The gotchas are behavioral, not install: existing environment variables win unless you pass override=True, the default upward .env search behaves differently in notebooks and frozen apps, and quoting plus ${VAR} expansion rules differ from docker compose env-file parsing just enough to bite. Version 1.2 requires Python 3.10+.

alternatives.name: pydantic-settings
alternatives.when: You want typed, validated settings with .env support; the better default in new FastAPI-era codebases

alternatives.name: environs
alternatives.when: You want env parsing with casting and validation built in, without adopting pydantic

alternatives.name: python-decouple
alternatives.when: Similar .env loading with casting and defaults; popular in Django projects

alternatives.name: dynaconf
alternatives.when: Config has outgrown one flat file: multiple formats, environments, and secrets backends

guide.verdict: The boring, correct choice for local development configuration in Python and safe to adopt anywhere. Keep .env out of git, and use real environment variables or a secrets manager in production.

apiStability.why: load_dotenv and dotenv_values have kept the same shape for years; the 1.x line ships small additive releases, and the biggest recent change was dropping old Python versions.

docsQuality.why: The README is the documentation and it covers the file format, expansion rules, CLI, and edge cases like valueless variables well; there is no dedicated docs site, and some behavior details live in issues.

maintenance.why: Two named maintainers, last push July 2026, 8.8k stars, 106 open issues and PRs; the release cadence is slow, but the surface is tiny so that rarely matters in practice.

ecosystem.why: 187M weekly downloads and de facto standard status: Flask CLI integration and uvicorn --env-file go through it, and nearly every Python deployment tutorial assumes a .env file.

patterns.title: Load .env into the environment
patterns.snippet:
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()  # searches from the caller's directory upward

db_url = os.getenv("DATABASE_URL")
patterns.note: Call it before any module reads os.environ; variables already set in the environment win unless you pass override=True.

patterns.title: Let the file beat the environment
patterns.snippet:
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv(override=True)
patterns.note: Default is override=False, so a variable exported in your shell silently shadows the .env value; this flips the precedence.

patterns.title: Parse without touching os.environ
patterns.note: Keys declared with no value come back as None, while KEY= gives an empty string; code that expects strings everywhere should handle both.

patterns.title: Merge shared, secret, and real env
patterns.snippet:
import os
from dotenv import dotenv_values

config = {
    **dotenv_values(".env.shared"),
    **dotenv_values(".env.secret"),
    **os.environ,  # real environment wins
}
patterns.note: Straight from the README; later spreads win, so keep os.environ last if the actual environment should take precedence.

patterns.title: Load a specific .env file
patterns.snippet:
from pathlib import Path
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv(dotenv_path=Path(__file__).parent / ".env")
patterns.note: The default upward search keys off the calling file, which misbehaves in notebooks, REPLs, and frozen binaries; an explicit path is deterministic.

patterns.title: Search from the working directory
patterns.snippet:
from dotenv import load_dotenv, find_dotenv

load_dotenv(find_dotenv(usecwd=True))
patterns.note: usecwd=True searches from the current working directory instead of the library call site; useful under pytest and console entry points.

patterns.title: Load config from a string or socket
patterns.snippet:
from io import StringIO
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv(stream=StringIO("USER=foo\nEMAIL=foo@example.org"))
patterns.note: Lets you load config fetched from a network source or secrets API without writing a temp file.

patterns.title: Interpolate variables inside .env
patterns.snippet:
# .env
DOMAIN=example.org
ADMIN_EMAIL=admin@${DOMAIN}
ROOT_URL=${DOMAIN}/app
patterns.note: Only braced ${VAR} references expand; a bare $VAR stays a literal string.

patterns.title: Manage .env from the command line
patterns.snippet:
pip install "python-dotenv[cli]"
dotenv set USER foo
dotenv list --format=json
dotenv run -- python app.py
patterns.note: The dotenv command is behind the [cli] extra; a plain install does not ship it.

patterns.title: Read and write .env entries from code
patterns.snippet:
from dotenv import set_key, get_key, unset_key

set_key(".env", "API_KEY", "abc123")
print(get_key(".env", "API_KEY"))
unset_key(".env", "API_KEY")
patterns.note: set_key rewrites the file while preserving other lines; fine for setup scripts, wrong for anything with concurrent writers.

patterns.title: Disable loading globally
patterns.snippet: export PYTHON_DOTENV_DISABLED=1
patterns.note: Stops load_dotenv() from loading files or streams; the escape hatch when third-party code calls it in environments where .env must not load.

guide.whatIs: PyYAML is the standard YAML parser and emitter for Python: yaml.safe_load turns YAML text into dicts, lists, and scalars, yaml.dump goes the other way. It is a dependency of half the Python ecosystem (Ansible, Docker Compose tooling, CI config readers, Kubernetes clients) and at roughly 300 million downloads a week it is one of the most installed packages on PyPI. It implements the YAML 1.1 spec, with optional C-accelerated parsing through LibYAML bindings.
useIf: You need to read YAML config files, Kubernetes manifests, CI definitions, or anything else the infrastructure world writes in YAML
You want the zero-surprise choice: every tutorial, linter, and tool assumes PyYAML semantics, and it is probably already in your dependency tree
You parse large YAML files and can install the LibYAML C bindings (yaml.CSafeLoader) for a substantial speedup over the pure-Python parser
You only need load and dump; for that job the API has been unchanged and reliable for years
skipIf: You need to edit YAML and write it back preserving comments, ordering quirks, and formatting: PyYAML throws all of that away on load, ruamel.yaml is the round-trip tool

You need YAML 1.2 behavior: PyYAML implements YAML 1.1, so unquoted 'yes', 'no', 'on', and 'off' become booleans and other 1.1 scalar rules apply, which regularly corrupts things like country code 'NO'
You are choosing a config format for a new project you control: TOML has stdlib support via tomllib since Python 3.11 and avoids YAML's footguns entirely

You are tempted by yaml.load on untrusted input: full load can construct arbitrary Python objects, which the README itself warns about; if a code reviewer will not catch that, prefer a parser without the dangerous mode
You need new spec features to arrive: the issue tracker has a 350+ open issue and PR backlog and YAML 1.2 support has been an open request for years
guide.setupReality: pip install pyyaml just works because binary wheels ship for CPython on Linux, macOS, and Windows. The catch is the C accelerator: the wheels include LibYAML bindings when available, but yaml.load defaults to the pure-Python loader anyway, so you must explicitly pass CSafeLoader (with a try/except ImportError fallback) to get the speed you installed. Building from source without wheels needs a compiler and libyaml-dev headers. Historical trivia that still bites: version 6.0 broke installs for months in 2023 because of a Cython 3 build interaction on old pinned versions.

alternatives.name: ruamel.yaml
alternatives.when: You need round-trip editing that preserves comments and formatting, or YAML 1.2 semantics

alternatives.name: strictyaml
alternatives.when: You want a restricted, schema-validated YAML subset that removes implicit typing footguns entirely

guide.verdict: For reading YAML that other tools produce, PyYAML is the boring correct answer and safe_load is the only load you should ever type. For editing YAML in place or for strict 1.2 semantics it is the wrong tool, and ruamel.yaml exists precisely because of that.

apiStability.why: The load/dump API has been essentially frozen for a decade; the one real break was 5.1 making bare yaml.load warn and 6.0 requiring an explicit Loader, both security-motivated.

docsQuality.why: The official documentation is a wiki page last restructured years ago; it covers the API but reads like 2009, and critical guidance like the safe_load rule is easy to miss. Most people learn PyYAML from Stack Overflow.

maintenance.why: Maintained by the YAML community with recent pushes and a 6.0.3 release, but movement is slow: 350+ open issues and PRs, years between releases, and no progress toward YAML 1.2.

ecosystem.why: Roughly 300M weekly downloads and a dependency of Ansible-class tooling; YAML-adjacent Python code overwhelmingly assumes PyYAML behavior.

patterns.title: Parse YAML from a file
patterns.snippet:
import yaml

with open('config.yml') as f:
    config = yaml.safe_load(f)
patterns.note: Always safe_load. Plain yaml.load with a full loader can execute arbitrary object construction from untrusted input.

patterns.title: Write a dict out as YAML
patterns.snippet:
import yaml

text = yaml.safe_dump(
    data,
    sort_keys=False,
    default_flow_style=False,
    allow_unicode=True,
)
patterns.note: sort_keys defaults to True and will alphabetize your keys; set it False to keep insertion order.

patterns.title: Read a multi-document stream
patterns.note: Kubernetes-style files separated by --- need load_all; empty documents come back as None, so filter them.

patterns.title: Use the LibYAML C parser when available
patterns.note: safe_load never uses the C parser on its own; you must pass CSafeLoader explicitly, with a fallback for wheels built without LibYAML.

patterns.title: Serialize a custom class
patterns.note: Register against SafeDumper if you dump with safe_dump; registering on the default Dumper alone silently does nothing for safe_dump.

patterns.title: Parse a custom tag safely
patterns.note: Adding constructors to SafeLoader keeps safe_load safe while supporting the one tag you actually need.

patterns.title: Avoid the yes/no/on/off boolean trap
patterns.note: This is YAML 1.1 behavior, not a bug; quote any value that could look like a boolean, and quote version numbers like 3.10 too or they load as floats.

patterns.title: Load from and dump to strings
patterns.snippet:
import yaml

data = yaml.safe_load('a: 1\nb: [2, 3]')
text = yaml.safe_dump(data)  # returns a str when no stream given
patterns.note: dump writes to the stream argument if given and returns None in that case; only the no-stream form returns the string.

patterns.title: Dump multi-line strings as literal blocks
patterns.note: Without this, multi-line strings dump as quoted scalars full of \n escapes instead of readable | blocks.

patterns.title: Know what happens with duplicate keys
patterns.snippet:
import yaml

yaml.safe_load('a: 1\na: 2')  # {'a': 2}, no error
patterns.note: PyYAML silently keeps the last duplicate key; if duplicates should be errors, validate separately or use a stricter parser.

patterns.title: Reuse blocks with anchors and merge keys
patterns.snippet:
import yaml

doc = '''
defaults: &d
  retries: 3
  timeout: 10
prod:
  <<: *d
  timeout: 30
'''
yaml.safe_load(doc)['prod']  # {'retries': 3, 'timeout': 30}
patterns.note: Merge keys (<<) work on load, but dump never re-creates anchors from shared structure in a readable way; round-tripping loses them.

guide.whatIs: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of components. You describe what each state of the UI looks like, and React updates the DOM when your data changes. Components hold their own state and compose into bigger UIs, logic lives in JavaScript rather than templates, and the same model renders in the browser, on the server via Node, and on mobile through React Native. Note that the react package itself is only the component runtime; the actual DOM rendering lives in react-dom.
useIf: You are building an app with lots of interactive, stateful UI (dashboards, editors, feeds) rather than mostly-static pages
You want the largest hiring pool, component ecosystem, and answered-questions surface in frontend
You plan to share skills or code with React Native mobile apps
You need SSR or React Server Components, which you get through a framework such as Next.js or React Router framework mode
skipIf: Your site is mostly static content; you would ship and hydrate a client runtime for pages that never needed one
You want one framework that decides routing, data fetching, and state for you; React alone decides none of that, so the surrounding stack is a series of choices you have to make and maintain
You are payload-sensitive for small widgets; the real weight is react-dom, many times larger than the 2.8 kB react package, while preact offers the same component model in a fraction of the size
Your team resents churn; hooks, concurrent rendering, and Server Components each reshaped idiomatic React, and long-lived codebases end up carrying all three eras at once
guide.setupReality: The react package renders nothing by itself: you also install react-dom at a matching version, and JSX needs a build step, so in practice everyone starts from Vite or a framework rather than wiring the transform by hand. StrictMode double-invokes renders and effects in development, which surprises newcomers with duplicate fetches. React itself upgrades cleanly; the pain lives in the ecosystem, where peer dependencies pinned to older React majors block upgrades.

alternatives.name: preact
alternatives.when: You need the React component model in a few kilobytes for widgets and embeds

alternatives.name: vue
alternatives.when: You want a progressive framework with official router and state libraries instead of assembling your own stack

alternatives.name: svelte
alternatives.when: You prefer compile-time components that ship less runtime JavaScript to the client

alternatives.name: solid-js
alternatives.when: You want JSX with fine-grained reactivity and no virtual DOM re-render model

guide.verdict: The default choice for interactive UIs, and the default is worth something: docs, hiring, and third-party libraries all point here. Just remember React is a rendering library, not a framework, so choosing the rest of the stack is still your job.

apiStability.why: The component and hooks API has been backward compatible for years; v19 removed only long-deprecated APIs, and changes like ref-as-prop were additive

docsQuality.why: react.dev has a real tutorial, conceptual guides like Thinking in React, and a complete API reference; among the best docs in frontend

maintenance.why: Full-time Meta engineers plus a large contributor base; the repo is pushed daily and majors arrive with codemods and upgrade guides

ecosystem.why: The largest UI ecosystem on npm: routers, data libraries, component kits, and 162M weekly downloads

patterns.title: Mount an app into the DOM

guide.whatIs: react-hook-form manages form state in React by registering inputs as mostly uncontrolled fields, so typing in one input does not re-render the whole form. You get validation (native HTML rules or schema libraries like Zod and Yup through resolvers), error tracking, dirty/touched state, dynamic field arrays, and submit handling from one useForm() hook. It has zero runtime dependencies and only React as a peer dependency.
useIf: You build forms with many fields where per-keystroke re-renders of controlled state become a visible performance problem
You want schema-based validation: official resolvers exist for Zod, Yup, AJV, Superstruct, and Joi via @hookform/resolvers
Your inputs are mostly native elements (input, select, textarea) where the register() spread pattern is genuinely minimal boilerplate
skipIf: Your form logic is moving server-side (Next.js server actions, Remix): native FormData plus server validation may need no client form library at all
Your UI is mostly controlled component libraries (MUI, Ant, react-select): every such input needs a Controller wrapper, and that boilerplate cancels much of the simplicity you came for
You need one form library across React, Vue, Solid, or Angular: this is React-only, TanStack Form is framework-agnostic
You dislike ref-and-proxy magic: form values live outside React state, so debugging why a value did not update means learning the subscription model first
guide.setupReality: Install is one package with no dependencies beyond the React peer. The real setup cost arrives later: schema validation requires the separate @hookform/resolvers package plus your schema library; every non-native widget needs a Controller with a render prop; and the TypeScript generics for useForm<FormValues> with deeply nested field paths produce long, confusing errors until you learn the shape. Code you find online mixes v6 and v7 register APIs, and the v7 spread form ({...register('name')}) is the only correct one today.

alternatives.name: formik
alternatives.when: You maintain a codebase already built on it; for new projects its development pace has fallen well behind

alternatives.name: @tanstack/react-form
alternatives.when: You want a headless, framework-agnostic form library with first-class TypeScript inference

guide.verdict: The default React form library in 2026 for good reason: small, fast, and stable across years of 7.x releases. Budget real extra time if your form is mostly controlled UI-kit widgets, and consider skipping it entirely for simple server-action forms.

apiStability.why: On major version 7 since 2021 with dozens of minor releases and no breaking rewrite since. The register-spread API introduced in v7 has held steady.

docsQuality.why: Dedicated docs site with live examples, an interactive form builder, and an FAQ. Advanced TypeScript scenarios around nested field paths and generic components are thinner than the basics.

maintenance.why: Pushed the day of this review with a steady release cadence, but the project is driven by a small core team around one lead maintainer rather than a company.

ecosystem.why: About 58 million weekly downloads, official resolvers for every major schema library, DevTools, and integration examples for all the big UI kits.

guide.whatIs: React Native brings React's declarative component model to iOS and Android: you write components in JavaScript or TypeScript, and they render as real native UI controls, not a webview. You get React's state and props model, live-reloading JavaScript during development, and full access to native platform APIs when you need to drop down. Apps can target iOS 15.1+ and Android 7.0 (API 24)+, and the same code can reach other platforms through out-of-tree renderers.
useIf: Your team already knows React and you need one codebase shipping real native UI on both iOS and Android
You want fast iteration: JavaScript changes reload in seconds without rebuilding the native app
You need access to native capabilities through an ecosystem of existing native modules, with the option to write your own
You are building a mostly standard app (lists, forms, navigation, media) where native look and feel matters more than pixel-identical custom rendering
skipIf: Nobody on the team can debug Xcode or Gradle: native build failures are a fact of life and the JavaScript layer will not shield you from them
Your app is dominated by heavy custom rendering, 3D, or per-frame animation work, where a fully native app or a game engine fits better
You cannot budget for upgrades: React Native is still on 0.x with frequent releases, and moving between versions regularly breaks native dependencies
Your product is already a working responsive web app: wrapping it with Capacitor is far less work than rebuilding the UI in React Native
You need to build iOS locally without a Mac: iOS builds require macOS unless you lean on Expo's cloud services
guide.setupReality: The docs steer new apps toward a framework, in practice Expo, which hides most of the native setup until you need a custom native module. Going bare means installing Xcode, Android Studio, JDK, SDK paths, and CocoaPods, and each of those can fail independently on a fresh machine. The package pins peer dependencies tightly (0.86 wants react ^19.2.3), so version mismatches surface as confusing install or runtime errors. The New Architecture is the default now, and older native libraries that never migrated may not work. Upgrades are their own project: the community upgrade-helper diff is the honest tool for the job.

alternatives.name: expo
alternatives.when: Almost always for new apps: it is the recommended framework layer over React Native and removes most native tooling pain.

alternatives.name: @capacitor/core
alternatives.when: You already have a web app and want it in the stores as a webview with native plugin access.

alternatives.name: nativescript
alternatives.when: You want direct JavaScript access to native APIs without the React model, with Angular or Vue flavors available.

guide.verdict: The proven way for React teams to ship both app stores from one codebase, backed by Meta and a large contributor ecosystem. Budget real time for native tooling and version upgrades, and start with Expo unless you have a specific reason not to.

apiStability.why: Still versioned 0.x with releases that regularly require native-side changes; the New Architecture migration and tight react peer-dependency pins mean upgrades are routine breaking events.

docsQuality.why: reactnative.dev covers components, APIs, and platform setup well, but the story is split across React docs, React Native docs, and Expo docs, and you often need all three.

maintenance.why: Developed by Meta with many partner companies, pushed the day this was written (August 2026), with numerous stable branches receiving patch releases in parallel.

ecosystem.why: Huge module ecosystem and 11M weekly downloads, but quality varies and libraries that never adopted the New Architecture quietly stop working; vetting dependencies is part of the job.

guide.whatIs: React Router is a multi-strategy router for React that you can use two very different ways. Library mode keeps your own build and gives you nested routes, links, params, and navigation state. Framework mode (the Remix lineage) adds a Vite plugin with route modules, loaders, actions, middleware, SSR, and pre-rendering, making it a full-stack framework. v8 is ESM-only, sits on an open governance model, and majors now ship on a planned yearly cadence each June.
useIf: Your SPA needs nested layouts, URL params, and data loading tied to routes rather than scattered in components
You want a full-stack React framework with loaders, actions, middleware, and SSR while staying on the React Router API
You are on v7 with the future flags adopted; the v8 upgrade is deliberately boring by design
skipIf: Your build cannot go ESM-only or meet the v8 baseline of Node 22.22+, React 19.2.7+, and Vite 7+
You want compile-time type-safe params and search params as the core design; that is TanStack Router's whole pitch
You already use Next.js or another framework with routing built in; adding this router on top is redundant
You pin dependencies for years; the planned yearly major cadence means a scheduled breaking release every June, and v6 to v7 to v8 each moved imports around
guide.setupReality: Library mode is one install and a router component. Framework mode is a different project shape: the @react-router/dev Vite plugin, a routes.ts file, generated route types, and entry files, so start from create-react-router instead of bolting it onto an existing Vite app. v8 removed the react-router-dom package entirely: RouterProvider and HydratedRouter now import from react-router/dom and everything else from react-router. Middleware is always enabled, and custom-server getLoadContext must return a RouterContextProvider, which breaks v7 servers that returned plain objects.

alternatives.name: @tanstack/react-router
alternatives.when: You want fully type-safe routes and search params checked at compile time

alternatives.name: wouter
alternatives.when: A minimal hook-based router covers your small SPA and you do not need loaders or data APIs

alternatives.name: next
alternatives.when: You want routing, SSR, RSC, and bundling as one integrated framework rather than assembled parts

guide.verdict: The default router for React and, in framework mode, a credible full-stack framework with the Remix ideas built in. Adopt future flags as they appear and the yearly majors stay boring; ignore them and each June becomes a migration project.

apiStability.why: The future-flag system genuinely de-risks majors for teams that adopt flags early, but the ecosystem still churns: react-router-dom was removed in v8 and v8 went ESM-only with a raised Node/React/Vite baseline

docsQuality.why: reactrouter.com has separate framework and library getting-started tracks, per-major upgrade guides, and a changelog maintained as one searchable file

maintenance.why: Open governance with a planned yearly release cadence, active daily development, and the Remix team's full attention since the projects merged

ecosystem.why: The assumed default in React tutorials and starters for a decade; official adapters for Node, Express, Cloudflare, and Architect ship from the same repo

guide.whatIs: node-redis is the official Redis client for Node.js, maintained by Redis Inc. It gives you every Redis command as a promise-returning method (both HGETALL and hGetAll spellings), plus transactions, pub/sub, scan iterators, clustering, sentinel, connection pooling, and client-side caching. The npm package 'redis' is the all-in-one build that bundles the JSON, search, bloom, and time-series module commands on top of the core client.
useIf: You want the official client that tracks new Redis server features first (client-side caching with RESP3, the 8.4 compare-and-set commands, OpenTelemetry metrics)
You need module commands (RedisJSON, RediSearch, time series, bloom filters) with typed APIs instead of hand-built sendCommand calls
You are on Redis Cloud or a Redis Stack deployment where matching the vendor's own client removes a class of compatibility questions
You like async iterators for SCAN and promise-native transactions instead of callback-era patterns
skipIf: Your team has ioredis muscle memory or an existing ioredis codebase: the APIs are incompatible enough that migrating is real work for little payoff
You deploy to serverless or edge runtimes with no TCP sockets (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge): you need an HTTP-based client like @upstash/redis instead

You are still on the v3/v4 API: each major has renamed core methods (quit/disconnect became close/destroy in v5, isolation pools became RedisClientPool), so upgrading is a migration project, not a version bump
You forget error listeners: by the maintainers' own warning, a client without an 'error' listener will throw on any network hiccup and take the whole Node process down
guide.setupReality: npm install redis pulls in five @redis/* packages; there is no native compilation and setup is genuinely quick. The real friction is operational: you must attach an error listener before connect or a dropped socket kills your process, connect() is explicit and async, reconnection strategy is your problem to configure, and the v4 to v5/v6 renames (disconnect to destroy, quit to close, pool extraction) mean most blog posts and older Stack Overflow answers show an API that no longer exists. The optional local digest helper additionally wants a @node-rs/xxhash native peer dependency.

alternatives.name: ioredis
alternatives.when: The long-time community standard; huge installed base and a different but mature API, though new feature work happens in node-redis

alternatives.name: @upstash/redis
alternatives.when: Serverless and edge runtimes where you need Redis over HTTP instead of a TCP connection

alternatives.name: iovalkey
alternatives.when: You run Valkey rather than Redis and want a client maintained for that fork

guide.verdict: The right default for new Node projects talking to Redis, especially with Stack modules or Redis Cloud. Budget real time for the v5+ API differences from every tutorial written before 2024, and never ship without an error listener.

apiStability.why: v3 to v4 was a full rewrite and v5 renamed core lifecycle methods again (quit to close, disconnect to destroy) and extracted pooling into RedisClientPool; the current API is good but history says majors break you.

docsQuality.why: The README covers the essentials well and dedicated guides exist for pub/sub, clustering, sentinel, pooling, and v4-to-v5 migration; the catch is that most third-party tutorials still show the old API, so you must read the repo docs, not blogs.

maintenance.why: Maintained by Redis Inc with pushes as recent as this week, a 6.2.0 release days old, and fast support for new server features like Redis 8.4 CAS/CAD commands.

ecosystem.why: 12.6M weekly downloads, official module packages for JSON/search/bloom/time-series, OpenTelemetry and diagnostics_channel integration; ioredis still owns a large share of existing deployments and third-party integrations.

patterns.title: Create and connect a client
patterns.note: The error listener is mandatory: without one, any socket error is thrown and exits the Node process.

patterns.title: Set a key with expiry and NX
patterns.note: Command modifiers are an options object, not extra string arguments like in redis-cli examples.

patterns.title: Store and read a hash
patterns.note: hGetAll on a missing key returns an empty object, not null; check Object.keys(user).length.

patterns.title: Run a MULTI/EXEC transaction
patterns.snippet:
const [setReply, count] = await client
  .multi()
  .set('key', 'value')
  .incr('counter')
  .exec();
patterns.note: Commands queue locally and run atomically on exec(); combine with client.watch() for optimistic locking.

patterns.title: Iterate keys without blocking Redis
patterns.note: The iterator yields batches of keys, not single keys; never use KEYS in production, SCAN exists for this.

patterns.title: Publish and subscribe
patterns.note: A subscribed connection cannot run other commands, so you must duplicate() a dedicated client for subscriptions.

patterns.title: Use a connection pool
patterns.note: v5 replaced the v4 'isolation pool' option with this class; use a pool when you need blocking commands like BLPOP without stalling other traffic.

patterns.title: Send a command the client does not know
patterns.snippet:
await client.sendCommand(['SET', 'key', 'value', 'NX']); // 'OK'
const raw = await client.sendCommand(['HGETALL', 'key']);
patterns.note: sendCommand returns raw flat replies (HGETALL gives an array, not an object) and the API differs on clusters.

patterns.title: Enable client-side caching
patterns.note: Requires RESP3; the server invalidates the local cache for you, which cuts round trips on hot read keys.

patterns.title: Batch commands in one round trip
patterns.note: Commands issued in the same tick pipeline automatically; use Promise.all so no rejection goes unhandled.

patterns.title: Close the connection cleanly
patterns.note: quit() and disconnect() are the deprecated v4 names; close() replaces quit and destroy() replaces disconnect.

patterns.title: Work with Buffers instead of strings
patterns.note: DUMP/RESTORE payloads corrupt if decoded as UTF-8 strings; map blob strings to Buffer first.

guide.whatIs: redis-py is the official Python client for the Redis key-value store (this page covers the PyPI package named redis; there is a separate npm package with the same name for Node.js). You install it, point it at a Redis server, and every Redis command becomes a Python method: r.set, r.get, r.hset, and so on. It ships sync and asyncio clients, connection pooling, pipelines, pub/sub, streams, and cluster support in one package, and it is the client that Celery, RQ, django-redis, and most other Python tooling build on.
useIf: You need caching, sessions, rate limiting, or counters backed by a Redis (or Redis-compatible) server
Your stack already depends on it indirectly through Celery, RQ, or django-redis and you want direct access too
You have an asyncio codebase; redis.asyncio mirrors the sync API almost method for method
You want pub/sub, distributed locks, or streams without adding a full message broker
skipIf: You only need per-process caching in one Python app: functools.lru_cache or diskcache does the job without running and monitoring a server
Your data is relational or needs ad hoc queries: Redis is a data-structure store, and forcing query workloads into it means rebuilding indexes by hand; use Postgres
You moved to Valkey over the Redis licensing changes: the valkey client is the fork's own package and tracks its server, not Redis Ltd's roadmap
You want an object-mapping layer: redis-py is deliberately low level, one method per command; redis-om adds models and validation on top if that is what you actually wanted
guide.setupReality: pip install redis takes seconds; the friction is everything around it. You need a running server (docker run -p 6379:6379 redis works). Responses come back as bytes unless you remember decode_responses=True, which bites almost every new user. Since 8.0 the wire protocol defaults to RESP3 while keeping legacy response shapes, and new projects are told to set legacy_responses=False, so there is now a compatibility flag to think about. Old tutorials still show hmset and the separate aioredis package, both long gone. For speed you want the hiredis extra, which is a compiled parser and one more thing in your lockfile.

alternatives.name: valkey
alternatives.when: You run the Valkey fork and want the client maintained by that project instead of Redis Ltd

alternatives.name: coredis
alternatives.when: You want an async-first client with typed responses rather than the sync-API-mirrored redis.asyncio

alternatives.name: redis-om
alternatives.when: You want declarative models and validation on top of Redis instead of raw command methods

guide.verdict: If you talk to Redis from Python, this is the client; it is official, everywhere, and actively maintained. The real decision is not the library but whether you run Redis or Valkey on the server side.

apiStability.why: Command methods map one to one to Redis and rarely change, but recent majors arrived quickly (6.x then 8.x) with a RESP3 wire default and a response-shape migration flag to track

docsQuality.why: readthedocs covers the API and has good asyncio and connection examples, but conceptual guides are split between redis.io and readthedocs, and migration notes assume you already know the RESP2/RESP3 story

maintenance.why: Official Redis Ltd project, pushed within the last day as of this review, regular releases tracking new server versions up to Redis 8.x

ecosystem.why: The default Redis client for Python; Celery, RQ, django-redis, and most caching and queue tooling in the ecosystem sit on top of it

patterns.title: Connect and read strings back
patterns.snippet:
import redis

r = redis.Redis(host="localhost", port=6379, db=0, decode_responses=True)
r.set("greeting", "hello")
print(r.get("greeting"))  # 'hello'
patterns.note: Without decode_responses=True every reply is bytes (b'hello'), which is the single most common surprise with this library.

patterns.title: Connect from a URL
patterns.snippet:
import redis

r = redis.Redis.from_url("redis://:s3cret@cache.internal:6379/1", decode_responses=True)
patterns.note: The database number rides in the path (/1). Use rediss:// (double s) for TLS; plain redis:// sends the password unencrypted.

patterns.title: asyncio client
patterns.snippet:
import asyncio
import redis.asyncio as redis

async def main():
    r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)
    await r.set("k", "v")
    print(await r.get("k"))
    await r.aclose()

asyncio.run(main())
patterns.note: The old standalone aioredis package was merged into redis-py years ago; ignore tutorials that import aioredis. Close with aclose(), not close().

patterns.title: Batch commands in a pipeline
patterns.snippet:
pipe = r.pipeline()
pipe.set("a", 1)
pipe.incr("a")
pipe.get("a")
results = pipe.execute()  # [True, 2, '2']
patterns.note: pipeline() wraps commands in MULTI/EXEC by default (transaction=True); pass transaction=False if you only want to save round trips without atomicity.

patterns.title: Store a dict as a hash
patterns.snippet:
r.hset("user:42", mapping={"name": "Keyoor", "plan": "pro"})
user = r.hgetall("user:42")  # {'name': 'Keyoor', 'plan': 'pro'}
patterns.note: hmset was removed; hset with mapping= is the current form. Hash values are always strings on the server, so numbers come back as strings.

patterns.title: Set with TTL and set-if-absent
patterns.snippet:
r.set("session:abc", "payload", ex=3600)      # expires in 1h
created = r.set("lock:init", "1", nx=True, ex=30)
print(r.ttl("session:abc"))
patterns.note: ex/px/nx/xx flags on set() replace the old setex and setnx commands. nx=True returns None (not False) when the key already exists.

patterns.title: Iterate keys without blocking the server
patterns.snippet:
for key in r.scan_iter(match="session:*", count=500):
    r.delete(key)
patterns.note: Never use r.keys() in production; it blocks the single-threaded server while it walks the whole keyspace. scan_iter pages through cursor-style.

patterns.title: Subscribe to a channel
patterns.snippet:
p = r.pubsub(ignore_subscribe_messages=True)
p.subscribe("alerts")
for message in p.listen():
    print(message["channel"], message["data"])
patterns.note: Without ignore_subscribe_messages you get a subscribe-confirmation message first. Pub/sub is fire-and-forget: subscribers that are offline miss messages; use streams if you need replay.

patterns.title: Distributed lock
patterns.snippet:
with r.lock("job:nightly-report", timeout=60, blocking_timeout=5):
    run_report()
patterns.note: timeout is how long the lock lives, not how long you wait; if the work runs longer than timeout the lock expires and a second worker can enter. blocking_timeout raises LockError if the lock cannot be acquired in time.

patterns.title: Share one connection pool
patterns.snippet:
pool = redis.ConnectionPool(host="localhost", port=6379, max_connections=20, decode_responses=True)
r1 = redis.Redis(connection_pool=pool)
r2 = redis.Redis(connection_pool=pool)
patterns.note: Each Redis() instance otherwise creates its own pool; in web apps make one module-level pool (or one client) instead of a client per request.

patterns.title: Customize connection retries
patterns.snippet:
from redis.retry import Retry
from redis.backoff import ExponentialBackoff

r = redis.Redis(retry=Retry(ExponentialBackoff(), retries=5))
patterns.note: Recent majors retry failed connections automatically, so a brief server blip may add latency instead of raising; tune or disable this deliberately rather than discovering it during an incident.

patterns.title: Opt out of legacy response shapes (new projects)
patterns.snippet: r = redis.Redis(host="localhost", port=6379, legacy_responses=False, decode_responses=True)
patterns.note: Since 8.0 the wire protocol is RESP3 by default but replies keep old RESP2-style Python shapes for compatibility; legacy_responses=False gives the unified shapes the maintainers recommend for new code.

guide.whatIs: requests is the standard synchronous HTTP client for Python. It wraps urllib3 in an API that reads like the HTTP you mean: requests.get(url, auth=(user, pass)) returns a Response with .status_code, .headers, and .json(). Sessions add connection pooling, cookie persistence, and shared defaults. It supports Python 3.10+ and, per its own README, is depended on by over 4 million repositories, which makes it close to a de facto part of the language.
useIf: You need to call HTTP APIs from scripts, cron jobs, or synchronous backends with zero learning curve
You want Sessions with connection pooling, cookie persistence, and mountable retry behavior from urllib3
You need streaming downloads, multipart uploads, digest auth, or SOCKS proxies without hunting for extra libraries
You are writing example code or docs that other people must be able to run anywhere
skipIf: Your code is async. requests is blocking only; httpx gives you a nearly identical API with async support, and aiohttp is the asyncio native option
You need HTTP/2 or HTTP/3; requests speaks HTTP/1.1 only
You assume retries and timeouts are built in. There is no default timeout (a classic production incident) and retries require manually mounting an HTTPAdapter
You want a library that is still growing. requests is deliberately conservative; fixes land, new features mostly do not
guide.setupReality: pip install requests pulls in urllib3, certifi, charset_normalizer, and idna and works on any Python 3.10+ without native builds. The friction is policy, not packaging: no timeout is applied unless you pass one on every single call, retries mean wiring an HTTPAdapter with a urllib3 Retry object yourself, and .json() raises on non-JSON bodies so error paths need care. None of it is hard; all of it is on you.

alternatives.name: httpx
alternatives.when: When you need async or HTTP/2 with a requests-like API

alternatives.name: aiohttp
alternatives.when: When you are all-in on asyncio and may also need the server or websocket side

alternatives.name: urllib3
alternatives.when: When you want one fewer layer and are comfortable with a lower-level API

guide.verdict: Still the right default for synchronous HTTP in Python: boring, everywhere, and documented to death. Reach for httpx the moment async or HTTP/2 enters the picture.

apiStability.why: The 2.x line has held backward compatibility since 2013; code written a decade ago still runs unchanged.

docsQuality.why: requests.readthedocs.io is one of the most imitated docs sites in Python, with a quickstart and an advanced guide that cover nearly every feature.

maintenance.why: Maintained under the PSF with pushes the day before this review, but intentionally in low-feature mode; do not expect new capabilities like HTTP/2.

ecosystem.why: 417M weekly downloads and 4M+ dependent repositories per the README; virtually every Python HTTP answer online assumes it.

patterns.title: GET a URL and parse JSON
patterns.snippet:
import requests

r = requests.get("https://api.example.com/items", timeout=10)
r.raise_for_status()
data = r.json()
patterns.note: r.json() raises if the body is not JSON; check r.status_code or call raise_for_status() first so you fail on the real error.

patterns.title: POST a JSON body
patterns.snippet:
import requests

r = requests.post(
    "https://api.example.com/items",
    json={"name": "widget", "qty": 3},
    timeout=10,
)
patterns.note: Use json=, not data=; json= serializes and sets the Content-Type header for you, data= sends form encoding.

patterns.title: Always set a timeout
patterns.snippet:
import requests

# (connect timeout, read timeout)
r = requests.get("https://api.example.com/slow", timeout=(3.05, 27))
patterns.note: There is no default timeout; a request without one can hang a worker forever. This is the most common requests bug in production.

patterns.title: Reuse a Session for connection pooling
patterns.snippet:
import requests

s = requests.Session()
s.headers.update({"Authorization": "Bearer TOKEN"})

for page in range(1, 6):
    r = s.get("https://api.example.com/items", params={"page": page}, timeout=10)
    r.raise_for_status()
patterns.note: A Session keeps TCP connections alive across calls; calling requests.get in a loop reopens a connection every time.

patterns.title: Retry failed requests with backoff
patterns.snippet:
import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry

s = requests.Session()
retry = Retry(
    total=3,
    backoff_factor=0.5,
    status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504],
)
s.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))

r = s.get("https://api.example.com/data", timeout=10)
patterns.note: Retries are not built into requests itself; you mount urllib3's Retry. By default only idempotent methods are retried.

patterns.title: Stream a large file to disk
patterns.snippet:
import requests

with requests.get(url, stream=True, timeout=30) as r:
    r.raise_for_status()
    with open("file.zip", "wb") as f:
        for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):
            f.write(chunk)
patterns.note: Without stream=True the entire body is read into memory before you see it; with it, always use a with block so the connection is released.

patterns.title: Upload a file as multipart form data
patterns.snippet:
import requests

with open("report.pdf", "rb") as f:
    r = requests.post(
        "https://api.example.com/upload",
        files={"file": ("report.pdf", f, "application/pdf")},
        timeout=60,
    )
patterns.note: Open the file in binary mode; passing files= sets the multipart boundary and Content-Type automatically.

patterns.title: Handle HTTP and network errors separately
patterns.note: A 404 does not raise by itself; requests only raises for network-level failures unless you call raise_for_status().

patterns.title: Send query string parameters
patterns.snippet:
import requests

r = requests.get(
    "https://api.example.com/search",
    params={"q": "blue widgets", "page": 2},
    timeout=10,
)
print(r.url)  # https://api.example.com/search?q=blue+widgets&page=2
patterns.note: Use params= instead of building the query string by hand; it handles encoding and lists correctly.

patterns.title: Authenticate with basic auth
patterns.snippet:
import requests

r = requests.get(
    "https://httpbin.org/basic-auth/user/pass",
    auth=("user", "pass"),
    timeout=10,
)
print(r.status_code)  # 200
patterns.note: auth=(user, pass) is basic auth; digest auth needs requests.auth.HTTPDigestAuth instead.

patterns.title: Route requests through a proxy
patterns.note: requests also honors HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY environment variables, which can surprise you in CI; SOCKS needs the socks extra installed.

guide.whatIs: Rich is the Python library for making terminal output look good. It gives you a drop-in print replacement with a bbcode-style markup for color and styling, plus ready-made renderables: tables, progress bars, spinners, trees, columns, markdown, syntax-highlighted code, and pretty tracebacks. It auto-detects terminal capability, word-wraps to the terminal width, works in Jupyter notebooks with no configuration, and pretty-prints any Python data structure. It is why so many modern Python CLIs (pip included) look the way they do.
useIf: You build CLI tools and want tables, progress bars, and colored output without writing ANSI escape codes
You want readable debugging: rich tracebacks and inspect() beat staring at plain repr output
You need progress reporting for long jobs, including multiple concurrent bars and spinners
Your output runs in mixed environments (Linux, macOS, Windows Terminal, Jupyter) and you want capability detection handled for you
skipIf: You are writing a library, not an application: forcing a display dependency on your users for a bit of color is poor manners, and logging plus plain text serves them better
Your output is consumed by machines or log aggregators: styled output must be disabled or stripped there, so if that is your main audience Rich adds surface without payoff
You need interactive UI (input handling, widgets, screens): that is Textual, Rich's sister project, not Rich
You are on classic Windows conhost and expect the screenshots: it is limited to 16 colors there per the README
You count dependencies in a minimal tool: Rich pulls in pygments and markdown-it-py, which is real weight for printing a colored warning
guide.setupReality: pip install rich and you are running in under a minute; python -m rich demos everything in your own terminal. There is no config. The gotchas are operational: Console(force_terminal=True) or the FORCE_COLOR conventions for CI where you DO want color, remembering markup like [bold] gets parsed in print calls (escape square brackets in user data), and major version bumps that arrive fairly frequently (v15 is current) occasionally adjust rendering details your snapshot tests may notice. Requires Python 3.9+ per current metadata.

alternatives.name: colorama
alternatives.when: You only need basic cross-platform colored text with near-zero footprint

alternatives.name: tqdm
alternatives.when: You only need a progress bar and want the lightest, most ubiquitous option

alternatives.name: textual
alternatives.when: You have outgrown printing and need a real interactive terminal UI with widgets and events

guide.verdict: The best-in-class way to make Python terminal output presentable, and the default choice for application CLIs. Skip it inside libraries and machine-facing tools, and reach for Textual once you need interaction rather than display.

apiStability.why: Console, Table, Progress, and the print API have been stable in shape for years, but major versions land often (v13 to v15 in about two years) with occasional rendering and signature changes.

docsQuality.why: readthedocs coverage of every renderable with examples, a runnable python -m rich demo, an examples directory in the repo, and the README alone is enough to get productive.

maintenance.why: Still released and pushed to in 2026 (v15.0.0 current, push June 2026), but Textualize's center of gravity moved to Textual and Toad, and over 360 issues sit open.

ecosystem.why: One of the most-downloaded packages on PyPI, a dependency of pip itself and of countless CLIs; the Console Protocol lets third-party objects render themselves.

patterns.title: Drop-in print with color markup
patterns.snippet:
from rich import print

print("[bold magenta]Deploy[/bold magenta] finished :rocket:")
print({"status": "ok", "replicas": 3})
patterns.note: Square brackets in user-supplied strings are parsed as markup; print untrusted text via rich.markup.escape() or console.print(text, markup=False).

patterns.title: Use a Console for real applications
patterns.snippet:
from rich.console import Console

console = Console()
console.print("Hello", "World!", style="bold red")
console.print("Where there is a [bold cyan]Will[/bold cyan] there [u]is[/u] a way.")
patterns.note: Create one Console at module level and share it; it owns terminal-width detection and color capability for the process.

patterns.title: Render a data table
patterns.snippet:
from rich.console import Console
from rich.table import Table

table = Table(show_header=True, header_style="bold magenta")
table.add_column("Date", style="dim", width=12)
table.add_column("Title")
table.add_column("Box Office", justify="right")
table.add_row("Dec 20, 2019", "Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker", "$375,126,118")

Console().print(table)
patterns.note: Columns auto-shrink and wrap to fit the terminal; cells accept any Rich renderable, including nested tables.

patterns.title: Progress bar around any loop
patterns.note: track() needs a sequence with a known length; for unknown totals use Progress with total=None or a status spinner.

patterns.title: Spinner for work with unknown duration
patterns.snippet:
from rich.console import Console

console = Console()
with console.status("[bold green]Working on tasks...") as status:
    for task in tasks:
        run(task)
        console.log(f"{task} complete")
patterns.note: console.log inside the status block prints above the live spinner without breaking it; run python -m rich.spinner to browse spinner styles.

patterns.title: Colorize the standard logging module
patterns.snippet:
import logging
from rich.logging import RichHandler

logging.basicConfig(
    level="INFO",
    format="%(message)s",
    datefmt="[%X]",
    handlers=[RichHandler()]
)
logging.getLogger("app").info("Server started")
patterns.note: Keep format minimal; RichHandler renders level, time, and caller location itself, so a full format string doubles the noise.

patterns.title: Install pretty tracebacks globally
patterns.snippet:
from rich.traceback import install

install(show_locals=True)

# any uncaught exception now renders with syntax highlighting
1 / 0
patterns.note: show_locals prints variable values at each frame, which is great for debugging and a secrets-leak risk in production logs.

patterns.title: Inspect any Python object
patterns.snippet:
from rich import inspect

my_list = ["foo", "bar"]
inspect(my_list, methods=True)
patterns.note: inspect(obj, help=True) includes full docstrings; it is a REPL power tool, not something to leave in committed code.

patterns.title: Render Markdown in the terminal
patterns.snippet:
from rich.console import Console
from rich.markdown import Markdown

with open("README.md") as readme:
    md = Markdown(readme.read())
Console().print(md)
patterns.note: Rendering is approximate by design; tables and headings translate well, raw HTML blocks inside the Markdown do not.

patterns.title: Print syntax-highlighted source code
patterns.snippet:
from rich.console import Console
from rich.syntax import Syntax

code = open("app.py").read()
syntax = Syntax(code, "python", theme="monokai", line_numbers=True)
Console().print(syntax)
patterns.note: Highlighting comes from pygments, so any pygments lexer name works as the language argument.

patterns.title: Pretty-print everything in the REPL
patterns.snippet:
>>> from rich import pretty
>>> pretty.install()
>>> ["data", {"structures": True}]
patterns.note: After install(), every evaluated expression is pretty-printed and highlighted; add it to PYTHONSTARTUP to make it permanent.

patterns.title: Keep color in CI or piped output
patterns.snippet:
from rich.console import Console

# CI pipes are not TTYs, so Rich disables color by default
console = Console(force_terminal=True, width=120)
console.print("[green]PASS[/green] 128 tests")
patterns.note: Fix the width too: without a TTY Rich cannot detect it and falls back to 80 columns, which mangles wide tables.

guide.whatIs: Rollup is the module bundler that made ES-module-first builds and tree shaking mainstream. You point it at an entry file and it emits a bundle in ESM, CommonJS, UMD, or IIFE format, keeping only the code that is actually imported. Its core niche today is building JavaScript libraries for npm, and it is also the production bundler inside Vite. Since v4 the parser is native Rust code shipped as per-platform binaries, which made it faster and made installation touchier in some environments.
useIf: You are publishing a library to npm and want clean ESM plus CJS output with the most mature tree shaking available
You need precise control over output: multiple formats, preserved module structure, banners, manual chunks
You already use Vite and need to tune the production build, since Vite build options are Rollup options underneath
You want an official plugin suite (@rollup/*) covering TypeScript, CommonJS interop, node resolution, JSON, and minification
skipIf: You are building an application, not a library: Vite gives you a dev server, HMR, and sane defaults on top of Rollup and you will finish faster
Raw build speed is your bottleneck: esbuild does comparable bundling far faster because Rollup does much more per-module analysis
Your dependency tree is heavy CommonJS: everything goes through @rollup/plugin-commonjs, and its interop edge cases can eat an afternoon
You are picking a long-term default in 2026: the Vite team is building Rolldown, a Rust rewrite aimed at exactly this niche, so check its status before committing a new toolchain
guide.setupReality: npm install rollup lists 27 optional platform packages and the right native binary is picked at install time. The classic failure is npm's optional-dependency bug: move a lockfile or node_modules across OS, libc, or CPU arch (macOS to Alpine Docker, x64 to arm64) and you get "Cannot find module @rollup/rollup-linux-x64-gnu" until you delete the lockfile and reinstall. Config lives in rollup.config.mjs (a .js config inside a CJS package needs --bundleConfigAsCjs), and TypeScript, CommonJS deps, JSON imports, and minification each need a separate @rollup/* plugin, so a real library build ends up with four to six plugins. Requires Node 18+.

alternatives.name: vite
alternatives.when: You are building an app and want a dev server and defaults; it uses Rollup for production builds anyway

alternatives.name: esbuild
alternatives.when: Build speed matters more than fine-grained output control or maximum tree shaking

alternatives.name: rolldown
alternatives.when: You want the Rust successor the Vite team is building for this exact role; newer and still stabilizing

alternatives.name: webpack
alternatives.when: You need its ecosystem-specific features like module federation or deeply custom loader chains

guide.verdict: Still the best tool for bundling libraries and the engine under Vite production builds. For apps use Vite, for raw speed use esbuild, and keep an eye on Rolldown, which is being built to take over this niche.

apiStability.why: v4 shipped in October 2023 and the config and plugin APIs have been stable across majors; v3 to v4 was mostly a parser swap plus config-format cleanup. Plugins written years ago still work.
