useIf: You are accepting payments with Stripe from a Node, Deno, or serverless backend; this is the official, always-current SDK
You want webhook signature verification (webhooks.constructEvent) instead of writing your own HMAC check
You need to walk large lists (customers, charges) and want for-await auto-pagination instead of manual cursor handling
You want typed request/response params: TypeScript definitions ship with the package and track the latest Stripe API version
skipIf: You are not using Stripe as your payment processor; this SDK is useless outside Stripe's API
You need it in the browser or React Native; it is server-side only and embedding it would leak your secret key
You need types pinned to an old Stripe API version: types only reflect the latest version, and the README's own advice for older versions is scattering @ts-ignore comments through your code

You dislike frequent majors: Stripe cuts a new major with every backwards-incompatible API version (v22 now), and minor upgrades can surface new TypeScript errors by design under their versioning policy
guide.setupReality: npm install stripe is trivial (zero runtime dependencies, Node 18+ required) but the integration around it is where the time goes. You need a secret key from the dashboard, and since v17 instantiating the client at import time without the key present breaks build steps, so you end up writing a lazy getter. Webhooks are the classic trap: constructEvent needs the raw request body, so Express/Next.js body parsing must be disabled for that route or verification fails. Telemetry to Stripe is on by default. Testing means juggling sk_test keys and the Stripe CLI for webhook forwarding.

alternatives.name: braintree
alternatives.when: Your processor is Braintree/PayPal; its official Node SDK covers similar ground for that platform

alternatives.name: square
alternatives.when: You are on Square for payments, especially with in-person/POS needs

alternatives.name: @paypal/paypal-server-sdk
alternatives.when: You only need PayPal buttons and orders rather than a full billing stack

guide.verdict: If you use Stripe on a Node backend there is no real debate: this is the SDK, it is actively maintained (pushed within the last day), and the retry/webhook/pagination helpers are worth it. Budget real time for webhook raw-body handling and for TypeScript churn across API version upgrades.

apiStability.why: Majors track Stripe API versions, so breaking releases are frequent by policy (v22 now), and even minor bumps may introduce new type errors the README explicitly says you must resolve with type guards.

docsQuality.why: Stripe's API reference has per-method Node examples for every endpoint, plus a long README covering retries, webhooks, pagination, proxies, and TypeScript edge cases.

maintenance.why: Pushed August 4, 2026, releases land near-weekly with the API, and only 49 issues are open on a 17.5M weekly download package.

ecosystem.why: 17.5M weekly downloads, official samples repos, Stripe CLI tooling, and framework guides everywhere; the ecosystem is deep but entirely bound to one vendor.

patterns.title: Initialize the client safely
patterns.note: Since v17, constructing Stripe at module top level fails builds where the env var is absent; the README recommends this lazy pattern or a placeholder key.

patterns.title: Create a PaymentIntent
patterns.note: Amounts are integers in the smallest currency unit; passing 20.00 for twenty dollars is the classic first-week bug.

patterns.title: Verify a webhook signature (Express)
patterns.note: constructEvent needs the raw body exactly as received; any global express.json() middleware on this route breaks verification with a signature error.

patterns.title: Create a hosted Checkout session
patterns.note: The literal {CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID} placeholder is substituted by Stripe; do not template it yourself.

patterns.title: Iterate all results with auto-pagination
patterns.note: autoPagingToArray refuses unbounded collection; you must pass a limit, and for-await is the safer default for big lists.

patterns.title: Make a create call idempotent
patterns.note: Reusing the same key within 24 hours returns the original response instead of double-charging; derive it from your own order ID, not a random UUID per attempt.

patterns.title: Configure automatic network retries
patterns.note: Since v13 the default is already 1 retry with idempotency keys added automatically; set 0 to disable, and remember the default timeout is a long 80 seconds.

patterns.title: Expand a nested object in one call
patterns.note: Expandable fields are typed as string | Object, so TypeScript forces a cast; without expand you only get the id string.

patterns.title: Act on behalf of a Connect account
patterns.note: stripeAccount is a per-request option, not a param; putting it inside the first argument is silently wrong.

patterns.title: Handle declined cards and API errors
patterns.note: Card declines are thrown as errors, not returned as statuses; log err.requestId when contacting Stripe support.

patterns.title: Mock a signed webhook event in tests
patterns.note: This tests your verification path without the Stripe CLI; for live-ish local testing use 'stripe listen --forward-to localhost:3000/webhook'.

guide.whatIs: Svelte is a UI framework that works as a compiler: you write declarative components in .svelte files and it compiles them into plain JavaScript that updates the DOM directly, with no virtual DOM diffing at runtime. Since version 5, reactivity is explicit through 'runes' ($state, $derived, $effect), which replaced the older implicit let-and-$: reactivity. The result is small output, fast updates, and components that read close to plain HTML, CSS, and JS. Most real apps pair it with SvelteKit, its official app framework.
useIf: You want less framework ceremony: state is a plain variable with $state, templates are HTML-like, and styles are scoped per component by default
Runtime payload and update performance matter; compiled output is small (the runtime the compiler injects is around 10.8 KB gzipped) and updates are targeted, not diffed
You are building a content site or app with SvelteKit and want SSR, routing, and progressive enhancement handled by the official stack
Your team is small or includes people closer to HTML/CSS than to React idioms; the learning curve to productive is short
skipIf: You need the biggest hiring pool and component-library market; React's ecosystem (component kits, job candidates, Stack Overflow answers, AI training data) is several times larger
Your team has deep React investment; Svelte 5 runes are a different mental model and the migration cost buys you little if React already works for you

You rely on lots of pre-2024 Svelte tutorials and libraries: Svelte 5 changed the core model (runes, snippets, event attributes), so much older content and some older libraries teach deprecated patterns
You want to render components without a build step; Svelte is a compiler, so there is no realistic drop-a-script-tag usage the way Vue or Preact allow
guide.setupReality: You never install just svelte in practice; you scaffold with npx sv create (SvelteKit) or a Vite template, which wires the compiler plugin for you. That part is smooth. The real friction in 2026 is the version 4 to 5 transition: docs and runes are current, but a large share of blog posts, Stack Overflow answers, and third-party components still show pre-runes syntax (export let, on:click, slots), so beginners constantly hit deprecated patterns. Runes only work in .svelte and .svelte.js/.svelte.ts files, which trips people up when they try to share reactive state from a plain .ts module.

alternatives.name: react
alternatives.when: You want the largest ecosystem, hiring pool, and third-party component supply, and accept more boilerplate

alternatives.name: vue
alternatives.when: You want a similar single-file-component feel with a bigger ecosystem and optional no-build usage

alternatives.name: solid-js
alternatives.when: You want fine-grained signal reactivity like runes but with JSX instead of a template compiler

alternatives.name: preact
alternatives.when: You need React compatibility at a tiny size rather than a different component model

guide.verdict: Technically excellent and genuinely pleasant to write; with SvelteKit it is a complete, actively developed stack (87.8K stars, pushed this week). The honest tradeoff is ecosystem size and the Svelte 5 content gap: you trade React's endless libraries and answers for cleaner code you will write more of yourself.

apiStability.why: Svelte 5 (late 2024) replaced the reactivity model wholesale; legacy syntax still compiles and a migration tool exists, but the ecosystem is mid-transition and old patterns are deprecated.

docsQuality.why: svelte.dev has a full interactive tutorial, live playground, and reference that is current for runes; among the best docs of any frontend framework.

maintenance.why: Very active monorepo (pushed August 2, 2026, version 5.56.x cadence is near-weekly) with full-time maintainers funded via Open Collective and Vercel.

ecosystem.why: 5.3M weekly downloads and a healthy SvelteKit ecosystem, but component libraries, integrations, and hiring depth are far behind React and Vue, and some libraries lag on Svelte 5 support.

patterns.title: Declare reactive state with $state
patterns.snippet:
<script>
  let count = $state(0);
</script>

<button onclick={() => count++}>
  clicked {count} times
</button>
patterns.note: Runes like $state are compiler keywords, not imports; they only work in .svelte and .svelte.js/.svelte.ts files.

patterns.title: Compute a value from other state
patterns.snippet:
<script>
  let count = $state(0);
  let doubled = $derived(count * 2);
  let big = $derived.by(() => {
    // multi-line derivations use $derived.by
    return count > 10 ? 'big' : 'small';
  });
</script>
patterns.note: This replaces Svelte 4's $: label syntax; $derived values are read-only and recompute lazily.

patterns.title: Run a side effect when state changes
patterns.snippet:
<script>
  let query = $state('');
  $effect(() => {
    const id = setTimeout(() => search(query), 300);
    return () => clearTimeout(id); // cleanup runs before re-run and on destroy
  });
</script>
patterns.note: $effect tracks whatever it reads synchronously; values read inside setTimeout or await are not tracked, a common surprise.

patterns.title: Accept props with $props
patterns.snippet: {name}
patterns.note: This replaces 'export let name' from Svelte 4; defaults and rest props come straight from destructuring.

patterns.title: Bind an input, and make a prop bindable
patterns.snippet:
<!-- Input.svelte -->
<script>
  let { value = $bindable('') } = $props();
</script>
<input bind:value />

<!-- Parent.svelte -->
<script>
  import Input from './Input.svelte';
  let name = $state('');
</script>
<Input bind:value={name} />
patterns.note: In Svelte 5 a component prop must be declared $bindable() before a parent may bind: to it; plain props are one-way.

patterns.title: Handle DOM events and component callbacks
patterns.snippet:
<script>
  let { onRemove } = $props(); // callback prop instead of createEventDispatcher
</script>

<button onclick={() => onRemove?.()}>remove</button>
<input oninput={(e) => console.log(e.currentTarget.value)} />
patterns.note: Svelte 5 uses plain event attributes (onclick, oninput); the on:click directive and createEventDispatcher are deprecated in favor of callback props.

patterns.title: Render a keyed list
patterns.snippet:
{#each todos as todo (todo.id)}
  • {todo.text}
    • {:else}
  • Nothing to do
    • {/each}
patterns.note: The (todo.id) key matters: without it Svelte patches rows by index, which breaks animations and input state on reorder.

patterns.title: Conditionals and awaiting promises in markup
patterns.note: {#await} re-runs if the promise expression changes; in SvelteKit, prefer load functions for data that needs SSR.

patterns.title: Pass markup to a component with snippets
patterns.snippet:
{@render header?.()} {@render children?.()}
{#snippet header()}

Title

{/snippet}

Body content becomes the children snippet
patterns.note: Snippets replace Svelte 4 slots; content not wrapped in a named {#snippet} arrives as the implicit children snippet.

patterns.title: Share reactive state across components
patterns.note: The file must be named *.svelte.js or *.svelte.ts for runes to compile, and you must export an object and mutate its properties; reassigning an exported binding breaks reactivity.

patterns.title: Get a DOM node and run mount logic
patterns.snippet:
<script>
  import { onMount } from 'svelte';
  let canvas; // populated via bind:this

  onMount(() => {
    const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
    ctx.fillRect(0, 0, 100, 100);
    return () => {/* cleanup on destroy */};
  });
</script>

<canvas bind:this={canvas} width="200" height="200"></canvas>
patterns.note: onMount still exists in Svelte 5 and only runs in the browser, which makes it the standard place for DOM-only code under SSR.

guide.whatIs: Tailwind CSS is a utility-first CSS framework: instead of writing custom stylesheets you compose small single-purpose classes like flex, pt-4, and text-center directly in your markup. A build step scans your source files for class names and generates only the CSS you actually use, so the shipped stylesheet stays small even though the framework covers most of modern CSS. Since v4, configuration lives in CSS itself (the @theme block) rather than a JavaScript config file.
useIf: You want spacing, color, and type scales enforced by a design-token system instead of ad hoc CSS values scattered across files
Your team ships React, Vue, or server-rendered templates and is tired of naming, organizing, and dead-code-hunting CSS files
You rely on copy-paste component ecosystems like shadcn/ui or Tailwind UI, which assume Tailwind classes
You are on v4-era tooling (Vite, PostCSS, or the standalone CLI) and can adopt the CSS-first @theme configuration
skipIf: Your markup is generated by a CMS or a third party you do not control; Tailwind can only style class attributes you can edit
Long class strings in markup bother your team more than separate stylesheets do; that tradeoff is permanent, not a learning-curve phase
You have a large stable v3 codebase: v4 replaced tailwind.config.js with CSS config, and plenty of plugins, tutorials, and answers online still assume v3 syntax
You are styling HTML email, where most clients need inlined CSS rather than a utility build step
guide.setupReality: Fresh v4 setup on Vite is genuinely short: install tailwindcss and @tailwindcss/vite, add the plugin, and put a single @import "tailwindcss" line in your CSS. The real cost is migration and stale knowledge: the PostCSS plugin moved to a separate @tailwindcss/postcss package, tailwind.config.js gave way to @theme blocks in CSS, and a large share of tutorials still show v3. The scanner also only sees class names that appear literally in source, so dynamically concatenated class strings silently produce no CSS, which surprises every team exactly once.

alternatives.name: unocss
alternatives.when: Same utility-first idea with an on-demand engine and fully custom rule presets

alternatives.name: bootstrap
alternatives.when: Prebuilt components with no build-step scanning, when you want standard-looking pages up fast

alternatives.name: open-props
alternatives.when: Plain CSS custom properties when you want design tokens without utility classes

guide.verdict: Still the default answer for styling new web projects, with an ecosystem no competitor matches. Pick it for new work; think twice before migrating a large, stable v3 codebase until you have a concrete reason.

apiStability.why: v4 was a breaking rewrite of configuration, but utility names stay stable within a major and v3 is kept alive on a v3-lts dist-tag (currently 3.4.19).

docsQuality.why: tailwindcss.com documents every utility with live examples and fast search; the repo README just points there. The docs effectively double as a CSS reference for the whole ecosystem.

maintenance.why: Built by Tailwind Labs, a funded company; the repo shows near-daily pushes (last push 2026-08-04) and releases across both the v4 line and the v3 LTS line.

ecosystem.why: First-party Vite/PostCSS plugins and an official editor extension, plus a huge component layer (shadcn/ui, Tailwind UI, daisyUI) and 118M weekly downloads.

patterns.title: Install with Vite (v4)
patterns.note: v4 has no init command and no tailwind.config.js by default; the CSS import is the whole entry point.

patterns.title: Install with PostCSS
patterns.note: In v4 the PostCSS plugin lives in @tailwindcss/postcss, not in the tailwindcss package; old v3 configs break here first.

patterns.title: Define design tokens in CSS
patterns.note: @theme replaces the theme section of the old tailwind.config.js; tokens also become plain CSS variables you can read anywhere.

patterns.title: Class-toggled dark mode
patterns.note: By default dark: follows prefers-color-scheme; you need @custom-variant to switch it to a class toggle.

patterns.title: Add a custom utility
patterns.note: @utility registers the class with the engine, so variants like hover: and lg: work; a plain CSS class would not get them.

patterns.title: One-off arbitrary values
patterns.snippet: ...
patterns.note: Fine for one-offs, but if the same bracket value keeps repeating, promote it to a @theme token.

patterns.title: Scan extra source paths
patterns.note: v4 auto-detects your project files but ignores node_modules unless you add a path with @source explicitly.

patterns.title: Conditional classes that survive the scanner
patterns.note: The scanner matches literal strings in source files; any runtime string building produces class names with no CSS behind them.

patterns.title: Reuse styles with @apply
patterns.note: Using @apply from a separate CSS file may need @reference at the top so it can see your theme; overusing it also recreates the naming problem Tailwind exists to remove.

patterns.title: Upgrade a v3 project
patterns.snippet: npx @tailwindcss/upgrade
patterns.note: The codemod handles most of the config-to-CSS migration; run it on a clean git branch and review the diff, plugin-heavy configs need manual work.

guide.whatIs: TanStack Query's React bindings manage server state: the data you fetch over the network but do not own. useQuery gives you caching, request deduplication, background refetching, and staleness tracking keyed by a query key; useMutation handles writes plus cache invalidation. It replaces hand-rolled useEffect fetching and most of the store code teams wrote just to hold API responses. It is protocol agnostic, so it works with REST, GraphQL, or anything that returns a promise.
useIf: Multiple components fetch the same data and you keep rebuilding loading, error, and refetch logic by hand
You need caching, deduplication, and background refetch without adopting an entire data framework
You talk to REST or any promise-returning API and do not want to be pushed toward GraphQL
You want pagination, infinite scroll, and optimistic updates as documented patterns instead of bespoke code
skipIf: Your problem is client state (forms, UI flags, wizards): this is a server cache, not a Zustand or Redux replacement
Your framework already owns data fetching, like Next.js server components or Remix loaders: a second client cache means two sources of truth to keep honest
Your app makes a handful of fetches on one page: query keys, staleTime, and gcTime are real learning overhead for something a small fetch hook covers
You need normalized caching where different queries share the same cached entities: Apollo Client's normalized store fits GraphQL data better
guide.setupReality: Install is easy: one package with a single react peer dependency, wrap the app in QueryClientProvider, done. The cost shows up later. The default staleTime of 0 refetches on every window focus, so you tune defaults early or watch the network tab churn. You need a query key convention the whole team actually follows. SSR requires prefetch plus dehydrate plus HydrationBoundary wiring per route. And the v4 to v5 migration renamed a lot (cacheTime to gcTime, status loading to pending, object-only signatures), so pre-2024 blog posts and old Stack Overflow answers actively mislead.

alternatives.name: swr
alternatives.when: You want the same stale-while-revalidate idea with a smaller API surface and you are already in the Vercel ecosystem.

alternatives.name: @apollo/client
alternatives.when: You are all-in on GraphQL and want a normalized cache where entities are shared across queries.

alternatives.name: @reduxjs/toolkit
alternatives.when: You already run Redux and want data fetching (RTK Query) inside the store you have instead of a second cache.

guide.verdict: If a React app talks to an API without a framework-owned data layer, this is the default choice and deserves to be. Budget real time for query key discipline, and do not bolt it onto a framework that already caches for you.

apiStability.why: v5 has been the current major since late 2023 and minors ship weekly without breakage; the v4 to v5 jump was a genuine rename-everything migration though.

docsQuality.why: tanstack.com/query has guides, full API reference, framework-specific docs, and an official v5 migration guide; examples exist for nearly every pattern.

maintenance.why: Pushed the day before this review, 50k stars, active core team plus paid partners; 209 open issues and PRs is modest for its usage.

ecosystem.why: Official devtools, a shared query-core powering React, Vue, Solid, Svelte, and Angular adapters, and years of community answers for every edge case.

patterns.title: Fetch and cache data with useQuery
patterns.note: v5 only accepts the object form, and v4's isLoading is now isPending; fetch does not reject on 404/500, so throw on !res.ok yourself.

patterns.title: Create the client with sane defaults
patterns.note: The default staleTime is 0, meaning a refetch on every mount and window focus; set a real value unless you want that.

patterns.title: Write data, then invalidate the cache
patterns.note: invalidateQueries marks matching queries stale and refetches the active ones; it matches key prefixes, so ['todos'] also hits ['todos', 5].

patterns.title: Run a query only when its input exists
patterns.note: A disabled query reports status pending with fetchStatus idle, so do not treat isPending alone as a spinner signal.

patterns.title: Load pages with useInfiniteQuery
patterns.note: initialPageParam is required in v5; returning undefined (not null) from getNextPageParam is what sets hasNextPage to false.

patterns.title: Keep old data visible while a new page loads
patterns.note: The v4 keepPreviousData boolean option is gone in v5; import the keepPreviousData function and pass it to placeholderData.

patterns.title: Update the UI before the server confirms
patterns.note: cancelQueries matters: without it an in-flight refetch can land after your setQueryData and overwrite the optimistic value.

patterns.title: Prefetch on the server and hydrate on the client
patterns.note: Create a fresh QueryClient per request on the server or you leak data between users; v4's Hydrate component is now HydrationBoundary.

patterns.title: Define a query once with queryOptions
patterns.note: queryOptions keeps key, fetcher, and types in one place, so useQuery, prefetchQuery, and getQueryData stop drifting apart.

patterns.title: Use Suspense instead of isPending checks
patterns.note: data is never undefined here, but you must provide both a Suspense boundary and an error boundary or failures bubble to the root.

patterns.title: Refetch on an interval
patterns.note: Returning false from the refetchInterval function stops polling; by default polling pauses when the tab is backgrounded unless refetchIntervalInBackground is set.

guide.whatIs: TensorFlow is Google's end-to-end machine learning framework: tensors and autodiff at the bottom, the Keras API for building and training models on top, and a deployment story (SavedModel, TensorFlow Serving, TFLite/LiteRT for mobile, TF.js for browsers) that is still its strongest card. You define models in Python, train on CPU/GPU/TPU, and export artifacts that run in production far from Python.
useIf: You need the deployment pipeline more than the research flexibility: SavedModel plus TF Serving, or on-device inference via the LiteRT/TFLite toolchain, is mature and battle-tested
You work in the Google ecosystem: TPUs, Vertex AI, or an org already standardized on TFX pipelines
You want the high-level Keras workflow (compile, fit, callbacks) where standard supervised training is a few dozen lines
You maintain existing TensorFlow models; the 2.x API is stable and 2.21 keeps shipping regular releases
skipIf: You are doing research or following current papers: the research community has largely moved to PyTorch and JAX, so new architectures, reference implementations, and tutorials appear there first and TF ports lag or never arrive
You care about install weight: the Linux x86_64 wheel for 2.21.0 is about 572 MB before dependencies, and the CUDA extras multiply that; tensorflow-cpu exists but is still heavy
You want current native Windows GPU training: the pip GPU path is aimed at Linux, and Windows GPU work generally means WSL2 or the DirectML plugin rather than a plain pip install
You just want to run or fine-tune LLMs: the modern tooling for that (HF transformers ecosystem, vLLM, llama.cpp) is overwhelmingly PyTorch-first
You are learning ML from scratch in 2026: unless your target job or codebase is TF, starting with PyTorch gives you more transferable material
guide.setupReality: pip install tensorflow works cleanly on CPU. GPU is where the pain lives: you need a CUDA-enabled card and matching CUDA/cuDNN stack, and the version compatibility matrix between TF release, CUDA, cuDNN, and your driver is unforgiving; pip's cuda extra helps on Linux but Windows users are pushed toward WSL2 and macOS users toward the separate tensorflow-metal plugin. Expect a multi-hundred-megabyte download, a slow first import, and a wall of log noise on startup. Also note the ABI surface: numpy and protobuf version conflicts with the rest of your environment are a recurring theme, so use a dedicated virtualenv.

alternatives.name: torch
alternatives.when: Default choice for research, LLM work, and most new deep learning projects; largest community momentum

alternatives.name: jax
alternatives.when: You want composable function transforms (grad, jit, vmap) and best-in-class TPU performance

alternatives.name: keras
alternatives.when: Keras 3 standalone runs the same model code on TensorFlow, PyTorch, or JAX backends, decoupling you from this choice

alternatives.name: onnxruntime
alternatives.when: You only need fast inference on an exported model, not a training framework

guide.verdict: Still a serious, actively developed framework with the best production and on-device story, and the right call inside Google-stack shops or existing TF codebases. For new projects without those constraints, the gravity of the field is with PyTorch and JAX, and pretending otherwise wastes your time.

apiStability.why: TF promises backward compatibility for stable Python APIs within 2.x and has held to it since 2019; the residual churn comes from the Keras 3 switch in 2.16, which changed saving formats and broke some tf.keras-era code.

docsQuality.why: tensorflow.org has extensive API references, tutorials, and install guides, but the sheer volume of outdated 1.x and pre-Keras-3 material in search results and the ecosystem makes finding the currently correct way harder than it should be.

maintenance.why: Google ships regular minor releases (2.21.0 current), pushes daily, and runs security programs including fuzzing; the 3000+ open issue and PR count and slower response on non-Google priorities reflect its scale, and heavy investment visibly flows to JAX as well.

ecosystem.why: Massive installed base, TFX, TF Serving, LiteRT, TF.js, tensorflow_hub, and 196k GitHub stars; but the research-and-LLM ecosystem now standardizes on PyTorch, so newest models and libraries frequently skip TF.

patterns.title: Build and train a classifier with Keras
patterns.snippet:
import tensorflow as tf

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(128, activation='relu'),
    tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.2),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(10),
])
model.compile(
    optimizer='adam',
    loss=tf.keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True),
    metrics=['accuracy'],
)
model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=5, validation_split=0.1)
patterns.note: from_logits=True with no final softmax is numerically safer; adding softmax AND from_logits=True is a classic silent accuracy killer.

patterns.title: Feed training with tf.data
patterns.snippet:
ds = (
    tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((features, labels))
    .shuffle(10_000)
    .batch(32)
    .prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)
)
model.fit(ds, epochs=5)
patterns.note: Order matters: shuffle before batch, prefetch last; forgetting prefetch often leaves the GPU idle waiting on input.

patterns.title: Save and reload a model
patterns.snippet:
model.save('model.keras')            # Keras v3 format
reloaded = tf.keras.models.load_model('model.keras')

# for TF Serving, export a SavedModel instead
model.export('serving/1')
patterns.note: Since Keras 3 (TF 2.16+), .keras is the native format and model.export() produces the SavedModel for serving; old H5 files still load but are legacy.

patterns.title: Custom training step with GradientTape
patterns.snippet:
optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3)

@tf.function
def train_step(x, y):
    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
        logits = model(x, training=True)
        loss = loss_fn(y, logits)
    grads = tape.gradient(loss, model.trainable_variables)
    optimizer.apply_gradients(zip(grads, model.trainable_variables))
    return loss
patterns.note: Everything you differentiate must happen inside the tape context; pass training=True yourself, nothing does it for you here.

patterns.title: Verify GPU visibility and limit memory grab
patterns.snippet:
gpus = tf.config.list_physical_devices('GPU')
print(gpus)
for gpu in gpus:
    tf.config.experimental.set_memory_growth(gpu, True)
patterns.note: By default TF reserves nearly all GPU memory at startup; memory growth must be set before any op touches the GPU.

patterns.title: Load an image dataset from folders
patterns.snippet:
train_ds = tf.keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory(
    'data/train',
    image_size=(180, 180),
    batch_size=32,
    validation_split=0.2,
    subset='training',
    seed=42,
)
patterns.note: Class labels come from folder names in alphabetical order; use the same seed and validation_split for the 'validation' subset call or the splits overlap.

patterns.title: Stop early and keep the best weights
patterns.note: Without restore_best_weights=True you end training holding the last (worse) weights, not the best ones.

patterns.title: Fine-tune a pretrained backbone
patterns.snippet:
base = tf.keras.applications.EfficientNetV2B0(
    include_top=False, weights='imagenet', pooling='avg'
)
base.trainable = False  # phase 1: train the head only

inputs = tf.keras.Input(shape=(224, 224, 3))
x = base(inputs, training=False)
outputs = tf.keras.layers.Dense(num_classes)(x)
model = tf.keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
patterns.note: Call the frozen base with training=False so BatchNorm stays in inference mode; skipping that quietly wrecks fine-tuning.

patterns.title: Compile a hot function to a graph
patterns.note: Every new Python-side argument shape or dtype triggers a retrace; pass tensors, not Python scalars, or performance craters.

patterns.title: Convert a model for on-device inference
patterns.snippet:
converter = tf.lite.TFLiteConverter.from_keras_model(model)
converter.optimizations = [tf.lite.Optimize.DEFAULT]
tflite_model = converter.convert()
open('model.tflite', 'wb').write(tflite_model)
patterns.note: Optimize.DEFAULT enables quantization that shrinks the file but can shift accuracy; validate the converted model before shipping.

patterns.title: Train faster with mixed precision
patterns.snippet:
tf.keras.mixed_precision.set_global_policy('mixed_float16')

model = build_model()
# keep the final layer in float32 for numeric stability
outputs = tf.keras.layers.Activation('linear', dtype='float32')(x)
patterns.note: Set the policy before building the model, and force the output layer to float32 or the loss can go NaN.

patterns.title: Make runs repeatable
patterns.snippet:
import tensorflow as tf

tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(42)   # python, numpy, tf seeds
tf.config.experimental.enable_op_determinism()
patterns.note: Op determinism slows training and a few ops will raise errors because they have no deterministic implementation.

guide.whatIs: React Testing Library renders your React components into a DOM (usually jsdom) and gives you queries that find elements the way a user would: by role, label, or visible text. The whole point is testing behavior instead of implementation details, so refactors that do not change what the user sees do not break tests. It is the de facto standard for React component tests and what the React docs themselves point to.
useIf: You write unit or integration tests for React components in Jest or Vitest and want tests that survive refactors
You want accessibility pressure built into testing: getByRole fails when your markup has no proper roles or labels, which catches real a11y problems
You test user flows inside a component tree (fill form, click submit, assert the result) without paying for a real browser
You are on React 18 or 19; v16 supports both and tracks new React versions quickly
skipIf: You need to test real browser behavior: jsdom has no layout engine, so anything involving CSS, element sizes, scrolling, drag-and-drop, or media will silently not work; use Playwright or Cypress component tests instead
You want to assert on state, instance methods, or shallow-render one level deep, enzyme-style; RTL deliberately refuses to expose any of that and fighting the philosophy is miserable
Your components are mostly thin wrappers over heavy visual libraries (canvas, WebGL, charts); there is nothing meaningful for DOM queries to find
You have not budgeted time for the async model: act() warnings, findBy vs getBy, and waitFor misuse are the top source of flaky React tests for teams new to it
guide.setupReality: Since v16 you install @testing-library/react plus @testing-library/dom yourself as a peer dependency, and @types/react / @types/react-dom on TypeScript projects; forgetting the dom package is the classic post-upgrade error. You still need a test runner with a jsdom environment (jest-environment-jsdom or Vitest with environment: 'jsdom'), @testing-library/jest-dom for readable matchers, and usually a custom render wrapper for your providers. None of it is hard, all of it is fiddly, and every project rebuilds the same setup file.

alternatives.name: @playwright/test
alternatives.when: You want component or end-to-end tests in a real browser instead of jsdom

alternatives.name: cypress
alternatives.when: Your team prefers an interactive browser test runner with time-travel debugging

alternatives.name: enzyme
alternatives.when: Only for maintaining legacy test suites; it is unmaintained and has no official adapter beyond React 16

guide.verdict: If you test React components in a Node test runner, this is the correct default and the alternatives are worse. Just accept the philosophy: if you find yourself reaching for internals, you either restructure the test or move that case to a real browser.

apiStability.why: The query API has been stable for years; major bumps mostly track React itself. v16 did break setups by making @testing-library/dom a peer dependency you install yourself.

docsQuality.why: testing-library.com is excellent: query priority guide, common mistakes article, framework-specific examples, and an active FAQ. The 'which query do I use' page answers the question everyone has.

maintenance.why: Actively maintained under the testing-library org with prompt React 19 support and 82 open issues and PRs; releases are steady though the surface is intentionally small and slow-moving.

ecosystem.why: 51M weekly downloads, the whole @testing-library family (user-event, jest-dom, hooks patterns), first-class docs in Jest, Vitest, and the React docs, and every CI template assumes it.

patterns.title: Render a component and assert on output
patterns.note: Prefer screen over destructuring render's return; toBeInTheDocument needs @testing-library/jest-dom registered in setup.

patterns.title: Click and type like a real user
patterns.note: Use userEvent.setup() and await every call; fireEvent skips real event sequences (focus, keydown, pointer) and hides bugs.

patterns.title: Wait for content that appears after a fetch
patterns.note: findBy = getBy + waitFor with a 1000ms default timeout; using getBy for async content is the number one cause of 'works locally, fails in CI'.

patterns.title: Assert an element is NOT there
patterns.note: getBy throws when nothing matches, so absence checks must use queryBy.

patterns.title: Wrap renders with app providers
patterns.note: Create a fresh QueryClient (or store) per test, or state leaks between tests in ways that only fail when run together.

patterns.title: Pick the right query
patterns.note: If getByRole cannot find your element, the markup is usually the bug: a div with onClick has no role.

patterns.title: Test a prop change on the same instance
patterns.note: rerender keeps component state; a second render() call would mount a fresh tree instead.

patterns.title: Test a custom hook directly
patterns.note: renderHook moved into @testing-library/react in v13; the separate react-hooks package is dead, do not install it.

patterns.title: Wait for an assertion to pass
patterns.note: Keep exactly one assertion inside waitFor and never put side effects (clicks, renders) in the callback; it retries the whole block.

patterns.title: See what actually rendered
patterns.snippet:
render(<App />);
screen.debug();                 // prints the DOM
screen.debug(undefined, 30000); // raise the truncation limit
logRoles(container);            // prints every ARIA role present
patterns.note: When getByRole fails, logRoles shows you the roles that exist; the error message also suggests close matches.

patterns.title: Query inside one section of the page
patterns.note: within() is the clean fix when getByRole matches multiple elements across the page.

guide.whatIs: three.js is the dominant JavaScript 3D library. It wraps WebGL and WebGPU in a scene graph of cameras, meshes, materials, and lights so you can build 3D in the browser without writing shader plumbing by hand. The npm build ships the WebGL and WebGPU renderers; SVG and CSS3D renderers, model loaders, and camera controls live in the addons folder. It powers most 3D on the web, from product configurators to browser games to data visualization.
useIf: You are building interactive 3D in the browser: product viewers, configurators, games, or visualizations
You want one ecosystem with maintained loaders (GLTF, DRACO), controls, and hundreds of official live examples
You need WebGPU rendering today with WebGL still available behind a similar API
You work in React and can pair it with @react-three/fiber and its ecosystem
skipIf: You need a stable API across upgrades. three uses 0.x versioning and ships breaking changes in its roughly monthly releases; the wiki maintains a permanent migration guide because you will need it
Your project is 2D. You would carry a 178 KB gzipped core for a scene graph you do not need; pixi.js is the better fit
You expect an engine rather than a library: there is no built-in physics, no editor-driven asset pipeline, and no game framework conventions
Your team has no 3D math background and the deadline is short; cameras, matrices, and lighting have a real learning curve that no library removes
guide.setupReality: npm install three is the easy part. Anything beyond a spinning cube (OrbitControls, GLTFLoader, post-processing) is imported from three/addons, which requires a bundler that understands package exports or a hand-written import map. Releases land about monthly under 0.x versioning, so pin your version and read the wiki migration guide before every upgrade. TypeScript types come from the separate @types/three package. And plan to learn manual disposal of geometries, materials, and textures, or long-lived apps will leak GPU memory.

alternatives.name: @babylonjs/core
alternatives.when: When you want a batteries-included engine with physics integration and an inspector

alternatives.name: pixi.js
alternatives.when: When your project is 2D and you do not need a 3D scene graph

alternatives.name: @react-three/fiber
alternatives.when: When you are in React and want to declare three scenes as components (it still uses three underneath)

guide.verdict: The default 3D library on the web for good reason: unmatched examples, ecosystem, and momentum, now including WebGPU. Budget real time for the learning curve and for keeping up with monthly breaking releases.

apiStability.why: 0.x versioning with deliberate breaking changes in regular monthly releases; the project keeps a permanent migration guide in its wiki.

docsQuality.why: Full API docs, a long-form manual, and hundreds of live examples at threejs.org; knowing whether an answer lives in docs, manual, examples, or forum takes practice.

maintenance.why: Pushed the day of this review, 114k stars, and a monthly release cadence sustained for over a decade.

ecosystem.why: About 13.7M weekly downloads plus a satellite ecosystem (react-three-fiber, drei, threlte, loaders, editors) larger than most competing libraries entirely.

patterns.title: Render a spinning cube
patterns.note: Use renderer.setAnimationLoop instead of requestAnimationFrame; it is required for WebXR and handles the loop for you.

patterns.title: Load a glTF model
patterns.note: Loaders live in three/addons, not the core package; glTF is the format the project recommends for the web.

patterns.title: Add orbit camera controls
patterns.note: With enableDamping you must call controls.update() every frame or the camera freezes.

patterns.title: Keep the canvas correct on window resize
patterns.note: Forgetting camera.updateProjectionMatrix() is the classic bug: the canvas resizes but the image stays stretched.

patterns.title: Pick the object under the mouse with a raycaster
patterns.note: Pointer coordinates must be normalized to -1..1 with Y flipped; raw pixel coordinates silently pick nothing.

patterns.title: Add lights and enable shadows
patterns.note: Shadows are opt-in three times over: on the renderer, on each light, and on each mesh. Miss one and nothing renders wrong, it just casts no shadow.

patterns.title: Load a texture and put it on a material
patterns.note: Set colorSpace = SRGBColorSpace on color textures or everything looks washed out under the default color management.

patterns.title: Draw thousands of copies with InstancedMesh
patterns.note: One InstancedMesh is one draw call; ten thousand separate Meshes will bury your frame rate in overhead.

patterns.title: Play animations baked into a glTF file
patterns.note: Nothing moves unless you call mixer.update(delta) every frame with real elapsed time from a Clock.

patterns.title: Free GPU memory when removing objects
patterns.note: scene.remove() alone does not free GPU memory; geometries, materials, and textures each need an explicit dispose() call.

guide.whatIs: PyTorch is the dominant deep learning framework for Python: a tensor library with NumPy-like operations that run on GPUs, tape-based automatic differentiation, the torch.nn module system for building networks, and utilities for data loading and distributed training. Models are ordinary imperative Python, so debugging stays normal (print, pdb, readable stack traces), and torch.compile JIT-compiles that same code when you want speed. It is the substrate most modern ML work runs on, including nearly everything on Hugging Face.
useIf: You are training or fine-tuning neural networks: it is the research and industry default, and most papers and pretrained checkpoints assume it
You need GPU-accelerated tensor math with autograd on NVIDIA (CUDA), AMD (ROCm), Intel GPUs, or Apple silicon (MPS)
You build on the Hugging Face, torchvision, or Lightning ecosystem, which all target PyTorch first
You want model code you can step through imperatively instead of a static graph you cannot inspect
skipIf: You are doing classical ML (trees, regressions, clustering) on tabular data: scikit-learn is lighter and the right tool, and PyTorch adds nothing there
Install size matters: default Linux wheels bundle CUDA libraries and pull in gigabytes, which is a lot for a small inference service that onnxruntime could serve
You only need to call a hosted model API: no local deep learning framework is required at all
You deploy to constrained mobile or edge targets: the full framework is heavy and the mobile path (ExecuTorch) is a separate toolchain to learn
guide.setupReality: pip install torch works, but which build you get matters: the default Linux wheel bundles CUDA libraries and weighs gigabytes, while CPU-only or specific CUDA/ROCm builds come from PyTorch's own index URL that the selector on pytorch.org generates for you. Python 3.10+ is required. GPU use adds driver and CUDA version matching, and Apple silicon runs through the MPS backend where a few ops still fall back to CPU. Building from source is a real project (CMake, MKL, optional magma and triton) that almost nobody needs to attempt.

alternatives.name: jax
alternatives.when: Functional composable transforms (jit, grad, vmap) and TPU-first research code

alternatives.name: tensorflow
alternatives.when: Production pipelines already standardized on TF, Keras, and TFX

alternatives.name: scikit-learn
alternatives.when: Classical ML on tabular data where deep learning is overkill

guide.verdict: If you are doing deep learning in Python this is the default, and fighting the default is rarely worth it. Just do not reach for it when scikit-learn or a hosted API already solves your problem.

apiStability.why: The 2.x line has kept the core tensor/nn/optim API steady since 2023; compiler-adjacent surfaces (torch.compile, export) still move faster and each minor release carries deprecations like the torch.cuda.amp to torch.amp rename

docsQuality.why: pytorch.org docs and tutorials are extensive and the official forum is active; the surface area is so large that finding the current best practice for compile, AMP, or distributed takes real digging

maintenance.why: Linux Foundation project with Meta and broad industry backing, commits landing around the clock and a regular release train (2.13.0 current); 18k+ open issues and PRs reflects project scale, not neglect

ecosystem.why: The center of the Python ML world: Hugging Face, torchvision/torchaudio, Lightning, and vLLM all target PyTorch first, and 22M weekly PyPI downloads undercount conda and custom-index installs

patterns.title: Create tensors
patterns.snippet:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]])
z = torch.zeros(3, 4)
r = torch.randn(2, 3)
patterns.note: torch.tensor copies data and infers dtype; use torch.from_numpy to share memory with an existing NumPy array.

patterns.title: Pick the best available device
patterns.snippet:
device = (
    'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available()
    else 'mps' if torch.backends.mps.is_available()
    else 'cpu'
)
model = model.to(device)
batch = batch.to(device)
patterns.note: Every tensor in an op must live on the same device; the 'expected all tensors to be on the same device' error is almost always a missing .to(device).

patterns.title: Define a model with nn.Module
patterns.note: Invoke the model as model(x), not model.forward(x); the call path runs hooks that a bare forward() skips.

patterns.title: Write a training loop
patterns.snippet:
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

model.train()
for xb, yb in loader:
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
patterns.note: Forgetting opt.zero_grad() silently accumulates gradients across steps; it is the classic PyTorch bug.

patterns.title: Load batches with Dataset and DataLoader
patterns.note: num_workers > 0 spawns worker processes; on Windows and macOS guard the entry point with if __name__ == '__main__' or spawning recurses.

patterns.title: Save and load model weights
patterns.snippet:
torch.save(model.state_dict(), 'model.pt')

model = Net()
model.load_state_dict(
    torch.load('model.pt', map_location='cpu')
)
model.eval()
patterns.note: Save the state_dict, not the whole model object; whole-model pickles break when your class or file layout changes.

patterns.title: Run inference correctly
patterns.snippet:
model.eval()
with torch.inference_mode():
    preds = model(batch)
patterns.note: model.eval() switches dropout and batchnorm behavior while inference_mode disables autograd; correct inference needs both.

patterns.title: Speed up a model with torch.compile
patterns.snippet:
model = torch.compile(model)
out = model(x)  # first call triggers compilation
patterns.note: The first call per input shape is slow while kernels compile; heavy Python dynamism in forward() can silently fall back to eager.

patterns.title: Train with automatic mixed precision
patterns.snippet:
scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler('cuda')

for xb, yb in loader:
    opt.zero_grad()
    with torch.amp.autocast('cuda'):
        loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()
    scaler.step(opt)
    scaler.update()
patterns.note: Use the torch.amp namespace; the old torch.cuda.amp spelling is deprecated. GradScaler is for fp16 and unnecessary in bf16 training.

patterns.title: Freeze a backbone for fine-tuning
patterns.note: Setting requires_grad False skips those gradients; also filtering them out of the optimizer avoids wasted optimizer state memory.

patterns.title: Accumulate gradients for a bigger effective batch
patterns.snippet:
accum = 4
opt.zero_grad()
for i, (xb, yb) in enumerate(loader):
    loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb) / accum
    loss.backward()
    if (i + 1) % accum == 0:
        opt.step()
        opt.zero_grad()
patterns.note: Divide the loss by the accumulation steps or your effective learning rate quietly multiplies by that factor.

guide.whatIs: Hugging Face's model-definition library: the standard way to download, run, and fine-tune pretrained models for text, vision, audio, video, and multimodal tasks in PyTorch. Over one million checkpoints on the Hugging Face Hub load through its Auto classes and pipeline() API, and its model definitions are the common format that vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, Axolotl, and most of the training and inference ecosystem build against. v5 targets Python 3.10+ and PyTorch 2.5+.
useIf: You want to run or fine-tune open-weights models from the Hugging Face Hub in a few lines of Python
You need one API (pipeline, AutoModel, AutoTokenizer) that spans text, vision, audio, and multimodal tasks
You are fine-tuning: Trainer plus the surrounding stack (PEFT, TRL, Accelerate) is the standard tooling
You need the reference model definition that inference engines and export formats are built from
skipIf: You are serving LLMs in production: plain transformers generation is far slower than dedicated engines like vLLM; prototype here, serve there
You only need text embeddings: sentence-transformers wraps this with a simpler purpose-built API
You run on CPU or edge hardware: GGUF models via llama.cpp bindings are lighter and faster there
You want a small dependency: the install plus PyTorch runs to gigabytes before you download a single model
Your codebase is pinned to TensorFlow or JAX: v5 targets PyTorch, so you would be stuck maintaining aging 4.x pins
guide.setupReality: pip install "transformers[torch]" in a fresh venv; the heavy lift is PyTorch itself, whose CUDA wheels are multi-gigabyte and must match your driver stack. First use of any model downloads weights into ~/.cache/huggingface, which fills disks fast, and gated models like Llama need a Hub token plus an accepted license before from_pretrained stops throwing 401s. GPU out-of-memory errors are the standard rite of passage: expect to reach for dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto", and quantization before larger models fit.

alternatives.name: vllm
alternatives.when: Production LLM serving where throughput and batching matter

alternatives.name: sentence-transformers
alternatives.when: You only need embeddings for search or similarity

alternatives.name: llama-cpp-python
alternatives.when: CPU or edge inference on quantized GGUF models

guide.verdict: The center of gravity for open-source ML; nothing else matches its Hub integration and task breadth. Use it to load, experiment, and fine-tune, then hand heavy production serving to a dedicated engine.

apiStability.why: The core surface (pipeline, Auto classes, from_pretrained) has survived every major; v5 removed long-deprecated paths and per-model kwargs still shift between releases

docsQuality.why: Extensive official docs with task guides, API reference, and free courses; at this breadth quality varies by page and older examples drift out of date

maintenance.why: One of the most active repos on GitHub: 163k stars, pushes within the hour, frequent releases, backed by Hugging Face; 2.3k open issues and PRs is the cost of that scale

ecosystem.why: Over 1M compatible checkpoints on the Hub; PEFT, TRL, Accelerate, vLLM, and most training frameworks consume its model definitions directly

patterns.title: Generate text with a pipeline
patterns.snippet:
from transformers import pipeline

generator = pipeline(task="text-generation", model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B")
print(generator("the secret to baking a really good cake is "))
patterns.note: The model downloads and caches on first use; pin an explicit model name because task-only defaults can change between versions.

patterns.title: Chat with an instruct model
patterns.snippet:
import torch
from transformers import pipeline

chat = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise assistant."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Fun things to do in New York?"},
]

pipe = pipeline(task="text-generation", model="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct",
                dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto")
out = pipe(chat, max_new_tokens=512)
print(out[0]["generated_text"][-1]["content"])
patterns.note: Passing a list of role/content dicts applies the model's chat template automatically; Llama models are gated and need a logged-in Hub token.

patterns.title: Load a model and tokenizer directly
patterns.snippet:
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto")

inputs = tokenizer("Explain ASGI in one line.", return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=60)
print(tokenizer.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True))
patterns.note: In v5 the argument is dtype=, replacing the older torch_dtype= you will see in pre-v5 tutorials.

patterns.title: Apply a chat template manually
patterns.snippet:
messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Write a haiku about compilers."},
]
inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages, add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt"
).to(model.device)
out = model.generate(inputs, max_new_tokens=60)
patterns.note: Skipping the chat template on an instruct model is the top cause of garbage output; never hand-format the prompt string yourself.

patterns.title: Fit a large model on limited GPU memory
patterns.snippet:
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3",
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device_map="auto",
)
patterns.note: device_map="auto" (via accelerate) shards layers across GPUs and CPU; anything offloaded to CPU runs much slower, so watch the printed device map.

patterns.title: Load a model in 4-bit to halve memory again
patterns.snippet:
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig

bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3",
    quantization_config=bnb,
    device_map="auto",
)
patterns.note: Requires the separate bitsandbytes package and a CUDA GPU; quantized weights cannot be trained directly, only used with adapters like LoRA.

patterns.title: Transcribe audio with Whisper
patterns.snippet:
from transformers import pipeline

asr = pipeline(task="automatic-speech-recognition", model="openai/whisper-large-v3")
print(asr("meeting.flac")["text"])
patterns.note: Audio decoding needs ffmpeg installed on the system; for files over 30 seconds pass chunk_length_s to avoid truncation.

patterns.title: Classify an image
patterns.snippet:
from transformers import pipeline

clf = pipeline(task="image-classification",
               model="facebook/dinov2-small-imagenet1k-1-layer")
print(clf("parrots.png"))
patterns.note: Accepts local paths, URLs, or PIL images; install pillow if you are not already depending on it.

patterns.title: Save and reload a model locally
patterns.snippet:
model.save_pretrained("./my-model")
tokenizer.save_pretrained("./my-model")

# later, fully offline:
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("./my-model")
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("./my-model")
patterns.note: Set HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 in air-gapped environments so nothing tries to phone the Hub for version checks.

patterns.title: Chat or serve a model from the command line
patterns.snippet:
# interactive chat in the terminal
transformers chat Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct

# OpenAI-compatible local server
transformers serve
patterns.note: Handy for smoke-testing a checkpoint before writing code; it is not a production serving stack.

guide.whatIs: @trpc/server is the server half of tRPC, which gives you end-to-end typesafe APIs in TypeScript without schemas or code generation. You define procedures (queries, mutations, subscriptions) in a router; the client imports only the router's type and gets compile-time checking and autocomplete on inputs, outputs, and errors. There is no codegen step and no runtime schema on the wire, and the server package itself has zero dependencies.
useIf: Your client and server are both TypeScript in the same repo or monorepo and you own both ends
You are tired of hand-written fetch wrappers and API types drifting out of sync with the backend
You want middleware, auth context, and input validation with types flowing through automatically
You are on Next.js or another full-stack TS setup where the official adapters (Next, Express, Fastify, Fetch) drop in
skipIf: Anyone outside your TypeScript codebase consumes the API (mobile teams, partners, other languages): tRPC has no schema to hand them, so use OpenAPI or GraphQL
Client and server live in separate repos with separate deploys: sharing the AppRouter type across them is clumsy and version skew bites at runtime
You are building a public API: RPC-shaped endpoints coupled to procedure names are fine internally and hostile externally
Your router is huge and your machines are not: TypeScript inference over large routers measurably slows tsserver and editor feedback
guide.setupReality: It is a family of packages, not one install: @trpc/server plus a validator (usually zod) on the back end, @trpc/client and typically the TanStack Query integration on the front end. First-time wiring of the context function, an adapter, and the shared AppRouter type export takes a real afternoon. The v10 to v11 migration renamed client entry points, so tutorials written before 2024 will steer you into APIs that no longer exist, and editor slowness on big routers is a known, documented cost you design around by splitting routers.

alternatives.name: @orpc/server
alternatives.when: You want tRPC-style typesafety but with OpenAPI output for non-TS consumers built in.

alternatives.name: @ts-rest/core
alternatives.when: You prefer a contract-first REST approach that still shares types between client and server.

alternatives.name: hono
alternatives.when: You want a plain typed web framework with an RPC client mode and fewer layers than the tRPC stack.

guide.verdict: The best developer experience available for TypeScript-only, same-repo APIs; batching, middleware, and typed errors come along free. The moment a non-TypeScript consumer appears its core advantage evaporates, so choose based on who will call the API.

apiStability.why: v11 is the current line with frequent minor releases (11.18 now) and no breaking churn within the major; the v10 to v11 jump did rename core client APIs, and old content still circulates.

docsQuality.why: trpc.io covers concepts, every adapter, and framework integrations with example apps; versioned docs help, but search results still land on outdated v10 pages often enough to cost time.

maintenance.why: Pushed July 2026 with three named project leads and steady releases; 260 open issues and PRs on a 40k-star project is normal, but the bus factor is thinner than the download count suggests.

ecosystem.why: Official adapters for Next, Express, Fastify, and the Fetch API, a community add-on list, and deep TanStack Query integration; everything stops at the TypeScript border by design.

patterns.title: Create a router with a typed procedure
patterns.note: Export only the type to the client; importing the router value client-side drags server code into your bundle.

patterns.title: Build per-request context from headers
patterns.note: Call initTRPC.context<Context>() before .create(); adding context later means retyping every procedure.

patterns.title: Protect procedures with middleware
patterns.note: Returning next() with a narrowed ctx is what makes ctx.user non-nullable in every procedure downstream; skip it and you null-check forever.

patterns.title: Validate a mutation input with zod
patterns.note: Invalid input rejects with a BAD_REQUEST error before your handler runs; the input type in the handler is inferred from the schema.

patterns.title: Serve the router from a Fetch-based runtime
patterns.note: This one adapter covers Next.js route handlers, Bun, Deno, and edge runtimes; export both GET and POST or batched requests fail.

patterns.title: Mount tRPC inside an Express app
patterns.note: The express adapter gets req and res in createContext instead of a Fetch Request, so context code is adapter-specific.

patterns.title: Call the API from a plain TypeScript client
patterns.note: v11 renamed createTRPCProxyClient to createTRPCClient; httpBatchLink combines parallel calls into a single HTTP request.

patterns.title: Throw typed errors and log them centrally
patterns.note: Plain thrown Errors surface as INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR with the message hidden in production; use TRPCError codes for anything client-facing.

patterns.title: Validate what leaves the server
patterns.note: output() strips or rejects extra fields, which is cheap insurance when handlers return raw database rows with password hashes attached.

patterns.title: Stream events with an async generator subscription
patterns.note: v11 subscriptions run over Server-Sent Events with httpSubscriptionLink on the client, so WebSockets are no longer required for streaming.

guide.whatIs: Typer is a Python library for building command-line apps from type hints, made by the FastAPI author and built on top of Click. You write a normal function with typed parameters and Typer turns it into a CLI with argument parsing, validation, generated --help, error messages and shell completion. It scales from typer.run(main) on a single function up to nested subcommand trees, and it ships a typer command that can run even plain un-decorated Python scripts as CLIs. Output is styled with Rich when it is installed.
useIf: You are building a CLI with options, arguments and subcommands and want parsing, validation and --help generated from type hints instead of written by hand
You already think in FastAPI idioms; Typer uses the same Annotated-based declaration style and the same documentation voice
You want free shell autocompletion for bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell via --install-completion
You want pretty terminal output and error panels without wiring Rich yourself
skipIf: It is a small internal script: argparse is in the standard library and adds zero dependencies, while Typer pulls in click, rich and shellingham
You need rock-solid API stability: Typer is still 0.x and idioms have shifted (the Annotated style replaced the old default-value style), so tutorials and old codebases disagree
You need Click-level control or its plugin ecosystem directly (custom parameter types, complex context passing); dropping down from Typer's abstraction gets awkward
Startup latency matters (shell prompts, completion hooks): importing typer plus rich is noticeably slower than argparse
guide.setupReality: pip install typer gets you the library plus rich and shellingham, and a hello-world CLI is genuinely three lines. The friction: the docs now assume uv and its examples run through the typer command, which confuses people who just want python main.py; shell completion needs a per-shell install step (--install-completion) and only works properly for installed packages, not loose scripts; boolean options auto-generate --flag/--no-flag pairs that surprise first-timers; and because the project is pre-1.0 you will find two option-declaration styles in the wild, the old typer.Option default-value style and the current Annotated style, and mixing them in one signature is an error-prone mess.

alternatives.name: click
alternatives.when: You want the mature, decorator-based foundation Typer is built on, with more control and a huge plugin ecosystem

alternatives.name: cyclopts
alternatives.when: You like the type-hint approach but want stricter typing behavior and some Typer paper cuts fixed

alternatives.name: fire
alternatives.when: Zero-effort CLI over an existing module or class for internal tooling; not for polished user-facing CLIs

guide.verdict: The nicest developer experience for Python CLIs today, especially if you know FastAPI. Accept the 0.x churn and the extra dependencies; for stdlib-only scripts argparse still earns its keep.

apiStability.why: Still 0.x after six years; the move to Annotated-based declarations changed the recommended idiom and older examples no longer match the docs. Changes are managed with deprecation periods, but they happen.

docsQuality.why: typer.tiangolo.com is a full tutorial in the FastAPI style: every feature has a runnable example with the expected terminal output shown inline.

maintenance.why: Active (pushed within a day of this review, regular releases) and now under the fastapi GitHub org with team members, but direction still concentrates on one lead maintainer and the issue backlog is substantial.

ecosystem.why: Sits on Click so its ecosystem mostly applies, testing via CliRunner is built in, and Rich integration is first-class; native Typer-specific plugins are few because Click fills that role.

patterns.title: Smallest possible CLI
patterns.note: typer.run wraps one function as a complete CLI; the moment you need a second command, switch to typer.Typer().

patterns.title: App with multiple commands
patterns.note: Command names come from function names with underscores turned into hyphens; a single @app.command still requires the command name on the CLI unless it is the only one.

patterns.title: Option with help text (current Annotated style)
patterns.snippet:
from typing import Annotated
import typer


def main(
    name: str,
    greeting: Annotated[str, typer.Option(help="Greeting word")] = "Hello",
):
    print(f"{greeting} {name}")
patterns.note: Annotated is the recommended style; the old greeting: str = typer.Option("Hello") form still works but the docs have moved on.

patterns.title: Required and documented positional arguments
patterns.snippet:
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Annotated
import typer


def main(
    src: Annotated[Path, typer.Argument(exists=True, readable=True,
                                        help="Input file")],
):
    print(src.read_text()[:100])
patterns.note: Path parameters get free validation: exists=True makes Typer error out before your function runs.

patterns.title: Boolean flags
patterns.note: A bare bool option auto-creates a --x/--no-x pair; pass explicit flag names to get a plain switch instead.

patterns.title: Prompt for input and passwords
patterns.snippet:
from typing import Annotated
import typer


def main(
    user: Annotated[str, typer.Option(prompt=True)],
    password: Annotated[str, typer.Option(prompt=True, hide_input=True,
                                          confirmation_prompt=True)],
):
    print(f"Logging in {user}")
patterns.note: Prompts only fire when the option is missing from the command line, so scripts can still pass --password (with the usual shell-history caveat).

patterns.title: Nested subcommands (git-style)
patterns.snippet:
import typer

app = typer.Typer()
users_app = typer.Typer()
app.add_typer(users_app, name="users")


@users_app.command("create")
def users_create(name: str):
    print(f"user {name} created")

# CLI: mytool users create ada
patterns.note: Each Typer instance can carry its own callback for group-level options; help text nests correctly for free.

patterns.title: Fail with a proper exit code
patterns.note: raise typer.Exit, do not call sys.exit inside commands; typer.Abort() prints Aborted and exits 1 for cancel flows.

patterns.title: App-level options via callback
patterns.note: Callback options must come before the command on the CLI: mytool --verbose run, not mytool run --verbose.

patterns.title: Progress bar over an iterable
patterns.snippet:
import time
import typer


def main():
    items = range(100)
    with typer.progressbar(items, label="Processing") as progress:
        for _ in progress:
            time.sleep(0.01)
patterns.note: Fine for simple loops; for spinners, multiple bars or fancy rendering use rich.progress directly, it is already installed.

patterns.title: Test a CLI without spawning a process
patterns.snippet:
from typer.testing import CliRunner
from mytool.main import app

runner = CliRunner()


def test_create():
    result = runner.invoke(app, ["create", "ada"])
    assert result.exit_code == 0
    assert "Creating ada" in result.output
patterns.note: CliRunner needs a typer.Typer app object; if you only used typer.run, wrap the function in an app to make it testable.

guide.whatIs: TypeScript is a static type layer on top of JavaScript plus the compiler that checks it. You write .ts files, the tsc compiler verifies the types and emits plain readable JavaScript that runs anywhere JS runs. It is a dev-time tool: types vanish at runtime, so it catches wrong arguments, nulls and typos before you ship, not after. Version 7 is a ground-up native rewrite of the compiler focused on speed; the language itself is unchanged.
useIf: The codebase is touched by more than one person or will live longer than a month; types are the cheapest documentation you will ever write
You consume big third-party APIs (AWS SDK, React, Node) and want autocomplete and compile-time errors instead of runtime surprises
You maintain a public library; shipping .d.ts types is table stakes for adoption in 2026
You are refactoring a large JS codebase and want the compiler to find every call site you broke
skipIf: You are writing a throwaway script or tiny prototype; a build step and tsconfig ceremony slow you down for zero payoff, and JSDoc comments with checkJs get you 80% of the safety with no compiler

Your tooling depends on the TypeScript 5.x compiler API (custom transformers, ts-morph style codegen); the 7.0 native compiler changes that surface and the old repo now only takes a narrow class of fixes, so audit your toolchain before upgrading
Your team will fight the checker with any and as casts everywhere; badly typed TypeScript is worse than honest JavaScript because it lies with confidence
guide.setupReality: npm install -D typescript then npx tsc --init, and the compiler itself just works. The pain is tsconfig: module vs moduleResolution (nodenext vs bundler) confuses everyone, ESM/CJS interop errors are cryptic, and untyped dependencies need @types packages or hand-written declarations. Also note the 6/7 transition: development moved to the typescript-go repo and the original repo only accepts limited fixes, so some ecosystem tools lag behind 7.0.

alternatives.name: esbuild
alternatives.when: You only need TS syntax stripped and bundled fast; it never checks types, so pair it with tsc --noEmit in CI

alternatives.name: @swc/core
alternatives.when: Same idea as esbuild as a Rust-based transpiler, common inside Next.js and Jest setups

alternatives.name: flow-bin
alternatives.when: Almost never for new work; Meta's type checker lost the ecosystem war and mainly matters in legacy Meta-adjacent codebases

guide.verdict: The default for any JavaScript codebase that has to be maintained, and the 260M weekly downloads say the argument is over. Adopt strict mode from day one; the only real caution right now is the 7.0 compiler transition if you rely on compiler-API tooling.

apiStability.why: The language almost never breaks user code, but 7.0 replaces the compiler implementation; anything built on the old compiler API needs migration, and feature work is paused until the transition completes.

docsQuality.why: The handbook, playground and release notes are among the best docs in the ecosystem; nearly every error message has a searchable answer.

maintenance.why: Microsoft-funded, pushed daily, with a public roadmap. Development now happens in the typescript-go repo while this one takes crash and security fixes only.

ecosystem.why: Every major framework ships types, DefinitelyTyped covers the long tail, and editors bundle the language server by default.

patterns.title: Install and create a tsconfig
patterns.snippet:
npm install -D typescript
npx tsc --init
npx tsc --noEmit   # type-check without emitting JS
patterns.note: tsc --init writes a heavily commented tsconfig; keep strict true and delete options you do not understand yet.

patterns.title: A sane tsconfig for modern Node
patterns.note: Use module nodenext when Node runs the output, bundler when Vite/esbuild does; mixing them causes the classic ESM import errors.

patterns.title: Handle a caught error safely
patterns.note: catch variables are unknown under strict mode; narrow before touching properties instead of casting to any.

patterns.title: Model success or failure with a tagged union
patterns.note: Checking the shared literal field narrows the whole object; add a never-typed default case in switches to catch missed variants at compile time.

patterns.title: Write a custom type guard
patterns.note: The compiler trusts your guard blindly; a wrong guard silences the checker, so use a schema validator like zod at real I/O boundaries.

patterns.title: Check a shape without widening the type
patterns.note: Use satisfies instead of a type annotation when you want validation plus the narrowest inferred type.

patterns.title: Derive types instead of duplicating them
patterns.snippet:
type User = { id: string; name: string; email: string }

type UserPatch = Partial<Omit<User, 'id'>>
type PublicUser = Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>
type ById = Record<string, User>
patterns.note: Derived types update automatically when the source type changes; hand-copied interfaces drift.

patterns.title: Constrain a generic to keys of a type
patterns.note: K extends keyof T rejects invalid keys at the call site and infers the exact return type.

patterns.title: Add types for an untyped dependency
patterns.note: Check for an @types/legacy-lib package on DefinitelyTyped first; only hand-write declarations when none exists.

patterns.title: Run TypeScript without a build step
patterns.snippet:
npx tsx src/main.ts
# or with recent Node versions (type stripping):
node src/main.ts
patterns.note: Node's built-in stripping only handles erasable syntax (no enums or namespaces), and neither path checks types; keep tsc --noEmit in CI.

guide.whatIs: Undici is the HTTP/1.1 client the Node.js project wrote from scratch, and it is what powers the fetch() built into Node since v18. Installing it as a module gets you the newest version of that engine plus the low-level APIs the built-in fetch hides: request, stream, pipeline, and dispatch, along with connection pools, pipelining, interceptors for retry and caching, ProxyAgent and Socks5Agent for proxying, and MockAgent for network-free tests. It has zero runtime dependencies and, in the project's own benchmarks, undici.request runs several times faster than node-fetch and clearly ahead of axios and got.
useIf: You need connection pooling control, HTTP/1.1 pipelining, or interceptors (retry, cache, DNS) that Node's built-in fetch does not expose
Service-to-service HTTP performance matters; the project's benchmarks put undici.request at roughly 3.5x node-fetch on the same workload
You need MockAgent to intercept requests in tests without touching the network, or ProxyAgent/Socks5Agent for outbound proxying
You want a newer fetch implementation than the one bundled with your Node runtime (check process.versions.undici to see what you have)
skipIf: Simple GET/POST calls are all you do; Node's built-in fetch is already undici under the hood and needs zero dependencies
Your code must also run in browsers, Deno, or edge runtimes; undici is Node-only, and the portable answer is the standard fetch you already have

You want a batteries-included client; got and ky ship retries, hooks, and pagination as defaults, while undici's request API is deliberately low-level and you assemble those behaviors from interceptors yourself
You are on an older Node LTS: undici 8 requires Node >= 22.19.0, which rules it out for a lot of production fleets still on 20
Your team will mix undici's fetch/FormData with the global ones; the README explicitly warns that mixing implementations breaks request bodies, and it is an easy mistake to make
guide.setupReality: npm i undici is clean: zero runtime dependencies, no build step, no peer deps. The catches are elsewhere. Version 8 requires Node >= 22.19.0, a real cliff if you are on Node 20 or 22 pre-.19. The request API hands you a body stream that you must consume (or call .dump()) even on error paths, otherwise the connection is not released back to the pool and things stall under load. Composing dispatchers (Agent, compose, interceptors) is its own mental model and the docs assume you will read them. Error shapes also differ between undici.fetch, which wraps failures in TypeError per the spec, and undici.request, which throws undici's own error classes.

alternatives.name: axios
alternatives.when: You want the most widely known API with interceptors and browser support in one package

alternatives.name: got
alternatives.when: You want retries, hooks, and pagination built in for Node scripts and backends
